1.summary: The opening psalm sets two ways side by side: the person who delights in Yahweh's law and flourishes like a watered tree, and the wicked who blow away like chaff.
1.lookfor: Watch the three verbs walk, stand and sit in the first verse, the contrast between the tree and the chaff, and the word "way" that frames the whole poem.

insights.title: The doorway to the Psalter
insights.body: Psalms 1 and 2 have no titles and work together as an introduction to the whole book. Psalm 1 opens with "Blessed" and Psalm 2 ends with the same word (Psalm 2:12), framing the pair. Some ancient manuscripts of Acts even cite Psalm 2 as "the first psalm", and the Talmud treats the two as one.

insights.title: Torah means instruction
insights.body: The word translated "law" (1:2) is torah, which means teaching or instruction, not only rules. The psalm places the person of God's instruction at the head of a book of prayers, suggesting the psalms themselves are to be read as torah. Jewish tradition noticed that the Psalter has five books, like the five books of Moses.

insights.title: Meditating aloud
insights.body: "Meditates" (1:2) translates hagah, a verb for low, audible sound: a lion growling over its prey or a dove moaning. Ancient reading was usually spoken under the breath. To meditate is to murmur the words over and over until they become one's own.

insights.title: Walk, stand, sit
insights.body: The first verse moves from walking in the counsel of the wicked, to standing on the path of sinners, to sitting in the seat of scoffers (1:1). Each step settles a person more firmly into bad company. The blessed person is defined first by what they refuse and then by what they love (1:2).

insights.title: The tree by the water
insights.body: Jeremiah uses almost the same picture of a tree planted by water whose leaf stays green in drought, for the one who trusts in Yahweh. In a dry land a tree that keeps its leaves must have roots that reach a hidden stream. The image is about steady life drawn from a source outside oneself.

insights.title: Chaff on the threshing floor
insights.body: After harvest, grain was threshed on an open, often raised floor and tossed into the wind with a fork. The heavy kernels fell back while the light husks blew away (1:4). John the Baptist uses the same scene to describe judgment.

insights.title: Known by Yahweh
insights.body: "Yahweh knows the way of the righteous" (1:6) uses yada, a verb of close relationship and care rather than simple awareness. The wicked are not said to be destroyed by a blow; their way simply perishes, like a path that runs out in the desert.

insights.title: Whatever he does shall prosper
insights.body: The psalm promises that the righteous person prospers in whatever they do (1:3). Later psalms, such as Psalm 73, wrestle with righteous people who suffer while the wicked thrive. How might this opening promise be read alongside those honest complaints?

2.summary: Nations plot against Yahweh and his anointed king, but Yahweh laughs, announces that he has installed his King on Zion as his son, and warns the rulers of the earth to submit.
2.lookfor: Listen for the different speakers: the rebel kings, Yahweh, the king reporting God's decree, and the final warning to the rulers.

names.name: Zion
names.gloss: The hill of Jerusalem where David's palace and later the temple stood; often a name for Jerusalem itself.

insights.title: A coronation psalm
insights.body: Psalm 2 was probably used when a king of David's line was crowned. In the ancient Near East, subject nations often rebelled when a new king took the throne, hoping to throw off their tribute (2:3). The psalm answers that the king's authority comes from Yahweh himself.

insights.title: Today I have become your father
insights.body: "You are my son. Today I have become your father" (2:7) uses the language of adoption at the moment of enthronement. It echoes God's promise to David that his heir would be like a son to him. Egyptian and Mesopotamian kings were also called sons of gods, but here sonship is a covenant relationship given on a particular day.

insights.title: Messiah
insights.body: "His Anointed" (2:2) translates mashiach, the source of the word Messiah; the Greek equivalent is christos. Kings and priests were anointed with oil when they took office. After the monarchy ended, psalms like this fed the hope for a future anointed king.

insights.title: Quoted by the early church
insights.body: The first believers in Jerusalem prayed the opening verses of this psalm when their leaders were threatened. The New Testament applies the decree of verse 7 to Jesus at his resurrection and to his superiority over angels, and the voice at Jesus' baptism echoes it.

insights.title: Break them or shepherd them
insights.body: The Hebrew says the king will break the nations with a rod of iron (2:9). The ancient Greek translation read the same consonants with different vowels as shepherd them, and Revelation follows that reading when it applies the verse to Christ. The rod is a shepherd's staff and a royal sceptre at once.

insights.title: Kiss the son
insights.body: "Give sincere homage to the Son" (2:12) is a difficult line; WEB's footnote gives the literal "Kiss the son". The word for son here is bar, the Aramaic form, which is unusual, so some scholars translate "kiss purely" or emend the text. Kissing a king's hand or feet was a common act of submission.

insights.title: God laughs
insights.body: "He who sits in the heavens will laugh" (2:4) is one of the boldest images in the Psalms. What does it suggest about how great human powers look from God's point of view, and why does the psalm end with an invitation rather than a threat alone (2:12)?

3.summary: A king in danger, hunted by many enemies who say God will not help him, calls on Yahweh as his shield and sleeps in peace.
3.lookfor: Notice the repeated word "many", the move from fear to sleep, and the way the psalm ends by praying for the whole people.

insights.title: Fleeing from Absalom
insights.body: The title links this psalm to David's flight from Jerusalem when his son Absalom seized the throne. It is the first of thirteen psalms whose titles name an event in David's life. Most scholars think these titles were added by later editors, but they show how early readers learned to read the psalms against real lives.

insights.title: Selah
insights.body: "Selah" (3:2) appears 71 times in the Psalms and three times in Habakkuk, but no one knows exactly what it means. It may mark a musical interlude, a pause, or a call to lift the voice. Many readers simply pause at it.

insights.title: Many against one
insights.body: The word "many" is repeated three times in the opening lines (3:1-2), and the enemies' taunt is that "There is no help for him in God." The answer piles up three titles for God: shield, glory, and the one who lifts up my head (3:3). Lifting the head is what happens to a person restored to honour.

insights.title: A morning prayer
insights.body: "I laid myself down and slept. I awakened" (3:5) made this a traditional morning psalm. In the Eastern Orthodox morning service it is the first of the six psalms read at the start of Matins. A man fleeing a coup can sleep because Yahweh, not his guards, sustains him.

insights.title: Broken teeth
insights.body: Striking the enemies on the cheek and breaking their teeth (3:7) pictures them as wild animals made harmless. A blow to the cheek was also a public insult. The prayer asks God to disarm and shame the attackers.

insights.title: Salvation belongs to Yahweh
insights.body: The closing cry (3:8) is echoed almost exactly by Jonah inside the fish. Both prayers come from people with no other way out. The psalm then turns outward to bless the people, including those who followed the rebel.

insights.title: Sleeping in danger
insights.body: The psalmist's enemies have not gone away, yet he sleeps and wakes (3:5-6). What is the difference between the absence of danger and the peace this psalm describes?

4.summary: The psalmist asks God to answer, warns opponents to stop chasing falsehood, and ends with a quiet joy that lets him lie down and sleep in safety.
4.lookfor: Watch who is being spoken to in each section, the question "Who will show us any good?", and the closing picture of sleep.

insights.title: An evening psalm
insights.body: Because it ends with lying down to sleep (4:8), this psalm has long been prayed at night. The Rule of St Benedict sets it at Compline, the last service of the day, together with Psalms 91 and 134. It pairs naturally with the morning prayer of Psalm 3.

insights.title: For the Chief Musician
insights.body: This is the first psalm whose title is addressed to the Chief Musician, a Hebrew word that probably means the leader or director of the temple music. It appears in 55 psalm titles and at the end of Habakkuk's prayer. Titles like this show the psalms were sung, with instruments, in organised worship.

insights.title: Be angry, and don't sin
insights.body: "Stand in awe, and don't sin" (4:4) uses a verb that means to tremble or be stirred, whether with fear or anger. The Greek Old Testament read it as anger, and Paul quotes that version: "Be angry, and don't sin." Both readings point to strong feeling that does not turn into wrongdoing.

insights.title: The light of your face
insights.body: "Let the light of your face shine on us" (4:6) echoes the priestly blessing that Aaron's sons spoke over Israel. A shining face meant favour, as with a king who looks kindly on a petitioner. The psalm turns the blessing into a prayer.

insights.title: Grain and new wine
insights.body: The psalmist's joy is greater than the joy of a bumper harvest (4:7). Some scholars think the psalm was prayed during a drought, when people were tempted to seek rain from other gods; the "vanity" and "falsehood" of verse 2 often describe idols elsewhere. Others read it as a dispute with personal slanderers.

insights.title: Speaking to opponents
insights.body: In the middle of a prayer the psalmist turns and addresses people directly (4:2-5), telling them to search their hearts, offer right sacrifices and trust Yahweh. Prayer here is not only private; it becomes a word to others.

insights.title: Be still on your bed
insights.body: The psalm invites people to search their hearts on their beds and be still (4:4). What might it look like to end a day this way, before the sleep of verse 8?

5.summary: A morning prayer asks Yahweh, who cannot live with evil, to lead the psalmist through enemies who lie, and to make all who take refuge in him rejoice.
5.lookfor: Look for the morning setting, the description of the enemies' mouths, and the closing image of a shield.

insights.title: Laying out requests
insights.body: "In the morning I will lay my requests before you" (5:3) uses the verb arak, to set in order. It is used for arranging wood and offerings on the altar and for laying out a case in court. The psalmist arranges the prayer and then watches expectantly, like a lookout.

insights.title: Bowing toward the temple
insights.body: "I will bow toward your holy temple" (5:7) reflects the custom of praying toward God's house. Solomon asked God to hear prayers made toward the temple, and Daniel prayed facing Jerusalem from Babylon. The word for temple is also used of the sanctuary at Shiloh before Solomon built his temple.

insights.title: Loving kindness
insights.body: "Loving kindness" (5:7) translates hesed, one of the key words of the Psalter, used more than a hundred times in the book. It means loyal, faithful love within a covenant, often translated steadfast love or mercy. The psalmist enters God's house not by his own merit but on the strength of that love.

insights.title: An open tomb
insights.body: "Their throat is an open tomb" (5:9) pictures speech that smells of death. Paul quotes this line in Romans in a chain of psalm texts showing that all people stand under sin. In the psalm it describes a particular group of liars; Paul widens it to all humanity.

insights.title: Hold them guilty
insights.body: This is the first of many psalms that ask God to punish enemies (5:10). The prayer does not take revenge into the psalmist's own hands but asks God to let the liars fall by their own schemes. The reason given is that they have rebelled against God, not only against the speaker.

insights.title: A large shield
insights.body: The shield of verse 12 is the tsinnah, a large shield that covered the whole body, not the small round shield of Psalm 3:3. Goliath had one carried before him. God's favour surrounds the righteous on every side.

insights.title: Evil can't live with you
insights.body: The psalm says evil cannot live with God (5:4) and yet the psalmist enters God's house through God's loving kindness (5:7). How do these two truths fit together for someone who is not perfect?

6.summary: Sick, weeping and surrounded by enemies, the psalmist begs Yahweh not to discipline in anger, then suddenly declares that Yahweh has heard.
6.lookfor: Notice the cry "how long?", the nights of tears, and the sharp change of tone in the last three verses.

names.name: Sheol
names.gloss: The Hebrew name for the world of the dead, pictured as a silent place beneath the earth.

insights.title: First penitential psalm
insights.body: Since early Christian times Psalms 6, 32, 38, 51, 102, 130 and 143 have been grouped as the seven penitential psalms, prayed especially in Lent. Psalm 6 does not actually confess a sin, but its plea not to be disciplined in anger (6:1) made it a natural prayer of repentance.

insights.title: No praise in Sheol
insights.body: "In Sheol, who shall give you thanks?" (6:5) reflects the common Old Testament picture of the dead as cut off from the worship of the living. The psalmist argues that God loses a worshipper if he dies. Clearer hope of resurrection appears later, as in Daniel 12:2.

insights.title: An unfinished sentence
insights.body: "But you, Yahweh—how long?" (6:3) breaks off mid-thought. The cry "how long" recurs throughout the laments of the Psalms. The psalmist's body, bones and soul are all involved in the suffering (6:2-3).

insights.title: A sudden change
insights.body: After nights of tears (6:6), the psalmist suddenly declares that Yahweh has heard (6:8-9). Many scholars think something happened between the verses, such as a word of assurance from a priest; others see a shift of faith within the prayer itself. Many laments turn in this way.

insights.title: Depart from me
insights.body: The words telling evildoers to depart (6:8) are echoed by Jesus at the end of the Sermon on the Mount, when he tells false followers to depart from him. In the psalm the sufferer speaks them; in the Gospel the Judge does.

insights.title: The eight-stringed lyre
insights.body: The title mentions the sheminith, literally "the eighth", which WEB renders as an eight-stringed lyre. It may refer to an instrument, a tuning or a lower octave; no one is certain. Augustine read it as pointing to the eighth day of judgment beyond this age.

insights.title: Flooding the bed with tears
insights.body: The psalmist does not hide grief from God but describes it vividly (6:6-7). What does the presence of prayers like this in Scripture say about bringing raw feelings to God?

7.summary: Pursued by enemies and falsely accused, the psalmist swears his innocence, asks God to judge, and trusts that the wicked will fall into their own pit.
7.lookfor: Watch for the oath beginning "if I have done this", the picture of God as judge of the nations, and the wicked person who is pregnant with mischief.

insights.title: Cush the Benjamite
insights.body: The title links the psalm to the words of Cush, a Benjamite, who is otherwise unknown. As a Benjamite he may have been one of Saul's supporters, accusing David of treachery. He is not the Cushite messenger who brought David news of Absalom's death.

insights.title: A shiggaion
insights.body: WEB calls the psalm a meditation, translating the rare Hebrew shiggaion. The word may come from a root meaning to wander or reel, suggesting an intense or irregular song. Its plural appears at the head of Habakkuk's prayer.

insights.title: An oath of innocence
insights.body: "If I have done this... let the enemy pursue my soul" (7:3-5) is a self-curse, a common way of swearing innocence in the ancient world. Job uses the same form at length. The psalmist claims innocence in this case, not perfection in general.

insights.title: Minds and hearts
insights.body: "Their minds and hearts are searched" (7:9) literally reads hearts and kidneys. The kidneys stood for the hidden emotions and conscience, much as we use the heart. Revelation applies the phrase to the risen Christ, who searches minds and hearts.

insights.title: Pregnant with mischief
insights.body: The wicked person "travails with iniquity" and "has conceived mischief" (7:14), then digs a pit and falls into it (7:15). Evil is pictured as giving birth to its own downfall. Proverbs uses the same image of the digger falling into the pit.

insights.title: Yahweh Most High
insights.body: The psalm ends with "Yahweh Most High" (7:17), the first use in the Psalms of Elyon, Most High. The title first appears with Melchizedek, priest of God Most High in Salem. It presents Yahweh as ruler over all nations, not only Israel.

insights.title: Judge me by my righteousness
insights.body: The psalmist asks to be judged "according to my righteousness" (7:8), which can sound proud. When is it right to appeal to God about one's innocence, and how is that different from claiming to be sinless?

8.summary: A hymn that marvels at Yahweh's majesty in the heavens and at the surprising honour he gives frail human beings as rulers over his creation.
8.lookfor: Notice the refrain at the beginning and end, the question "what is man?", and the list of creatures placed under human feet.

insights.title: Genesis set to music
insights.body: Psalm 8 is a poetic meditation on the creation of humans in Genesis 1, where they are made in God's image and given rule over fish, birds and animals. The psalm lists the same creatures (8:7-8). It is the first hymn of praise in the Psalter.

insights.title: Lower than the angels
insights.body: "A little lower than the angels" (8:5) translates elohim, the ordinary word for God, which can also mean heavenly beings. The Greek translation chose angels, and Hebrews follows it. Many modern versions read a little lower than God.

insights.title: Son of man
insights.body: "What is the son of man" (8:4) uses ben adam, simply a human being, in parallel with enosh, a word that hints at frailty. Jesus' title the Son of Man draws mainly on Daniel 7, but Hebrews reads this psalm as fulfilled in him.

insights.title: Babes and infants
insights.body: When children shouted praise to Jesus in the temple, he answered his critics with verse 2, quoted in the Greek version, which speaks of perfected praise rather than strength. Paul quotes verse 6 about all things being put under Christ's feet.

insights.title: Royal language for everyone
insights.body: In the ancient Near East, kings were described as the image of a god and crowned with glory. Psalm 8 gives this royal language to every human being: crowned with glory and honour, ruler over the works of God's hands (8:5-6). The night sky (8:3) makes this honour all the more surprising.

insights.title: Framed by majesty
insights.body: The psalm begins and ends with the same line (8:1, 8:9). Human dignity sits in the middle, wrapped inside the praise of God's name. The structure itself says that human rule is under God's rule.

insights.title: What is man?
insights.body: Looking at the moon and stars makes the psalmist feel small, yet leads to wonder at human worth (8:3-5). How does seeing ourselves as both tiny and honoured shape the way we treat each other and creation?

9.summary: The psalmist thanks Yahweh, the righteous judge enthroned forever, for defeating enemy nations and remembering the afflicted, and asks him to rise again.
9.lookfor: Look for God's throne and judgment, the promise that the needy will not be forgotten, and the nations caught in their own net.

names.name: Zion
names.gloss: Jerusalem's temple hill, pictured as where Yahweh dwells.

names.name: Sheol
names.gloss: The realm of the dead.

insights.title: Psalms 9 and 10 belong together
insights.body: Psalms 9 and 10 form a single alphabetic poem, with lines starting with successive letters of the Hebrew alphabet, though some letters are missing. Psalm 10 has no title, and the Greek and Latin Bibles count the two as one psalm. That is why older Catholic and Orthodox Bibles number most later psalms one lower.

insights.title: A high tower
insights.body: "A high tower for the oppressed" (9:9) translates misgab, a high, secure place beyond the reach of attackers. The same word appears often in David's psalms of refuge. It suggests safety by height rather than by walls.

insights.title: Meditation. Selah.
insights.body: Verse 16 ends with two musical notes, "Meditation" (higgaion) and Selah. Higgaion comes from the same root as the meditating of Psalm 1:2 and may mean a quiet resounding sound. It marks a pause after the claim that the wicked are trapped by their own work.

insights.title: The afflicted and the needy
insights.body: "He doesn't forget the cry of the afflicted" (9:12) introduces the poor and oppressed, a major theme of the Psalms. The Hebrew words describe people who are humbled and without power. Yahweh is presented as their defender when no one else will be.

insights.title: He who avenges blood
insights.body: God is called "he who avenges blood" (9:12), the one who requires an account for every life taken, as he told Noah. Innocent blood cries out to God, as Abel's did. The psalm trusts that no victim is forgotten.

insights.title: The Death of the Son
insights.body: The title tells the musician to set the psalm to The Death of the Son, probably the name of a known tune. The Hebrew phrase is obscure, and ancient translators read it in several different ways. Such tune names show the psalms were sung to familiar melodies.

insights.title: Only men
insights.body: The psalm ends asking God to let the nations know "that they are only men" (9:20). Why might powerful people and nations need to learn this, and what might it look like for them to learn it?

10.summary: The psalmist asks why Yahweh seems far away while the arrogant prey on the helpless, then calls on him to rise, and ends trusting that the King hears the humble.
10.lookfor: Notice what the wicked say in their hearts, the hunting images of lion and net, and the turn at verse 12.

insights.title: Why do you stand far off?
insights.body: The psalm opens with one of the Bible's most direct complaints (10:1). It continues Psalm 9, which praised God as judge; now the psalmist asks why that judge seems absent while the weak suffer. Praise and protest sit side by side in the same poem.

insights.title: Practical atheism
insights.body: The wicked person does not argue that God doesn't exist. He says "God has forgotten. He hides his face. He will never see it" (10:11), and "God won't call me into account" (10:13). The danger is living as though God never acts.

insights.title: Ambush near the villages
insights.body: The wicked lie in wait near villages and pounce like a lion or a hunter with a net (10:8-9). Unwalled villages were exposed to raiders and strongmen. The images also fit powerful people who trap the poor through debt and false accusations.

insights.title: The helpless
insights.body: The word translated "the helpless" (10:8, 10:10, 10:14) is found nowhere else in the Hebrew Bible. It seems to mean the unfortunate or wretched. The psalm gives a special name to the people the wicked ignore.

insights.title: A mouth full of cursing
insights.body: Paul quotes this psalm's description of a mouth full of cursing (10:7) in Romans 3, alongside other psalms. The Torah repeatedly names the fatherless, the widow and the stranger as people God personally protects; the psalm appeals to that care (10:14, 10:18).

insights.title: Yahweh is King
insights.body: The turning point comes with "Yahweh is King forever and ever!" (10:16). The kingship of God is a central theme of the Psalter, which becomes especially strong in Psalms 93–99. The psalm ends with confidence that the King hears the humble.

insights.title: Seeing and acting
insights.body: The wicked say God does not see, but the psalmist says "you do see trouble and grief" (10:14). How does believing that God sees change the way someone responds to injustice they cannot fix?

11.summary: Told to flee like a bird to the mountains, the psalmist refuses, because Yahweh is on his throne, sees everything, and will judge the wicked.
11.lookfor: Watch for the advice of the frightened friends, the question about foundations, and the eyes of Yahweh watching from heaven.

insights.title: Flee or stay?
insights.body: The psalm answers friends who say "Flee as a bird to your mountain!" (11:1). Their advice is sensible: hidden archers are aiming in the dark (11:2). The psalmist's answer is that he has already taken refuge in Yahweh, so running is not the only safety.

insights.title: If the foundations are destroyed
insights.body: "If the foundations are destroyed, what can the righteous do?" (11:3) is often quoted as the psalmist's own despair. In context it is probably still the voice of the fearful advisers, and the psalm's reply is that Yahweh is still on his throne (11:4). The foundations are the order of law and justice in society.

insights.title: Testing eyes
insights.body: Yahweh's eyes "examine" people (11:4-5), using bachan, a word for testing metal to see if it is pure. God is not only watching but assessing. The same word is used for God testing hearts in Jeremiah.

insights.title: Fire and sulfur
insights.body: Blazing coals, fire and sulfur (11:6) recall the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah. The "portion of their cup" pictures judgment as a drink measured out to each person, an image prophets use for the cup of God's wrath.

insights.title: Archers in the dark
insights.body: Bows were bent by stepping on one end to string them, and arrows were fitted to the string before an ambush (11:2). Shooting from darkness describes hidden attacks, perhaps slander or plots. The righteous cannot see their attackers, but Yahweh can.

insights.title: Seeing his face
insights.body: "The upright shall see his face" (11:7) is the psalm's final promise. To see a king's face meant being welcomed into his presence. Jesus promises the pure in heart that they will see God, and Revelation says his servants will see his face.

insights.title: Staying put
insights.body: Sometimes fleeing is wise, as David did from Saul. How does someone discern when trust in God means staying where they are and when it means leaving?

12.summary: In a world where everyone seems to lie, the psalmist asks Yahweh for help, hears Yahweh promise to rise for the needy, and contrasts human flattery with Yahweh's pure words.
12.lookfor: Notice how many times lips and tongues are mentioned, the words Yahweh himself speaks, and the image of refined silver.

insights.title: No one faithful left
insights.body: "The godly man ceases" (12:1) is a cry of loneliness in a society where honest speech seems to have vanished. Micah and Elijah express the same feeling that they alone are left. The psalm is a lament for a whole culture, not just one enemy.

insights.title: A double heart
insights.body: "Flattering lips" (12:2) are literally smooth lips, and "a double heart" is literally a heart and a heart. The liar says one thing while meaning another. James uses a similar idea for the double-minded person.

insights.title: Our lips are our own
insights.body: The boasters say "Our lips are our own. Who is lord over us?" (12:4). They treat speech as answerable to no one. The psalm answers by letting Yahweh speak (12:5).

insights.title: God speaks in the psalm
insights.body: In verse 5 Yahweh himself speaks, promising to arise for the weak and needy. Words like this may have been spoken by a prophet or priest during worship in answer to a lament. The divine word turns the psalm from complaint to confidence.

insights.title: Silver refined seven times
insights.body: Silver was purified by heating it in a clay crucible until impurities separated out (12:6). Repeating the process seven times, the number of completeness, would give the purest silver possible. Yahweh's words are contrasted with the slippery talk of verse 2.

insights.title: Lies and the tongue
insights.body: Psalms, Proverbs and James all treat speech as a moral matter of the first order. James says the tongue is a small part of the body that boasts great things. Psalm 12 shows what happens to a society when trust in words collapses.

insights.title: When vileness is honoured
insights.body: The psalm ends without resolution: the wicked roam when what is vile is exalted (12:8). What does it suggest that the psalm closes here rather than with a triumphant finish?

13.summary: In six short verses the psalmist moves from asking "How long?" four times, to pleading for an answer, to resting in Yahweh's loving kindness.
13.lookfor: Count the questions in the first two verses, notice what the psalmist fears the enemy will say, and watch where the tone changes.

insights.title: A lament in miniature
insights.body: Psalm 13 shows the usual shape of a lament in its smallest form: complaint (13:1-2), request (13:3-4), and trust and praise (13:5-6). About a third of the psalms are laments, more than any other type. The pattern gives a path through suffering without pretending it away.

insights.title: Four times how long
insights.body: "How long" appears four times in two verses (13:1-2), covering God's forgetting, God's hidden face, the psalmist's inner turmoil and the enemy's triumph. The complaint is about God, self and others at once. The repetition itself expresses how long the waiting has felt.

insights.title: Light to the eyes
insights.body: "Give light to my eyes, lest I sleep in death" (13:3) uses a common picture: dull eyes were a sign of weakness, illness or approaching death, and bright eyes a sign of renewed strength. When Jonathan ate honey after exhaustion, his eyes brightened.

insights.title: Hiding the face
insights.body: For God to hide his face (13:1) means to withdraw favour and help, the opposite of the priestly blessing in which God makes his face shine on his people. Many psalms plead with God not to hide his face.

insights.title: Nothing has changed outside
insights.body: The closing trust (13:5-6) is not explained by any visible rescue. The enemy is still there. The psalm moves because the psalmist remembers God's loving kindness and past goodness, not because the circumstances have shifted.

insights.title: Echoed in Jesus' prayer
insights.body: The cry of abandonment that opens Psalm 22, which Jesus prayed on the cross, is a deeper form of this psalm's question. In both, the one who complains still addresses God as "my God" (13:3).

insights.title: From how long to good
insights.body: The psalm begins by asking whether God will forget forever and ends by saying he has been good (13:6). Is this a contradiction, or is it possible to say both in the same prayer?

14.summary: The fool denies God and the corrupt devour God's people, but Yahweh looks down, sides with the poor, and the psalmist longs for salvation from Zion.
14.lookfor: Watch Yahweh looking down from heaven, the phrase "no, not one", and the final longing for Israel's restoration.

names.name: Zion
names.gloss: Jerusalem's temple hill, the place from which salvation is expected to come.

insights.title: The fool
insights.body: The fool (14:1) is nabal, a person who is morally senseless rather than unintelligent. Nabal is also the name of the rich man who insulted David in 1 Samuel 25, whose wife said his name suited him. To say there is no God in this sense is to live as though no one will hold you accountable.

insights.title: Psalm 53 is a twin
insights.body: Psalm 53 is almost identical to Psalm 14, but uses Elohim, God, where Psalm 14 uses Yahweh. Psalms 42–83 are often called the Elohistic Psalter because they prefer that name. The same song seems to have been preserved in two collections.

insights.title: No, not one
insights.body: Paul quotes the first verses of this psalm in Romans 3 to show that Jews and Gentiles alike are under sin. In the psalm, the corrupt are those who "eat up my people" (14:4), contrasted with the righteous. Paul extends the verdict to all humanity.

insights.title: God looks down
insights.body: Yahweh looking down from heaven to see if any understand (14:2) recalls the scene before the flood and at Babel, where God sees and comes down. The fool says there is no God, but God is the one doing the looking.

insights.title: Eating people like bread
insights.body: "Who eat up my people as they eat bread" (14:4) pictures the powerful exploiting the poor as casually as eating a meal. The prophets use similar language of rulers who strip the people.

insights.title: Restoring the fortunes
insights.body: "When Yahweh restores the fortunes of his people" (14:7) is a phrase often used for return from exile. Some scholars think this final verse was added when the psalm was sung during or after the exile; others see it as a general hope for renewal.

insights.title: Living as if
insights.body: The fool's denial is shown in deeds, not arguments (14:1, 14:4). In what ways can people who believe in God still live as though he does not see?

15.summary: A worshipper asks who may live in Yahweh's presence, and the answer lists marks of an honest, faithful life.
15.lookfor: Notice how many of the qualities have to do with speech and money, and the promise at the end.

insights.title: At the temple gate
insights.body: Psalm 15 is often called an entrance liturgy. A worshipper asks who may come into God's sanctuary (15:1), and the answer, perhaps given by a priest, describes the kind of person who belongs there. Psalm 24 has the same pattern.

insights.title: Ethics, not ritual
insights.body: The answer does not mention washing, sacrifices or offerings. Every condition concerns how one treats others: truthful speech, loyalty to friends, honest money (15:2-5). Worship and daily ethics are bound together.

insights.title: No usury
insights.body: Israel's law forbade charging interest on loans to a poor fellow Israelite, since loans were usually for survival rather than business. The Hebrew word for interest comes from a root meaning to bite. Taking a bribe against the innocent was also condemned (15:5).

insights.title: An oath that hurts
insights.body: The faithful person "keeps an oath even when it hurts, and doesn't change" (15:4). A promise is kept even when circumstances make it costly. Leviticus allowed substitutions for some vows, but forbade exchanging something for worse.

insights.title: The Torah in eleven lines
insights.body: The Talmud records a rabbinic teaching that the 613 commandments of the Torah were summed up by David in the eleven qualities of Psalm 15, then by Isaiah in six, Micah in three, and Habakkuk in one: the righteous shall live by faith.

insights.title: Truth in his heart
insights.body: "Speaks truth in his heart" (15:2) means truthfulness that goes all the way down, not just careful public speech. The Hebrew emet means firmness and reliability as well as truth.

insights.title: Who can stand?
insights.body: This psalm sets a high standard for coming near to God. How do its demands relate to the confidence of other psalms that God welcomes sinners who repent, such as Psalm 32?

16.summary: The psalmist takes refuge in Yahweh as his only good, his portion and inheritance, and trusts that God will not abandon him to death but show him the path of life.
16.lookfor: Look for the language of land and inheritance, the night-time counsel, and the confident final verses about Sheol and life.

names.name: Sheol
names.gloss: The realm of the dead.

insights.title: A miktam
insights.body: WEB calls this a Poem, translating the obscure title miktam, used for Psalm 16 and Psalms 56–60. Ancient guesses included an inscription or a golden poem. No one knows its exact meaning.

insights.title: The lines have fallen
insights.body: "The lines have fallen to me in pleasant places" (16:6) refers to measuring ropes used to mark out plots of land, which were assigned by lot. Israel's tribes received their land this way. The psalmist says his true allotment is Yahweh himself.

insights.title: The Levites' portion
insights.body: "Yahweh assigned my portion and my cup" (16:5) echoes what God told the priests and Levites, who received no tribal land: I am your portion and your inheritance. The psalmist claims for himself the privilege of the priestly tribe.

insights.title: Drink offerings of blood
insights.body: The psalmist refuses to pour out "drink offerings of blood" to other gods or even say their names (16:4). This may describe offerings to the dead or to gods of the land, which the law condemned.

insights.title: Peter's Pentecost sermon
insights.body: Peter quotes verses 8–11 at Pentecost, arguing that David died and was buried, so the promise not to see corruption (16:10) was fulfilled in the resurrection of Jesus. Paul makes the same argument at Pisidian Antioch. Both follow the Greek wording.

insights.title: My heart instructs me
insights.body: "My heart instructs me in the night seasons" (16:7) literally says my kidneys, the seat of inner feeling and conscience. The night is a time of reflection and listening. God's counsel and the psalmist's inner self are working together.

insights.title: Sheol and the path of life
insights.body: Whether the psalmist originally meant rescue from an early death or something beyond death is debated (16:10-11). Many Jewish and Christian readers have seen here one of the clearest Old Testament hopes of life with God that death cannot end. The "fullness of joy" is found in God's presence.

insights.title: No good apart from you
insights.body: "Apart from you I have no good thing" (16:2) is a sweeping claim. What would it mean in practice to treat God as one's portion rather than one of many good things?

17.summary: Protesting his innocence, the psalmist asks God to hear, to guard him as the apple of his eye under the shadow of his wings, and to deliver him from lion-like enemies.
17.lookfor: Look for the courtroom language at the start, the tender images of protection in the middle, and the contrast between the enemies' portion and the psalmist's hope.

insights.title: A plea in court
insights.body: The psalm opens like a legal appeal: "my righteous plea" and "Let my sentence come out of your presence" (17:1-2). Some scholars think people falsely accused could come to the temple to seek God's verdict. The psalmist has been tested by night and claims nothing was found (17:3).

insights.title: Apple of the eye
insights.body: "Keep me as the apple of your eye" (17:8) refers to the pupil, the most protected part of the body. The Hebrew phrase is literally the little man of the eye, the tiny reflection a person sees in someone else's pupil. Moses' song uses the same image for Israel.

insights.title: Under the shadow of wings
insights.body: "Hide me under the shadow of your wings" (17:8) may picture a mother bird or the outstretched wings of the cherubim over the ark in the temple. Boaz blesses Ruth as one who came to take refuge under Yahweh's wings, and Jesus longs to gather Jerusalem like a hen.

insights.title: A crouching lion
insights.body: The enemy is like a young lion lurking in secret places (17:12). Lions lived in the thickets of the Jordan valley in biblical times and were a real danger to flocks and travellers. They are one of the Psalms' standard images for violent enemies.

insights.title: A difficult verse
insights.body: Verse 14 is hard to translate. WEB reads it as describing worldly people whose portion is in this life, whose children are well provided for; other versions read it as a curse filling their bellies with punishment. Either way, it contrasts them with the psalmist's hope in verse 15.

insights.title: When I awake
insights.body: "I shall be satisfied, when I awake, with seeing your form" (17:15) may describe waking after a night of prayer at the sanctuary. Later Jewish and Christian readers also heard in it a hope of waking from death. The word for form is used of the form of God Moses saw.

insights.title: Nothing found
insights.body: The psalmist says God tested his heart by night and "found nothing" (17:3). How is this kind of confidence different from self-righteousness, and when might a believer honestly pray this way?

18.summary: David's long song of thanks recalls how Yahweh came down in storm and fire to rescue him from death and enemies, and gave him victory and a kingdom.
18.lookfor: Notice the names David gives God at the start, the earthquake and storm when God comes down, and how the psalm ends with God's faithfulness to David's descendants.

names.name: Sheol
names.gloss: The realm of the dead, pictured here as a hunter's snare.

insights.title: Also in 2 Samuel
insights.body: Almost the whole psalm appears again as 2 Samuel 22, near the end of David's story. The differences between the two copies are small but show that psalms could circulate in slightly different forms. Its title links it to David's rescue from Saul and all his enemies.

insights.title: Horn of my salvation
insights.body: The horn (18:2) is a symbol of strength, taken from a wild ox or ram with its horns raised. Zechariah, John the Baptist's father, uses the phrase horn of salvation for the Messiah from David's house.

insights.title: God rides the storm
insights.body: The rescue is told as a storm: earthquake, smoke, fire, thick cloud, thunder, hail and lightning (18:7-14), with God riding on a cherub. Canaanite poems from Ugarit described the storm god Baal as the rider on the clouds. The psalm claims that language for Yahweh, who uses it to save one man.

insights.title: Rescue from many waters
insights.body: "He drew me out of many waters" (18:16) uses the verb from which the name Moses comes. Deep waters are a common picture of death and chaos. The rescuer reaches down from on high and brings the psalmist into a large place (18:19).

insights.title: God mirrors the person
insights.body: "With the merciful you will show yourself merciful... With the crooked you will show yourself shrewd" (18:25-26). God's dealings fit the character of the one he deals with. Jesus teaches something similar about the measure we use being measured back.

insights.title: Deer's feet and a bronze bow
insights.body: Being given feet like a deer's (18:33) means sure footing on steep rocky heights, where deer and ibex move easily. A bow of bronze (18:34) may mean a bow reinforced with metal, too strong for an ordinary man to bend. Habakkuk uses the deer's feet image too.

insights.title: Praise among the nations
insights.body: Paul quotes verse 49 in Romans to show that the Gentiles were always meant to glorify God for his mercy. The psalm ends with loving kindness to David "and to his offspring, forever more" (18:50), echoing God's covenant with David.

insights.title: According to my righteousness
insights.body: David says Yahweh rewarded him for the cleanness of his hands (18:20-24), even though his story includes Bathsheba and Uriah. How might this claim be understood alongside his confession in Psalm 51?

19.summary: The skies proclaim God's glory without words, the sun runs its course, and Yahweh's law is even more precious, leading the psalmist to pray for forgiveness and pure words.
19.lookfor: Watch how the poem moves from the sky to the sun to the law, the six different names for God's law, and the prayer at the end.

insights.title: Two books of God
insights.body: The psalm sets God's revelation in creation (19:1-6) beside his revelation in the law (19:7-11). Christians later spoke of the book of nature and the book of Scripture. C. S. Lewis called this the greatest poem in the Psalter.

insights.title: The expanse
insights.body: "The expanse" (19:1) is raqia, the same word used in Genesis 1 for the dome of the sky that separates the waters. Older translations say firmament. The heavens declare God's glory by simply being what they are.

insights.title: The sun as a creature
insights.body: Neighbouring peoples worshipped the sun; in Mesopotamia the sun god Shamash was also the god of justice who saw everything. Psalm 19 makes the sun a creature living in a tent God set up, running like a bridegroom or a champion (19:4-5). Nothing escapes its heat, just as nothing escapes God's law.

insights.title: Their voice has gone out
insights.body: Paul quotes verse 4 in Romans 10, applying the worldwide voice of the heavens to the spread of the gospel message. The psalm says the skies speak in every language, even though there is "no speech nor language" in the ordinary sense (19:3).

insights.title: Six names for the law
insights.body: Verses 7–9 use six terms: law, testimony, precepts, commandment, fear and ordinances, each with "Yahweh's" and each with a benefit such as restoring the soul or enlightening the eyes. Psalm 119 will expand this pattern into 176 verses.

insights.title: Hidden and presumptuous sins
insights.body: The psalmist asks forgiveness for hidden errors and protection from presumptuous sins (19:12-13). The law distinguished between unintentional sins, which could be atoned for, and sins done defiantly, with a high hand. Facing the perfect law makes the psalmist aware of faults he cannot see.

insights.title: My rock and my redeemer
insights.body: The final verse (19:14) is often prayed before sermons. "Redeemer" is go'el, the relative who buys back a family member's land or freedom, as Boaz did for Ruth and Naomi. God is pictured as the kinsman who takes responsibility for his people.

insights.title: Sweeter than honey
insights.body: The psalmist finds God's law more desirable than gold and sweeter than honey (19:10). What would make law feel like a gift rather than a burden?

20.summary: The people pray for their king before battle, and a voice declares confidence that Yahweh saves his anointed, who trusts in God's name rather than chariots and horses.
20.lookfor: Notice who is speaking to whom, the sudden "Now I know" in verse 6, and the contrast between chariots and the name of Yahweh.

insights.title: Before the battle
insights.body: Psalm 20 seems to be a prayer said for the king as he offered sacrifices before going to war (20:3). The people pray for him in verses 1–5, and then a single voice, perhaps a priest or the king himself, declares that God will answer (20:6). Psalm 21 is its partner, giving thanks after victory.

insights.title: Now I know
insights.body: The shift to "Now I know that Yahweh saves his anointed" (20:6) may mean that an encouraging sign or word came during the ceremony, as when a sacrifice was accepted. Confidence comes before the battle is fought.

insights.title: Chariots and horses
insights.body: Chariots were the most advanced and expensive weapons of the age, used by Egypt, Canaan and Assyria. Israel's law warned its king not to multiply horses, and the prophets condemned trust in Egypt's cavalry. "Some trust in chariots... but we trust the name of Yahweh" (20:7) makes trust the deciding weapon.

insights.title: The name
insights.body: God's "name" appears three times (20:1, 20:5, 20:7). In the Bible a name stands for the person's character and presence. To trust the name of Yahweh is to rely on who he has shown himself to be.

insights.title: Setting up banners
insights.body: "We will set up our banners" (20:5) pictures standards raised by each unit in camp or in victory. The tribes of Israel camped by their banners in the wilderness. Raising them in God's name declares whose army this is.

insights.title: Prayed for every ruler
insights.body: In the synagogue, Psalm 20 is recited in the weekday morning service. Christians have often prayed it for those in authority, in line with the New Testament's call to pray for kings. It remains a model of praying for leaders before their great tests.

insights.title: Chariots today
insights.body: If chariots and horses were the most impressive power of that age, what might they stand for now, and what would it mean to trust God's name instead?

21.summary: The people thank Yahweh for the king's victory and long life, then declare that the king will defeat every enemy by Yahweh's power.
21.lookfor: Compare this psalm with Psalm 20, and watch for the crown, the long life, and the fire of judgment on the enemies.

insights.title: Prayer answered
insights.body: Psalm 20 prayed that Yahweh would grant the king his heart's desire (Psalm 20:4). Psalm 21 begins by thanking him for doing exactly that (21:2). The two were probably placed together as prayer and answer.

insights.title: A crown of fine gold
insights.body: "You set a crown of fine gold on his head" (21:3) recalls the heavy gold crown David took from the king of Rabbah. Crowns, thrones and long life were the standard blessings of kings in the ancient Near East. The psalm says all of them come from Yahweh.

insights.title: Life forever
insights.body: "He asked life of you, you gave it to him, even length of days forever and ever" (21:4). Wishing the king eternal life was a standard courtly formula of honour. In time Jewish and Christian readers heard here a promise fulfilled only in an everlasting king; the Aramaic Targum reads the king of verse 1 as the King Messiah.

insights.title: The king trusts
insights.body: The centre of the psalm is "the king trusts in Yahweh" (21:7). Everything before it describes gifts received, and everything after it describes victory. The king's power rests on his trust and on God's loving kindness.

insights.title: A fierce ending
insights.body: The second half (21:8-12) promises that the king will burn up his enemies and destroy their descendants. Such lines reflect the brutal warfare of the time and are hard for modern readers. They are framed as Yahweh's judgment on those who plotted evil against him (21:11).

insights.title: The Most High
insights.body: The king is steady "through the loving kindness of the Most High" (21:7). Pairing hesed, covenant love, with Elyon, the title of God as supreme over all nations, joins God's personal faithfulness with his universal power.

insights.title: Strength for whom?
insights.body: The psalm begins and ends with Yahweh's strength (21:1, 21:13), not the king's. What does it suggest about leadership when every success is credited to God?

22.summary: A sufferer who feels forsaken by God describes mockery, wasting and encircling enemies, then suddenly breaks into praise that spreads to the whole world and future generations.
22.lookfor: Watch the alternation between despair and memory of God's past faithfulness, the animals surrounding the sufferer, and the sudden turn in verse 21.

names.name: Bashan
names.gloss: A fertile plateau east of the Jordan and north of Gilead, famous for its strong cattle.

insights.title: My God, my God
insights.body: Jesus cried the first line of this psalm from the cross, in Aramaic, as recorded in Matthew and Mark. Since Jews often cited a psalm by its opening words, many interpreters think he was claiming the whole psalm, which ends in vindication, though the cry of abandonment is no less real for that.

insights.title: The scene at the cross
insights.body: The Gospels echo this psalm repeatedly: passers-by shaking their heads and mocking that God should rescue him (22:7-8), and soldiers dividing his clothes and casting lots (22:18). John says this happened to fulfil the psalm.

insights.title: They have pierced
insights.body: "They have pierced my hands and feet" (22:16) follows the ancient Greek translation. Most Hebrew manuscripts read like a lion, my hands and feet, which is hard to make sense of, and Jewish translations usually follow it. A Hebrew fragment from the Judean desert has a verb form instead, which supports a reading like pierced or dug.

insights.title: Bulls, lions and dogs
insights.body: The enemies are bulls of Bashan, roaring lions, dogs and wild oxen (22:12-21). Bashan's cattle were famous for their size. In the ancient world dogs were not pets but scavengers that roamed in packs.

insights.title: You have answered me
insights.body: In the middle of verse 21 the plea suddenly becomes "you have answered me". From there the psalm turns to praise in the assembly (22:22), to all Israel, to the ends of the earth (22:27), and to generations yet unborn (22:31). The circle of praise keeps widening.

insights.title: I will declare your name
insights.body: Hebrews quotes verse 22, putting it in the mouth of Christ who calls believers his brothers. The final words, "he has done it" (22:31), have often been compared with Jesus' last word in John, "It is finished".

insights.title: The Doe of the Morning
insights.body: The title sets the psalm to a tune called The Doe of the Morning, which may refer to the first light of dawn. Jewish tradition later applied the psalm to Queen Esther in her crisis. Christian tradition reads it especially on Good Friday.

insights.title: Praise inside abandonment
insights.body: Even in his darkest words the psalmist says "my God" and remembers that God is holy and enthroned on Israel's praises (22:1-3). What does it mean to keep addressing God while feeling forsaken by him?

23.summary: Yahweh is the psalmist's shepherd who provides, leads and protects through the darkest valley, and then his host who spreads a table and welcomes him home for good.
23.lookfor: Notice the change from talking about God to talking to God in verse 4, and the change of picture from shepherd to host in verse 5.

insights.title: Kings as shepherds
insights.body: In the ancient Near East, kings called themselves shepherds of their people, as Hammurabi of Babylon did. David was literally a shepherd before becoming king. To say "Yahweh is my shepherd" (23:1) is both personal and political: God is the true king who cares for his flock.

insights.title: Still waters
insights.body: "Still waters" (23:2) is literally waters of rest. Sheep drink poorly from fast streams, but the image is mainly of a place of refreshment and safety. "He restores my soul" (23:3) can also mean he brings me back, as a shepherd brings back a wandering sheep.

insights.title: The shadow of death
insights.body: "The valley of the shadow of death" (23:4) translates tsalmavet, which may mean deep darkness; the traditional reading divides it as shadow of death. Either way it describes a dark, dangerous ravine where a sheep cannot see what is coming.

insights.title: Rod and staff
insights.body: The rod was a short club for driving off wild animals; the staff was a long stick for guiding and leaning on. Both are signs of the shepherd's presence. The psalmist fears no evil not because there is none, but "for you are with me" (23:4).

insights.title: From shepherd to host
insights.body: In verse 5 the picture changes to a banquet: a table, oil for the head and an overflowing cup. In ancient hospitality the host was bound to protect a guest, even in the presence of enemies. The meal becomes a public sign that the guest belongs to the host.

insights.title: Goodness will pursue me
insights.body: "Goodness and loving kindness shall follow me" (23:6) uses radaph, a strong verb usually meaning pursue or chase, often used of enemies. Instead of enemies, God's goodness and hesed chase the psalmist all his days.

insights.title: The good shepherd
insights.body: Jesus calls himself the good shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep, and Revelation pictures the Lamb as a shepherd leading his people to springs of water. Hebrews calls him the great shepherd of the sheep.

insights.title: I shall lack nothing
insights.body: The psalm begins with a bold claim of contentment (23:1). What does it mean to say this while still walking through dark valleys and facing enemies?

24.summary: The earth belongs to Yahweh; only the clean-handed may climb his hill; and the ancient gates are told to lift their heads for the King of glory to come in.
24.lookfor: Watch the three parts: creation, the question of who may enter, and the call-and-response at the gates.

insights.title: A procession to the temple
insights.body: Psalm 24 seems to accompany a procession up to the sanctuary, perhaps with the ark, which represented Yahweh's throne. Many link it with David bringing the ark into Jerusalem. The questions and answers suggest singers at the gate and singers in the procession.

insights.title: Founded on the seas
insights.body: "He has founded it on the seas" (24:2) reflects the ancient picture of the land resting on waters below. Neighbouring myths told of gods defeating the sea to create the world. Here Yahweh simply owns and sets the earth in place.

insights.title: The earth is Yahweh's
insights.body: Paul quotes verse 1 when he tells Christians in Corinth that they may eat food sold in the market without asking where it came from. Everything belongs to God, so nothing is unclean in itself.

insights.title: Clean hands, pure heart
insights.body: The one who may ascend has "clean hands and a pure heart" (24:4): right actions and right inner motives. Like Psalm 15, the entrance requirements are about honesty, not ritual. Jesus blesses the pure in heart.

insights.title: Yahweh of Armies
insights.body: The answer to "Who is this King of glory?" is "Yahweh of Armies" (24:10), the first time this title appears in the Psalms. The armies may be heaven's hosts, the stars or Israel's forces. The title was closely linked with the ark, where Yahweh was enthroned on the cherubim.

insights.title: Gates lifting their heads
insights.body: The gates are told to lift their heads (24:7, 24:9), as if the doorways are too low for the King who is coming. Gates were the place of city life and judgment. Personifying them gives the scene a sense of cosmic welcome.

insights.title: Sunday's psalm
insights.body: The Mishnah lists Psalm 24 as the psalm the Levites sang in the temple on the first day of the week, and the Greek title says the same. Christians, who worship on that day, have long used it for Palm Sunday and the Ascension, reading the King of glory as Christ entering heaven.

insights.title: Who may ascend?
insights.body: The psalm asks who is fit to stand in God's holy place (24:3), then announces the King who enters. How might the King's entry change the answer to that question?

25.summary: An alphabet prayer in which the psalmist lifts his soul to Yahweh, asks to be taught his paths, begs forgiveness for old and great sins, and pleads for rescue from enemies.
25.lookfor: Notice the repeated requests to be taught and guided, the word "remember", and how the last verse widens the prayer to all Israel.

insights.title: An alphabet poem
insights.body: Psalm 25 is an acrostic: each verse begins with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet, with a few irregularities. The last verse (25:22) falls outside the pattern and turns from personal prayer to prayer for the nation, just as Psalm 34 does. The form suggests a prayer meant to be learned by heart.

insights.title: Lifting up the soul
insights.body: "To you, Yahweh, do I lift up my soul" (25:1) uses nephesh, which means the whole living self, including its desires and longings. To lift it up is to direct one's deepest wants toward God. The same opening appears in Psalms 86 and 143.

insights.title: Remember and don't remember
insights.body: The psalmist asks God to remember his mercies and loving kindness, but not the sins of his youth (25:6-7). God's memory is invoked selectively. In the Bible, for God to remember is to act on behalf of someone.

insights.title: The friendship of Yahweh
insights.body: "The friendship of Yahweh is with those who fear him" (25:14) translates sod, a word for confidential counsel or the inner circle of trusted friends. Amos says God reveals his secret counsel to his prophets; Job remembers when God's friendship was over his tent.

insights.title: Pardon, for it is great
insights.body: "Pardon my iniquity, for it is great" (25:11) gives an unusual reason for forgiveness: the size of the sin, not its smallness. The psalmist appeals to God's name, his reputation for mercy, rather than to any excuse.

insights.title: The Advent psalm
insights.body: In the Latin church this psalm's first verse, Ad te levavi, has been the opening chant of the First Sunday of Advent for centuries, beginning the church year. In some Jewish rites it is recited in the daily prayers of supplication.

insights.title: Teach me
insights.body: The psalmist asks to be taught God's ways five times while also asking forgiveness (25:4-5, 25:8-12). Why might learning and being forgiven belong together?

26.summary: The psalmist asks Yahweh to examine him, declares that he has walked in integrity and kept away from evildoers, and expresses his love for God's house.
26.lookfor: Look for the claims of integrity at the start and end, the washing of hands, and the love for the place where God's glory dwells.

insights.title: Seeking a verdict
insights.body: Like Psalms 7 and 17, this is the prayer of someone who believes he is falsely accused and asks God to judge (26:1). He invites God to test him thoroughly (26:2). The setting is the temple, where such cases might be brought before God.

insights.title: Examine, prove, try
insights.body: The three verbs in verse 2 come from testing metals and assaying their purity. "My heart and my mind" is literally my kidneys and my heart, the inner self. The psalmist welcomes a refining process.

insights.title: Washing the hands
insights.body: "I will wash my hands in innocence" (26:6) recalls rituals in which washing declared innocence of bloodshed, like the elders washing over the heifer in Deuteronomy. Pilate's hand-washing at Jesus' trial draws on the same symbol. In the traditional Latin Mass, the priest recited these verses while washing his hands.

insights.title: Where your glory dwells
insights.body: "The place where your glory dwells" (26:8) recalls the glory cloud filling the tabernacle and the temple. Later Jewish tradition used the word Shekinah for God's dwelling presence. The psalmist's love is for God's presence more than for the building.

insights.title: Not sitting with the wicked
insights.body: "I have not sat with deceitful men... and will not sit with the wicked" (26:4-5) echoes the opening of the Psalter, where the blessed person does not sit in the seat of scoffers.

insights.title: Bribes in the right hand
insights.body: The bloodthirsty have "their right hand... full of bribes" (26:10). Bribery of judges was a constant problem in the ancient world, and Israel's law and prophets condemn it repeatedly. The psalmist asks not to share their fate.

insights.title: Integrity and mercy
insights.body: The psalmist claims to walk in integrity, yet in the same breath asks God to redeem him and be merciful (26:11). How do claiming integrity and asking for mercy fit together?

27.summary: A confident song of trust in Yahweh, the psalmist's light and salvation, gives way to an urgent plea not to be forsaken, and ends with a call to wait for Yahweh.
27.lookfor: Compare the confident first half with the pleading second half, and notice the theme of seeking God's face.

insights.title: Two moods
insights.body: Verses 1–6 are full of confidence; verses 7–14 are an urgent plea. Some scholars think two psalms were joined; others see a single prayer that moves honestly between trust and fear. The final verse holds them together with "Wait for Yahweh" (27:14).

insights.title: One thing
insights.body: "One thing I have asked of Yahweh" (27:4) is to dwell in God's house and see his beauty. Jesus tells Martha that one thing is needed, and Mary has chosen it by sitting at his feet. Paul too speaks of the one thing he does.

insights.title: Hidden in his shelter
insights.body: "He will keep me secretly in his pavilion" (27:5) uses sukkah, the word for the booths Israel lived in at the Feast of Tabernacles. Jewish custom recites Psalm 27 daily from the month before the New Year until the end of that feast. The tent and the rock (27:5) are pictures of safe hiding.

insights.title: Seek my face
insights.body: "When you said, 'Seek my face,' my heart said to you, 'I will seek your face, Yahweh'" (27:8). The heart echoes back God's own invitation. To seek a king's face was to seek an audience; to seek God's face was to come to worship.

insights.title: Father and mother
insights.body: "When my father and my mother forsake me, then Yahweh will take me up" (27:10) may describe real abandonment or simply the worst imaginable loneliness. In a culture built on family loyalty, being forsaken by parents meant losing all protection. God takes up the abandoned like an adopting parent.

insights.title: False witnesses
insights.body: "False witnesses have risen up against me" (27:12) points to a legal threat. Israel's law required two or three witnesses and punished false witnesses with the penalty they sought for the accused.

insights.title: The land of the living
insights.body: "I will see the goodness of Yahweh in the land of the living" (27:13) means in this life, before going down to the grave. The psalmist expects to see God's goodness now, not only after death.

insights.title: Waiting with courage
insights.body: The psalm ends by connecting waiting with being strong and courageous (27:14). Why might waiting require more courage than acting?

28.summary: The psalmist cries for Yahweh not to be silent and not to count him with hypocrites, then blesses Yahweh for hearing and prays for the king and the people.
28.lookfor: Watch for the lifted hands toward the sanctuary, the sudden blessing in verse 6, and the final prayer for God's people.

insights.title: Hands toward the holy place
insights.body: "When I lift up my hands toward your Most Holy Place" (28:2) describes a common posture of prayer, with open hands raised. The Most Holy Place, at the back of the temple, held the ark. Solomon prayed with his hands spread out toward heaven, and Paul speaks of lifting holy hands.

insights.title: The pit
insights.body: "Those who go down into the pit" (28:1) is a common phrase for the dead. The pit (bor) was a cistern or dungeon, a fitting image for the grave. If God stays silent, the psalmist feels as good as dead.

insights.title: Peace on their lips
insights.body: The wicked "speak peace with their neighbors, but mischief is in their hearts" (28:3). The psalmist's fear is to be swept away with hypocrites. Jeremiah describes the same deceit.

insights.title: The turn to praise
insights.body: The prayer suddenly becomes "Blessed be Yahweh, because he has heard the voice of my petitions" (28:6). The same phrase, "the voice of my petitions", appears in verse 2 as a plea and in verse 6 as answered. Many laments turn this way, perhaps after a word of assurance in worship.

insights.title: From one to all
insights.body: The psalm ends praying for the king, Yahweh's anointed (28:8), and for the whole people (28:9). Personal prayer opens out into prayer for the community. The last verse was taken into the ancient Christian hymn Te Deum.

insights.title: Carried like sheep
insights.body: "Be their shepherd also, and bear them up forever" (28:9) pictures a shepherd lifting and carrying weak sheep. Isaiah uses the same image of God carrying lambs in his arms.

insights.title: Fear of God's silence
insights.body: For the psalmist, God's silence is more frightening than the enemies (28:1). Why might silence from God be so hard to bear, and what does the psalm do with it?

29.summary: Heavenly beings are called to praise Yahweh as his thundering voice sweeps across the sea, the mountains and the wilderness, and he sits enthroned as King forever.
29.lookfor: Count how many times "Yahweh's voice" appears, follow the storm as it moves across the land, and notice the quiet blessing at the end.

names.name: Lebanon
names.gloss: The mountain range north of Israel, famous for its great cedar forests.

names.name: Sirion
names.gloss: The Sidonian name for Mount Hermon, the high snow-capped mountain at Israel's northern edge.

names.name: Kadesh
names.gloss: A wilderness; either Kadesh in the southern desert or the region of Kadesh in Syria.

insights.title: Claiming the storm
insights.body: Many scholars believe Psalm 29 adapts the style of Canaanite hymns to Baal, the storm god, whose voice was thunder. Its repetitions closely resemble poems found at Ugarit in Syria. The psalm gives all that power to Yahweh alone.

insights.title: The sevenfold voice
insights.body: "Yahweh's voice" appears seven times, like seven claps of thunder (29:3-9). Some later Christian writers linked this to the seven thunders of Revelation. The voice moves from the waters to the cedars, to the northern mountains, to the southern wilderness.

insights.title: Sons of the mighty
insights.body: "You sons of the mighty" (29:1) translates bene elim, heavenly beings or angels. The psalm begins in heaven, with God's court called to give him glory, before the storm breaks on earth.

insights.title: Lebanon skipping
insights.body: Lebanon and Sirion skip "like a young, wild ox" (29:6), mountains shaking under the storm. Sirion is the Sidonian name for Mount Hermon. Even the greatest cedars, the most impressive trees of the ancient world, are shattered (29:5).

insights.title: Enthroned at the Flood
insights.body: "Yahweh sat enthroned at the Flood" (29:10) uses mabbul, a word found elsewhere only in the story of Noah's flood. The God who rules the storm also ruled over the greatest flood. His throne is above all chaos.

insights.title: Sung on the Sabbath
insights.body: In the synagogue, Psalm 29 is sung on the Sabbath as the Torah scroll is returned to the ark, and it is part of the Friday evening service welcoming the Sabbath. Its seven voices were linked by the rabbis with seven blessings in the Sabbath prayer.

insights.title: Storm then peace
insights.body: After all the thunder, the last word is "peace" (29:11). The power displayed in the storm becomes strength given to God's people. The same God who shakes the wilderness blesses with shalom.

insights.title: Glory!
insights.body: "In his temple everything says, 'Glory!'" (29:9). Where do people today sense God's power in nature, and how might that move them to worship rather than fear alone?

30.summary: The psalmist thanks Yahweh for healing him from near death, admits he had grown complacent in prosperity, and celebrates how God turned mourning into dancing.
30.lookfor: Notice the contrast between a moment and a lifetime, night and morning, and the words the psalmist used when he was overconfident.

names.name: Sheol
names.gloss: The realm of the dead.

insights.title: A dedication song
insights.body: The title calls this a song for the dedication of the temple, though the psalm itself is a personal thanksgiving for healing. It may have been reused at a dedication, perhaps of the second temple or at the rededication in 164 BC. Jews read it at Hanukkah, and many recite it daily in the morning service.

insights.title: Weeping stays the night
insights.body: "Weeping may stay for the night, but joy comes in the morning" (30:5). The verb for stay means to lodge, like a traveller who stays one night and moves on. Grief is pictured as a guest, not a permanent resident.

insights.title: I shall never be moved
insights.body: "I said in my prosperity, 'I shall never be moved'" (30:6) is a confession of complacency. The same words are boasted by the wicked in Psalm 10. When God hid his face, the psalmist discovered his security had come from God all along (30:7).

insights.title: Arguing with God
insights.body: "Shall the dust praise you?" (30:9) is a bold argument: if the psalmist dies, God loses a voice of praise. Such reasoning appears in other psalms and in Hezekiah's prayer, and it reflects an Old Testament view of Sheol as a place of silence.

insights.title: Sackcloth and dancing
insights.body: Mourners wore sackcloth, a coarse fabric often made of goat hair, while celebrations included dancing. "You have removed my sackcloth, and clothed me with gladness" (30:11) describes a change of clothes as well as mood.

insights.title: A moment and a lifetime
insights.body: "His anger is but for a moment. His favor is for a lifetime" (30:5) sets out a proportion found elsewhere: Isaiah speaks of a brief moment of abandonment and great compassion, and Paul of light momentary affliction and an eternal weight of glory.

insights.title: Not silent
insights.body: The healed psalmist's purpose is that his heart may sing and "not be silent" (30:12). What happens to gratitude that is never spoken aloud?

31.summary: Surrounded by plots, slander and grief, the psalmist commits his spirit into Yahweh's hand, trusts that his times are in God's hands, and calls others to take courage.
31.lookfor: Look for the famous words of commitment in verse 5, the description of being forgotten like a dead man, and the movement between plea and praise.

names.name: Sheol
names.gloss: The realm of the dead.

insights.title: Into your hand
insights.body: "Into your hand I commend my spirit" (31:5) were Jesus' last words on the cross in Luke, with "Father" added. Stephen echoed them as he was stoned. The verse is also used in Jewish bedtime prayer and in Christian night prayer, entrusting oneself to God before sleep.

insights.title: Terror on every side
insights.body: "Terror on every side" (31:13) is a phrase Jeremiah used repeatedly; his enemies even mocked him with it as a nickname. It captures the feeling of being surrounded by whispers and threats.

insights.title: Like broken pottery
insights.body: "I am forgotten from their hearts like a dead man. I am like broken pottery" (31:12). Broken pots were thrown away; the hills of ancient cities are full of their shards. The psalmist feels useless and discarded, even by his neighbours (31:11).

insights.title: My times are in your hand
insights.body: "My times are in your hand" (31:15) means the whole course of life, its seasons and its end, belongs to God. The same word "hand" runs through the psalm: the enemy's hand (31:8, 31:15) and God's hand (31:5, 31:15).

insights.title: Lying vanities
insights.body: "Those who regard lying vanities" (31:6) refers to idols, worthless gods. Jonah uses almost the same phrase in his prayer from the fish.

insights.title: Said in haste
insights.body: "I said in my haste, 'I am cut off from before your eyes'" (31:22). The psalmist admits that in panic he concluded God had abandoned him. He tells this so others can take courage (31:24).

insights.title: A strong city
insights.body: "He has shown me his marvelous loving kindness in a strong city" (31:21) may describe a besieged city or be a picture of protection. Walled cities were the safest places in war. For the psalmist, God's presence is the true fortified city.

insights.title: Commending one's spirit
insights.body: Jesus prayed this psalm at his death, and many believers pray it every night. What might it change to entrust oneself to God at the end of each day as practice for the end of life?

32.summary: The psalmist describes the joy of being forgiven after a time of hiding his sin, when guilt wasted his body, and urges others to come to God rather than be stubborn.
32.lookfor: Notice the different words for sin, the description of what silence did to him, and the voice that offers to teach in verse 8.

insights.title: Three words for sin
insights.body: The opening verses use three Hebrew words: pesha, rebellion or disobedience; chata'ah, sin as missing the mark; and avon, iniquity, a twisting or guilt. Matching them are three ways God deals with sin: forgiven, covered, not imputed (32:1-2). Verse 5 uses all three again.

insights.title: Paul and David
insights.body: Paul quotes verses 1–2 in Romans 4 as David's testimony to the blessing of the person to whom God counts righteousness apart from works. It is one of Paul's key Old Testament witnesses for justification by faith.

insights.title: The cost of silence
insights.body: "When I kept silence, my bones wasted away" (32:3). Unconfessed guilt is described as physical sickness, like strength drying up in summer heat (32:4). Confession brings release at once (32:5).

insights.title: A maskil
insights.body: The title calls this a contemplative psalm, translating maskil, a term used for thirteen psalms. It probably means a skilful or instructive song. Fittingly, the psalm goes on to teach: "I will instruct you" (32:8) uses the same root.

insights.title: Who is speaking?
insights.body: Verse 8, "I will instruct you and teach you", may be God speaking or the forgiven psalmist teaching others. Either way, the person who has experienced forgiveness now passes on what was learned.

insights.title: Horse and mule
insights.body: "Don't be like the horse, or like the mule" (32:9), which need bit and bridle to be brought near. Animals that could not be reasoned with had to be controlled by force. God desires people who come willingly.

insights.title: Augustine's wall
insights.body: Psalm 32 is the second of the seven penitential psalms. Augustine's friend and biographer Possidius records that in his last illness Augustine had the penitential psalms copied and fixed to the wall so he could read them from his bed.

insights.title: Why we hide
insights.body: The psalmist kept silent about his sin until it made him ill (32:3-4). Why do people often delay confessing, even when it costs them so much?

33.summary: A new song calls the righteous to praise Yahweh, whose word created the heavens, whose plans stand forever, and whose watchful eye, not armies or horses, keeps his people safe.
33.lookfor: Look for creation by word and breath, the contrast between the plans of nations and the plans of Yahweh, and the uselessness of horses.

insights.title: A psalm without a title
insights.body: Psalm 33 is one of few psalms in the first book with no title. Its first line picks up the last line of Psalm 32, calling the righteous to rejoice, so some think they were once read together. It has 22 verses, the number of letters in the Hebrew alphabet, but is not an acrostic.

insights.title: A new song
insights.body: "Sing to him a new song" (33:3) is the first of several calls to a new song in the Psalms. It means fresh praise for fresh acts of God. Revelation pictures the redeemed singing a new song to the Lamb.

insights.title: Created by word
insights.body: "By Yahweh's word, the heavens were made" (33:6) and "he spoke, and it was done" (33:9) summarise Genesis 1, where God speaks and things come to be. The word for breath, ruach, also means Spirit. Christians have connected this with John's prologue about the Word.

insights.title: Waters in a heap
insights.body: "He gathers the waters of the sea together as a heap" (33:7) uses a rare word found in the Song of the Sea, where the waters stood up as a heap at the Red Sea. Creation and exodus are joined in one image of God's control over the waters.

insights.title: Lyre and ten-stringed harp
insights.body: The lyre (kinnor) was a hand-held stringed instrument, David's instrument. The harp (nevel) of ten strings was probably larger, perhaps with a sound box. Temple worship was loud and skilful (33:3).

insights.title: No king saved by an army
