insights.body: The procession of tribes, led by little Benjamin (68:27), is followed by kings bringing presents and Ethiopia stretching out her hands to God (68:29-31). Acts tells of an Ethiopian official reading Isaiah on the road home from worship in Jerusalem.

insights.title: Daily burdens
insights.body: "Blessed be the Lord, who daily bears our burdens" (68:19) sits in the middle of a triumph song. What does it say that the God of great victories also carries ordinary daily loads?

69.summary: Sinking in deep waters and hated for his zeal for God, the psalmist cries for rescue, calls down judgment on his tormentors, and ends trusting that God will rebuild Zion.
69.lookfor: Watch the images of drowning and mire, the reasons the psalmist is mocked, the gall and vinegar, and the turn to praise at the end.

names.name: Zion
names.gloss: Jerusalem, which God will save.

insights.title: Quoted again and again
insights.body: Psalm 69 is one of the psalms most quoted in the New Testament. Its suffering speaker, mocked for loyalty to God, became a picture of Jesus' passion. The Gospels, Acts and Romans all draw on it.

insights.title: Waters to the neck
insights.body: "The waters have come up to my neck" (69:1) and "I sink in deep mire" (69:2) picture drowning in a muddy pit. Some have linked the psalm with Jeremiah, who was lowered into a cistern and sank in the mud.

insights.title: Zeal for your house
insights.body: "The zeal of your house consumes me" (69:9). John says the disciples remembered this verse when Jesus drove the traders out of the temple. Paul quotes the second half, about bearing others' reproaches, of Christ.

insights.title: Gall and vinegar
insights.body: "They also gave me gall for my food. In my thirst, they gave me vinegar to drink" (69:21). The Gospels describe Jesus being offered wine mixed with gall and later sour wine on the cross. Gall was a bitter, possibly poisonous plant.

insights.title: Restoring what he didn't take
insights.body: "I have to restore what I didn't take away" (69:4) describes being forced to pay back a theft he did not commit. The psalmist suffers not only hatred but injustice, and also admits his own foolishness (69:5).

insights.title: Harsh curses
insights.body: The psalmist prays that his enemies' table become a trap and their homes desolate (69:22-25). Paul applies verses 22–23 to Israel's hardening, and Acts applies verse 25 to Judas. These curses are among the hardest lines in the Psalter.

insights.title: The book of life
insights.body: "Let them be blotted out of the book of life" (69:28) uses the picture of God's register of the living. Moses asked to be blotted out of God's book for Israel's sake. Revelation speaks of names that will never be blotted out.

insights.title: Pain and praise
insights.body: "But I am in pain and distress" (69:29) is followed at once by praise that pleases God "better than an ox" (69:30-31). How can praise come from someone still in pain?

70.summary: A short, urgent cry for God to hurry to help, to shame those who seek the psalmist's life, and to gladden all who seek him.
70.lookfor: Compare this psalm with the end of Psalm 40 and notice how short and urgent it is.

insights.title: From Psalm 40
insights.body: Psalm 70 is almost identical to Psalm 40:13-17, mostly with God where Psalm 40 has Yahweh. Here it stands alone as a short prayer for quick help, without the thanksgiving that came before it in Psalm 40.

insights.title: More urgent
insights.body: Psalm 40 ended "May the Lord think about me", but Psalm 70 says "Come to me quickly, God" (70:5). The small change makes the prayer even more pressing. It begins and ends with hurry (70:1, 70:5).

insights.title: The opening of daily prayer
insights.body: For centuries Christian monastic prayer has begun each service with this psalm's first verse, O God, come to my assistance; O Lord, make haste to help me. The 5th-century monk John Cassian recommended repeating it constantly as a prayer for every situation.

insights.title: A reminder
insights.body: The title calls it a reminder, the same word in the title of Psalm 38. It may mean a prayer to bring the speaker to God's remembrance, or a psalm used with the memorial portion of an offering.

insights.title: Two groups
insights.body: Those who say "Aha! Aha!" (70:3) are contrasted with those who seek God and say "Let God be exalted!" (70:4). Each group is known by what it says. The psalmist places himself among the poor and needy (70:5).

insights.title: Short prayers
insights.body: Psalm 70 is only five verses long. What place do brief, urgent prayers have alongside longer, reflective ones?

71.summary: An old person who has trusted God since birth asks not to be abandoned in old age, and promises to tell the next generation of God's righteousness and power.
71.lookfor: Notice the references to youth, birth and old age, the enemies who say God has forsaken him, and the resolve to keep praising.

insights.title: A prayer for old age
insights.body: "Don't reject me in my old age. Don't forsake me when my strength fails" (71:9). The psalmist looks back on a life of trust from the womb (71:6) and forward to grey hair (71:18). It is one of the few biblical prayers specifically about ageing.

insights.title: Built from other psalms
insights.body: The opening verses repeat Psalm 31:1-3 almost word for word, and other lines echo Psalms 22, 35 and 40. The psalmist prays in the words of earlier prayers learned over a lifetime. Psalm 71 has no title and may continue Psalm 70.

insights.title: A marvel to many
insights.body: "I am a marvel to many" (71:7) uses mophet, a sign or portent. People may see the psalmist's long suffering as a warning sign of God's judgment, or as a wonder of survival. Either way, his life is on display.

insights.title: God has forsaken him
insights.body: The enemies say "God has forsaken him. Pursue and take him" (71:11). They read weakness and age as signs that God has left. The psalmist answers by asking God to come near quickly (71:12).

insights.title: To the next generation
insights.body: The reason to stay alive is "until I have declared your strength to the next generation" (71:18). Passing on faith to the young is a recurring duty in the Psalms. The older believer's story becomes the next generation's inheritance.

insights.title: Holy One of Israel
insights.body: "Holy One of Israel" (71:22) is the favourite title for God in Isaiah, where it appears about 25 times. In the Psalms it appears only here and in Psalms 78 and 89. It combines God's separateness with his commitment to Israel.

insights.title: Faith over a lifetime
insights.body: The psalmist says God has taught him "from my youth" (71:17). What does long faithfulness look like when strength is fading and the troubles have been "many and bitter" (71:20)?

72.summary: A prayer for the king to rule with God's justice, defend the poor, and reign over all nations with lasting peace and blessing; it closes Book 2 and the prayers of David.
72.lookfor: Look for the king's care for the poor and needy, the images of rain and harvest, the kings bringing gifts, and the closing note about David's prayers.

names.name: Tarshish
names.gloss: A distant port in the far west, probably in Spain.

names.name: Sheba
names.gloss: A rich kingdom in south-west Arabia, famous for gold and spices.

names.name: Seba
names.gloss: A distant land, probably in Africa, perhaps near Cush.

names.name: Lebanon
names.gloss: The mountains north of Israel, known for their tall cedars.

insights.title: For Solomon
insights.body: The title can mean by Solomon or for Solomon, and verse 20 attributes the collection to David. It may be David's prayer for his son, or a prayer used at the coronation of any king of David's line. Solomon's own request was for wisdom to judge.

insights.title: Justice for the poor first
insights.body: Before wealth or conquest, the psalm asks that the king defend the poor, save the needy and crush the oppressor (72:2, 72:4, 72:12-14). "Their blood will be precious in his sight" (72:14). The king's greatness is measured by how he treats the weakest.

insights.title: Rain on mown grass
insights.body: "He will come down like rain on the mown grass" (72:6). After a first cutting, rain makes the grass grow again. A just king is like rain: he brings life to the land. David's last words use a similar image.

insights.title: Kings bringing gifts
insights.body: "The kings of Sheba and Seba shall offer gifts" (72:10). The queen of Sheba brought gold and spices to Solomon. Christians have read this verse alongside the Magi's gifts to the infant Jesus, and it is sung at Epiphany.

insights.title: From sea to sea
insights.body: "He shall have dominion also from sea to sea, from the River to the ends of the earth" (72:8). The River is the Euphrates. Zechariah repeats the line for the humble king who comes riding on a donkey.

insights.title: Blessed through him
insights.body: "Men shall be blessed by him. All nations will call him blessed" (72:17) echoes God's promise to Abraham that all nations would be blessed through his offspring. The king becomes the channel of Abraham's blessing.

insights.title: End of Book 2
insights.body: A doxology closes the second book (72:18-19), followed by a note: "This ends the prayers by David, the son of Jesse" (72:20). Since more David psalms come later, the note probably marks the end of an earlier collection. The Targum read the king of this psalm as the Messiah.

insights.title: No king like this
insights.body: No king of Israel fully lived up to this prayer. How did that gap between ideal and reality shape the hope for a coming Messiah?

73.summary: Asaph admits he nearly lost his faith envying the carefree wicked, until in God's sanctuary he saw their end and discovered that God himself was his true good.
73.lookfor: Notice the opening statement, the long description of the wicked, the turning point in the sanctuary, and the confession of closeness to God at the end.

insights.title: Book 3 begins
insights.body: Psalm 73 opens the third book of the Psalter, mostly psalms of Asaph and the sons of Korah. Book 3 is the darkest part of the collection, with laments over the temple's destruction, and ends with the apparent failure of God's covenant with David in Psalm 89. Psalm 73 sets the tone by facing hard questions honestly.

insights.title: The prosperity of the wicked
insights.body: The psalmist confesses he was envious when he saw the arrogant thrive, healthy, rich and untroubled (73:3-12). Job and Jeremiah ask the same question. The psalm begins with the right answer, "Surely God is good" (73:1), but shows how hard it was to keep believing it.

insights.title: Not betraying the children
insights.body: "If I had said, 'I will speak thus'; behold, I would have betrayed the generation of your children" (73:15). The psalmist kept his doubts from spreading because of responsibility to the community. He wrestled honestly but carefully.

insights.title: Until I entered the sanctuary
insights.body: The turning point comes "Until I entered God's sanctuary, and considered their latter end" (73:17). Nothing outward changed; the psalmist's perspective did, through worship. He saw the wicked standing on slippery ground (73:18).

insights.title: Received to glory
insights.body: "You will guide me with your counsel, and afterward receive me to glory" (73:24) uses the same verb, take or receive, used of Enoch and in Psalm 49:15. Many readers find here a hope of life with God beyond death, though some take glory to mean honour in this life.

insights.title: Whom do I have in heaven?
insights.body: "Whom do I have in heaven? There is no one on earth whom I desire besides you" (73:25). The psalmist's reward is not the wealth he envied but God himself, his "portion forever" (73:26), the inheritance once given to the Levites. Paul says he counts everything loss compared with knowing Christ.

insights.title: Good to come close
insights.body: The psalm ends: "it is good for me to come close to God" (73:28). The opening said God is good to Israel; the ending says nearness to God is good for me. How is this second statement different from the first?

74.summary: The community laments that enemies have smashed and burned God's sanctuary, recalls God's ancient power over the sea and creation, and begs him to remember his covenant and rise up.
74.lookfor: Notice the eyewitness description of the destruction, the hymn about God's victory over sea monsters, and the repeated calls to remember.

names.name: Zion
names.gloss: Jerusalem's temple hill, where God lived.

insights.title: The temple in ruins
insights.body: Psalm 74 describes enemies smashing the sanctuary's carvings and burning it to the ground (74:6-7). Most scholars link it with the Babylonian destruction of the temple in 586 BC. Lamentations mourns the same catastrophe.

insights.title: Axes in the carved work
insights.body: The enemy hacked at the sanctuary "like men wielding axes, cutting through a thicket" (74:5). Solomon's temple was lined with cedar carved with cherubim, palm trees and flowers, overlaid with gold. The destruction of such work felt like an attack on God himself.

insights.title: No prophet
insights.body: "There is no longer any prophet, neither is there among us anyone who knows how long" (74:9). Silence from God added to the pain. Lamentations also says the prophets found no vision.

insights.title: Leviathan's heads
insights.body: "You broke the heads of Leviathan in pieces" (74:14). Canaanite poems from Ugarit describe a many-headed sea serpent, Lotan, defeated by Baal. The psalm uses this imagery to praise God's victory over chaos at creation and at the Red Sea (74:13). Isaiah and Revelation use the same picture.

insights.title: Creator of day and night
insights.body: In the middle of disaster the psalm remembers that day and night, sun, boundaries and seasons belong to God (74:16-17). The God who ordered creation is asked to restore order to his people. Jeremiah links God's fixed order of day and night with his faithfulness to his covenant.

insights.title: Your dove
insights.body: "Don't deliver the soul of your dove to wild beasts" (74:19) pictures Israel as a turtledove, small and defenceless. Hosea and the Song of Solomon also use the dove for God's people or beloved.

insights.title: Plead your own cause
insights.body: "Arise, God! Plead your own cause" (74:22). The psalm argues that God's own name is at stake in his people's suffering. How does seeing a disaster as an insult to God change the way one prays about it?

75.summary: The community gives thanks, and God speaks, promising to judge at the right time, warning the arrogant not to raise their horns, and holding out a cup of judgment for the wicked.
75.lookfor: Listen for where God speaks, the images of horns and of a cup, and who it is that lifts up and puts down.

insights.title: God speaks
insights.body: After the opening thanksgiving, God himself speaks: "When I choose the appointed time, I will judge blamelessly" (75:2). He holds the earth's pillars steady even when it shakes (75:3). The psalm gives a prophetic answer to the fear that injustice will go on forever.

insights.title: Lifting the horn
insights.body: "Don't lift up the horn" (75:4-5) uses the image of a wild bull raising its horns in strength and pride. To lift the horn is to boast in one's power. At the end, God cuts off the horns of the wicked and raises those of the righteous (75:10).

insights.title: He puts down, he lifts up
insights.body: "God is the judge. He puts down one, and lifts up another" (75:7) echoes Hannah's song. Mary's song in Luke says God has put down princes from their thrones and exalted the lowly.

insights.title: The cup of foaming wine
insights.body: "In Yahweh's hand there is a cup, full of foaming wine mixed with spices" (75:8). Mixed wine was stronger. The wicked must drink it down to the dregs. The prophets and Revelation use the same image of a cup of God's wrath.

insights.title: Not from east or west
insights.body: "Neither from the east, nor from the west, nor yet from the south, comes exaltation" (75:6). The north is not named, possibly because it was associated with God's own mountain. Promotion comes from no human direction, only from God.

insights.title: Your name is near
insights.body: "We give thanks, for your Name is near" (75:1). God's name stands for his presence. The thanksgiving rests on the conviction that God is not far off, even when judgment seems delayed.

insights.title: The appointed time
insights.body: God says he will judge "When I choose the appointed time" (75:2). How does trust in God's timing affect the way people wait for justice?

76.summary: A song of Zion praises God, who broke the weapons of the enemy at his dwelling place in Salem and rose to judge and save the afflicted of the earth.
76.lookfor: Notice the name Salem, the broken weapons and sleeping warriors, and the call to bring gifts to God.

names.name: Salem
names.gloss: An ancient name for Jerusalem, the city of Melchizedek.

names.name: Zion
names.gloss: Jerusalem's temple hill.

insights.title: Salem
insights.body: "His tabernacle is also in Salem" (76:2) uses the ancient name of Jerusalem, the city where Melchizedek was king and priest. Salem sounds like shalom, peace. Hebrews reflects on Melchizedek as king of Salem, king of peace.

insights.title: A lion's lair
insights.body: The words for God's tabernacle and dwelling (76:2) can also mean a lion's thicket and den. Many scholars think the psalm pictures God as a lion in his lair on Zion, which fits "mountains of game" (76:4). The poem is fierce as well as glorious.

insights.title: Concerning the Assyrian
insights.body: The Greek translation's title adds that the psalm concerns the Assyrian. Many readers have linked it with the sudden end of Sennacherib's siege of Jerusalem in 701 BC, when soldiers were found dead in the morning (76:5-6).

insights.title: Chariot and horse asleep
insights.body: "Both chariot and horse are cast into a dead sleep" (76:6). God defeats the enemy with a word of rebuke. The scene recalls the Red Sea, where horse and rider were thrown into the sea.

insights.title: The wrath of man praises you
insights.body: "Surely the wrath of man praises you" (76:10) is a hard line. It seems to say that even human rage ends up serving God's glory. Joseph told his brothers that what they meant for evil, God meant for good.

insights.title: Judgment that saves
insights.body: God rises to judgment "to save all the afflicted ones of the earth" (76:9). His judgment is not only punishment but rescue for the oppressed. The psalm moves from Jerusalem to the whole earth.

insights.title: Silent earth
insights.body: "The earth feared, and was silent" (76:8) when God judged. When might silence be the right response to God?

77.summary: In a sleepless night of trouble, Asaph asks whether God has forgotten to be gracious, then chooses to remember God's wonders, above all his leading of Israel through the sea.
77.lookfor: Notice the six anguished questions, the shift from "I" to "you" after verse 10, and the storm at the Red Sea.

insights.title: Six questions
insights.body: In verses 7–9 the psalmist asks six questions: will God reject forever, be favourable no more, has his loving kindness vanished, his promise failed, has he forgotten to be gracious, withheld compassion? Each challenges something God revealed about himself at Sinai.

insights.title: The years of the right hand
insights.body: Verse 10 is difficult. WEB reads "the years of the right hand of the Most High". It can also be translated this is my grief, that the right hand of the Most High has changed. Either the psalmist names his deepest pain, or he resolves to remember God's past years of power.

insights.title: From I to you
insights.body: The first half of the psalm is full of "I" and "my" (77:1-10). From verse 11 the focus shifts to God's deeds: "your wonders", "your work", "your way". Remembering God's acts turns the psalmist's attention outward.

insights.title: The waters saw you
insights.body: "The waters saw you, God... and they writhed" (77:16) retells the crossing of the sea as a storm with thunder, lightning and earthquake. Habakkuk's prayer pictures the same scene in similar language.

insights.title: Unseen footprints
insights.body: "Your way was through the sea... Your footsteps were not known" (77:19). God's path went through the water, and the waters closed over his tracks. His presence was real even when it left no visible trace.

insights.title: Sleepless nights
insights.body: "You hold my eyelids open" (77:4) describes insomnia caused by anxiety. The night was when the psalmist remembered his songs (77:6). Many psalms are prayers of the night watches.

insights.title: Remembering as a choice
insights.body: "I will remember Yah's deeds" (77:11) is a decision, not a feeling. How can remembering what God has done help when present experience seems to say he has forgotten?

78.summary: A long teaching poem retells Israel's history from Egypt to David, showing the people's repeated forgetting and rebellion, and God's repeated mercy, so the next generation will trust him.
78.lookfor: Watch the cycle of God's wonders, the people's forgetfulness, God's anger and his mercy, and how the story ends with Zion and David.

names.name: Zoan
names.gloss: An Egyptian city in the Nile delta, known to the Greeks as Tanis.

names.name: Ham
names.gloss: Noah's son, ancestor of the Egyptians; a poetic name for Egypt.

names.name: Shiloh
names.gloss: The town in Ephraim where the tabernacle stood before David's time.

names.name: Ephraim
names.gloss: The leading northern tribe, often a name for the northern kingdom.

insights.title: History as teaching
insights.body: With 72 verses this is the second longest psalm. It calls itself a teaching (78:1) and aims to pass on God's deeds so that the next generation will "set their hope in God" (78:7) and not be like their stubborn ancestors. Remembering is the cure for forgetting.

insights.title: Speaking in parables
insights.body: "I will open my mouth in a parable" (78:2). Matthew quotes this verse to explain Jesus' teaching in parables, calling Asaph a prophet. Chronicles calls Asaph a seer.

insights.title: Bread of angels
insights.body: Manna is called "the bread of angels" (78:25), literally bread of the mighty ones. Jesus' hearers quote this psalm's description of bread from heaven, and Jesus answers that he is the true bread from heaven.

insights.title: A different plague list
insights.body: The psalm lists the plagues of Egypt (78:44-51) but not in the order of Exodus and not all of them: gnats, boils and darkness are missing. Psalm 105 has its own selection. The poets retold the story freely to make their point.

insights.title: Shiloh abandoned
insights.body: God "abandoned the tent of Shiloh" and gave "his glory into the adversary's hand" (78:60-61), recalling the capture of the ark by the Philistines. Jeremiah later warned Jerusalem to go and look at Shiloh.

insights.title: Remembering they were flesh
insights.body: "He remembered that they were but flesh, a wind that passes away" (78:39). God's mercy is rooted in knowing human frailty. Psalm 103 says he remembers that we are dust.

insights.title: From sheepfold to throne
insights.body: The psalm ends with God rejecting Ephraim and choosing Judah, Zion and David, whom he "took... from the sheepfolds" (78:70) to shepherd his people. It explains why Jerusalem, not the northern sanctuaries, became the centre of worship.

insights.title: A daring image
insights.body: "Then the Lord awakened as one out of sleep, like a mighty man who shouts by reason of wine" (78:65). Why might the poet use such a bold, almost shocking picture for God's sudden action?

79.summary: After the nations destroy Jerusalem and leave the dead unburied, the community asks how long God will be angry, pleads for forgiveness, and calls for justice for the slain.
79.lookfor: Notice the scenes of desecration and unburied bodies, the plea not to be punished for ancestors' sins, and the concern for God's name among the nations.

insights.title: Jerusalem in heaps
insights.body: "They have laid Jerusalem in heaps" (79:1) echoes Micah's prophecy that Jerusalem would become heaps of ruins. Like Psalm 74, this lament most likely reflects the Babylonian conquest of 586 BC. The Jewish book of 1 Maccabees later quoted verses 2–3 about a massacre in its own time.

insights.title: No one to bury them
insights.body: Leaving the dead unburied, as food for birds and animals (79:2-3), was one of the worst disgraces in the ancient world. Proper burial was a sacred duty. Jeremiah warned this would happen to Jerusalem.

insights.title: Jeremiah's words
insights.body: Verses 6–7 are almost identical to Jeremiah 10:25: pour out your wrath on the nations that don't know you. Either the psalm and the prophet share a common prayer or one borrowed from the other.

insights.title: At the Passover door
insights.body: In the Passover Seder, when the door is opened for Elijah, many Jewish families recite verses 6–7, along with lines from Psalm 69 and Lamentations. The custom arose in the Middle Ages, a time of persecution.

insights.title: Not our fathers' sins
insights.body: "Don't hold the iniquities of our forefathers against us" (79:8). The survivors feel they are paying for previous generations. They also confess their own sins (79:9). Lamentations and Ezekiel wrestle with the same question.

insights.title: Into their bosom
insights.body: "Pay back to our neighbors seven times into their bosom" (79:12). The bosom was the fold of a robe used as a pocket, so to pay into the bosom was to pour into someone's lap. Jesus uses the same picture for generous measure poured into the lap.

insights.title: Where is their God?
insights.body: "Why should the nations say, 'Where is their God?'" (79:10). How should God's people think about their suffering when outsiders read it as proof that God is absent?

80.summary: The Shepherd of Israel is called to shine again on his people, pictured as a vine he brought out of Egypt and planted, now broken down and ravaged.
80.lookfor: Follow the refrain that returns three times, each time with a fuller name for God, and the long picture of the vine.

names.name: Joseph
names.gloss: Here the northern tribes descended from Joseph, especially Ephraim and Manasseh.

names.name: Ephraim
names.gloss: Joseph's younger son's tribe, the leading northern tribe.

names.name: Benjamin
names.gloss: The tribe descended from Rachel's younger son.

names.name: Manasseh
names.gloss: Joseph's elder son's tribe.

insights.title: A growing refrain
insights.body: The refrain "Turn us again... Cause your face to shine, and we will be saved" comes three times (80:3, 80:7, 80:19). Each time God's name grows: God, then God of Armies, then Yahweh God of Armies. The plea intensifies as the psalm goes on.

insights.title: The northern tribes
insights.body: The psalm names Joseph, Ephraim, Benjamin and Manasseh (80:1-2), the descendants of Rachel. In the wilderness these tribes camped together behind the tabernacle. Many link the psalm to the Assyrian destruction of the northern kingdom in 722 BC; the Greek title mentions the Assyrian.

insights.title: The vine from Egypt
insights.body: Israel is a vine God brought out of Egypt, planted and tended until it filled the land (80:8-11). Isaiah's song of the vineyard and Jesus' saying "I am the true vine" develop the same image.

insights.title: The boar from the forest
insights.body: "The boar out of the wood ravages it" (80:13). Wild boars could destroy a vineyard overnight, rooting up plants and trampling vines. Later Jewish interpreters read the boar as a symbol of Rome.

insights.title: The middle of the Psalter
insights.body: In the Hebrew text of verse 13, the letter ayin in the word for forest is written raised above the line. The Talmud explains that it marks the middle letter of the book of Psalms, a sign of how carefully scribes counted the text.

insights.title: Man of your right hand
insights.body: "Let your hand be on the man of your right hand, on the son of man whom you made strong" (80:17) probably refers to Israel's king. The phrase plays on Benjamin, whose name means son of the right hand. The Aramaic Targum read it of the Messiah, and Christians of Christ.

insights.title: Turn us again
insights.body: The people ask God to turn them back (80:3), not just to change their circumstances. What is the connection between being restored and being turned?

81.summary: A festival begins with music and trumpet, and then God speaks, recalling how he freed Israel from slavery and lamenting that his people would not listen to him.
81.lookfor: Notice the festival instructions, the sudden shift to God's voice, and the longing "Oh that my people would listen to me".

names.name: Joseph
names.gloss: Here a name for the people of Israel, descended from Jacob's son Joseph.

names.name: Meribah
names.gloss: The place in the wilderness where Israel quarrelled with God over water.

insights.title: New moon and full moon
insights.body: "Blow the trumpet at the New Moon, at the full moon, on our feast day" (81:3). The trumpet is the shofar. The seventh month began with a trumpet day at the new moon and reached the Feast of Tabernacles at the full moon. Jewish tradition uses this verse for the New Year, Rosh Hashanah, and the Mishnah makes it the temple's Thursday psalm.

insights.title: An unknown language
insights.body: "I heard a language that I didn't know" (81:5) is obscure. It may be the psalmist hearing God's voice in a new oracle, which then follows, or Israel hearing a foreign tongue in Egypt. Either way, what follows is God speaking.

insights.title: Freed from the basket
insights.body: "His hands were freed from the basket" (81:6) recalls the baskets used to carry clay and bricks in Egypt. Wall paintings from Egyptian tombs show slaves carrying bricks in baskets. God remembers the physical burden he lifted.

insights.title: The first commandment
insights.body: "There shall be no strange god in you... I am Yahweh, your God, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt" (81:9-10) echoes the opening of the Ten Commandments. The festival is a renewal of the covenant.

insights.title: Open wide
insights.body: "Open your mouth wide, and I will fill it" (81:10) pictures a baby bird with its beak open, waiting for food. God's generosity is limited only by his people's willingness to receive.

insights.title: Given over to their hearts
insights.body: "So I let them go after the stubbornness of their hearts" (81:12). God's judgment can mean letting people have what they insist on. Paul describes the same pattern in Romans 1.

insights.title: Honey from the rock
insights.body: The psalm ends with what might have been: the finest wheat and "honey out of the rock" (81:16), echoing Moses' song. God's disappointment is not anger only but grief at blessings refused.

insights.title: If only
insights.body: "Oh that my people would listen to me" (81:13) shows God longing. What does it suggest about God that he speaks of his people with such regret?

82.summary: God stands up in the divine council and condemns the "gods" who have judged unjustly and neglected the weak, declaring that they will die like mortals.
82.lookfor: Notice the courtroom setting, the list of duties toward the weak, and the verdict on the "gods".

insights.title: Who are the gods?
insights.body: "He judges among the gods" (82:1). Interpreters differ. Many modern scholars see the heavenly beings God set over the nations, who have failed. Many Jewish and Christian interpreters read it of human judges, who are sometimes called elohim because they judge on God's behalf.

insights.title: The divine council
insights.body: "God presides in the great assembly" (82:1). Ancient Near Eastern texts often describe a council of gods. The Bible uses this picture for God's heavenly court, as in Job and the vision of Micaiah, but here all the members are put on trial by the one true God.

insights.title: Duties to the weak
insights.body: The charge is specific: "Defend the weak, the poor, and the fatherless. Maintain the rights of the poor and oppressed" (82:3-4). The test of any power, human or heavenly, is how it treats the defenceless.

insights.title: Foundations shaken
insights.body: "All the foundations of the earth are shaken" (82:5). Injustice is not only a moral failure but a threat to the order of creation. When judges walk in darkness, the world itself becomes unstable.

insights.title: I said, you are gods
insights.body: Jesus quotes verse 6 when he is accused of blasphemy for calling himself the Son of God. He argues that if Scripture calls those to whom God's word came gods, he cannot be accused for claiming to be God's Son.

insights.title: Tuesday's psalm
insights.body: The Mishnah says the Levites sang Psalm 82 in the temple on the third day of the week. Its final cry, "Arise, God, judge the earth" (82:8), calls the true Judge to take over from those who have failed.

insights.title: Die like men
insights.body: "Nevertheless you shall die like men" (82:7). How might remembering that all power is temporary shape the way people in authority use it?

83.summary: As a coalition of neighbouring nations plots to wipe Israel off the map, Asaph asks God not to stay silent but to defeat them as in the days of the judges, so that they will know he alone is the Most High.
83.lookfor: Look for the list of ten enemy peoples, the memories from the book of Judges, and the purpose stated at the end.

names.name: Ishmaelites
names.gloss: Desert tribes descended from Abraham's son Ishmael.

names.name: Hagrites
names.gloss: A people east of the Jordan, perhaps linked to Hagar.

names.name: Gebal
names.gloss: Probably the Phoenician port of Byblos, north of Beirut.

names.name: Amalek
names.gloss: A nomadic people of the southern desert, Israel's old enemy.

names.name: Endor
names.gloss: A village near Mount Tabor, close to the site of Barak's battle.

names.name: Oreb
names.gloss: A Midianite prince killed by the Ephraimites in Gideon's time.

names.name: Zalmunna
names.gloss: A Midianite king captured and killed by Gideon, along with Zebah.

insights.title: A ring of enemies
insights.body: The psalm lists ten peoples allied against Israel: Edom, Ishmaelites, Moab, Hagrites, Gebal, Ammon, Amalek, Philistia, Tyre and Assyria (83:6-8). No known event matches the whole list. Some link it with the alliance against King Jehoshaphat; others see a poetic picture of encirclement.

insights.title: The children of Lot
insights.body: Assyria "helped the children of Lot" (83:8), meaning Moab and Ammon, who traced their descent from Abraham's nephew Lot. Many of these enemies were Israel's distant relatives.

insights.title: As in the days of the judges
insights.body: The psalm asks God to repeat his victories over Midian under Gideon and over Sisera and Jabin under Deborah and Barak (83:9-11). Oreb, Zeeb, Zebah and Zalmunna were Midianite leaders killed in Gideon's campaign.

insights.title: Like tumbleweed
insights.body: "Make them like tumbleweed; like chaff before the wind" (83:13). The Hebrew word suggests a whirling wheel, probably the dried head of a thistle that breaks off in late summer and rolls across the fields in the wind.

insights.title: So that they may seek
insights.body: The fierce prayer has a surprising aim: "Fill their faces with confusion, that they may seek your name, Yahweh" (83:16), and "that they may know that you alone... are the Most High" (83:18). The goal of the enemies' defeat is their recognition of God.

insights.title: Don't keep silent
insights.body: The psalm opens with three ways of asking God not to be silent (83:1). Israel's enemies are loud and active (83:2); God seems quiet. This is the last of the twelve psalms of Asaph and closes the group of psalms that prefer the name Elohim.

insights.title: Wiping out a name
insights.body: The enemies say, "let's destroy them as a nation, that the name of Israel may be remembered no more" (83:4). How have such words echoed through later history, and how should this psalm be prayed in light of that?

84.summary: A pilgrim longs for the courts of Yahweh, envies the birds nesting near the altar, blesses those who journey to Zion, and declares one day there better than a thousand elsewhere.
84.lookfor: Notice the birds at the altar, the pilgrims passing through the dry valley, and the contrast between doorkeeper and tent-dweller.

names.name: Zion
names.gloss: Jerusalem's temple hill, goal of the pilgrims.

insights.title: Birds at the altar
insights.body: "The sparrow has found a home, and the swallow a nest for herself... near your altars" (84:3). Small birds nested in the temple's walls and eaves. The psalmist envies them for living where he longs to be.

insights.title: A pilgrim's song
insights.body: "Blessed are those... who have set their hearts on a pilgrimage" (84:5), literally whose hearts are on the highways. Israelites went up to Jerusalem for the great festivals. The psalm captures the longing of the road.

insights.title: The valley of Weeping
insights.body: "Passing through the valley of Weeping, they make it a place of springs" (84:6). The Hebrew name, Baca, may mean weeping or refer to balsam trees that grow in dry places. The pilgrims' faith turns a dry valley into a place of springs, and the autumn rain blesses it.

insights.title: Strength to strength
insights.body: Unlike most travellers, who grow weaker on a long journey, the pilgrims "go from strength to strength" (84:7). The closer they come to God, the stronger they become. Isaiah says those who wait for Yahweh renew their strength.

insights.title: A doorkeeper
insights.body: "I would rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God, than to dwell in the tents of wickedness" (84:10). The sons of Korah, to whom the psalm is credited, served as gatekeepers of the temple. The lowest job in God's house beats the best home among the wicked.

insights.title: Sun and shield
insights.body: "Yahweh God is a sun and a shield" (84:11) is the only place in the Psalms where God is directly called a sun. Sun gods were worshipped all around Israel; the psalm uses the image for the life and light Yahweh gives.

insights.title: A thousand days
insights.body: "A day in your courts is better than a thousand" (84:10). What would have to be true of God for one day in his presence to be worth more than years elsewhere?

85.summary: The people thank Yahweh for restoring them in the past, ask him to revive them again now, and listen for his promise of peace, where mercy, truth, righteousness and peace meet.
85.lookfor: Compare the past restoration in verses 1–3 with the present plea, and notice the four virtues that meet and kiss.

insights.title: Restored, yet still waiting
insights.body: The psalm begins by thanking God for restoring Jacob's fortunes (85:1-3), then asks him to turn and revive them again (85:4-7). Many scholars read it as a prayer after the return from exile, when life in the land was still hard. Haggai and Zechariah describe that disappointing time.

insights.title: Listening for God
insights.body: "I will hear what God, Yahweh, will speak" (85:8). The psalm pauses to wait for a word from God, like a prophet on watch. The word that comes is peace, with a warning not to return to folly.

insights.title: Righteousness and peace kiss
insights.body: "Mercy and truth meet together. Righteousness and peace have kissed each other" (85:10). Medieval writers, including Bernard of Clairvaux, told an allegory of four daughters of God, Mercy, Truth, Justice and Peace, who argue over fallen humanity and are reconciled in the Incarnation.

insights.title: Glory dwelling in the land
insights.body: "That glory may dwell in our land" (85:9) hopes for the return of God's glory, which Ezekiel saw leave the temple and later return. John says the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we saw his glory.

insights.title: Earth and heaven meet
insights.body: "Truth springs out of the earth. Righteousness has looked down from heaven" (85:11). The picture is of heaven and earth coming together in harmony. Church fathers often read it of Christ's birth, and the psalm is used in Advent.

insights.title: Revive us again
insights.body: "Won't you revive us again" (85:6) uses a verb meaning make alive. It asks for more than better circumstances: renewed life and joy in God.

insights.title: Past mercy, present need
insights.body: The people remember past restoration but still need help now. How can remembering what God did before strengthen prayer for what is still lacking?

86.summary: David, poor and needy, asks God to hear and teach him, praises him as unique among the gods and merciful to all who call, and asks for a sign of his goodness.
86.lookfor: Notice how many lines echo other Scriptures, the prayer for an undivided heart, and the great confession of God's character in verse 15.

names.name: Sheol
names.gloss: The realm of the dead.

insights.title: Woven from older prayers
insights.body: Psalm 86, the only psalm credited to David in Book 3, is woven from phrases found in other psalms and in Exodus. The psalmist prays in the language of Scripture. Many believers do the same today.

insights.title: I am godly
insights.body: "Preserve my soul, for I am godly" (86:2) uses hasid, a person loyal to God's covenant. It is not a boast of perfection but a claim to belong to God, who is himself rich in hesed, loyal love (86:5).

insights.title: Merciful and gracious
insights.body: Verse 15 quotes God's self-description to Moses on Sinai: merciful and gracious, slow to anger, abundant in loving kindness and truth. It is the most quoted description of God in the Old Testament.

insights.title: An undivided heart
insights.body: "Make my heart undivided to fear your name" (86:11) is literally unite my heart. The psalmist knows his loyalties are split and asks God to gather them. Jeremiah promises one heart to fear God.

insights.title: All nations will worship
insights.body: "All nations you have made will come and worship before you" (86:9). Revelation echoes this verse in the song of those who conquered the beast.

insights.title: Son of your servant
insights.body: "Save the son of your servant" (86:16) is literally the son of your handmaid. A slave born in the household was the most loyal of servants, belonging to the master from birth. The psalmist pictures himself as born into God's service.

insights.title: A sign of goodness
insights.body: The psalmist asks for "a sign of your goodness, that those who hate me may see it" (86:17). What kind of sign might show others that God has helped someone?

87.summary: A short, surprising song declares that Yahweh loves Zion, and that even Israel's old enemies, Egypt, Babylon, Philistia, Tyre and Ethiopia, will be counted as born there.
87.lookfor: Look for the list of foreign peoples and the repeated phrase "This one was born there".

names.name: Rahab
names.gloss: A poetic name for Egypt, meaning arrogance or storm; not Rahab of Jericho.

names.name: Philistia
names.gloss: The land of the Philistines on the coastal plain.

names.name: Tyre
names.gloss: The great Phoenician trading city.

names.name: Ethiopia
names.gloss: Cush, the kingdom south of Egypt.

names.name: Zion
names.gloss: Jerusalem, pictured as mother of the nations.

insights.title: Rahab is Egypt
insights.body: "I will record Rahab and Babylon" (87:4). Rahab here is a poetic name for Egypt, meaning something like arrogance or blusterer, and is spelled differently in Hebrew from the name of Rahab of Jericho. Isaiah calls Egypt Rahab who sits still.

insights.title: Enemies made citizens
insights.body: Egypt and Babylon, Israel's two great oppressors, along with Philistia, Tyre and Ethiopia, are enrolled as people "born" in Zion (87:4-6). It is one of the Old Testament's boldest pictures of the nations joining God's people. Isaiah imagines Egypt and Assyria worshipping alongside Israel.

insights.title: The register of peoples
insights.body: "Yahweh will count, when he writes up the peoples" (87:6) uses the picture of a city's citizenship register. To be written in it gave the rights of a native. Isaiah speaks of those written for life in Jerusalem.

insights.title: Jerusalem our mother
insights.body: Paul writes that the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother. Hebrews speaks of the heavenly Jerusalem and the assembly of the firstborn enrolled in heaven. Psalm 87 lies behind this picture of Zion as the mother of believers from every nation.

insights.title: Glorious things
insights.body: "Glorious things are spoken about you, city of God" (87:3) gave John Newton the opening line of his 1779 hymn Glorious Things of Thee Are Spoken. The psalm itself is so short and abrupt that some think parts have been lost.

insights.title: All my springs
insights.body: The psalm ends with singers and dancers saying "All my springs are in you" (87:7). Zion is pictured as the source of life and joy for all its citizens, Israelite and foreign alike.

insights.title: Born there
insights.body: The former enemies are counted as if born in Zion (87:4). What does it mean to belong to God's people by his declaration rather than by birth?

88.summary: The darkest psalm: a lifelong sufferer cries day and night to God, feels already among the dead and abandoned by friends, and ends with no word of hope, only darkness.
88.lookfor: Notice the steady cry to God despite no answer, the questions about the dead, and the final word.

names.name: Sheol
names.gloss: The realm of the dead.

names.name: Destruction
names.gloss: Abaddon, another name for the place of the dead.

insights.title: No happy ending
insights.body: Almost every lament in the Psalms turns to trust or praise. Psalm 88 does not. In Hebrew its last word is darkness (88:18). Its presence in Scripture tells sufferers that there is room before God for prayers that do not resolve.

insights.title: Heman the Ezrahite
insights.body: The title credits the psalm to Heman the Ezrahite, a name also given to a famous wise man in Solomon's time and to one of David's chief singers. It is also linked with the sons of Korah. It may come from a person with a long illness.

insights.title: Afflicted from youth
insights.body: "I am afflicted and ready to die from my youth up" (88:15). Friends shun him as an abomination (88:8) and he is confined (88:8). Some think of a skin disease that forced isolation under the law; whatever the cause, the suffering is lifelong.

insights.title: Abaddon
insights.body: "Your faithfulness in Destruction" (88:11) translates Abaddon, a name for the place of the dead. Revelation gives it as the name of the angel of the abyss. The departed spirits (88:10) are the Rephaim, the shades of the dead.

insights.title: Prayer that keeps going
insights.body: Even with no answer the psalmist keeps praying: day and night (88:1), daily with hands spread out (88:9), in the morning (88:13). Calling God "the God of my salvation" (88:1) is itself an act of faith.

insights.title: Prayed on Fridays
insights.body: In the Roman Catholic Liturgy of the Hours, Psalm 88 is prayed at Night Prayer on Fridays, the day of the crucifixion. Christians have long heard in it the darkness Christ entered.

insights.title: Darkness as a companion
insights.body: The psalm ends with friends gone and darkness left (88:18). What does it mean that someone in this state still addresses God?

89.summary: A long psalm celebrates God's faithfulness and his everlasting covenant with David, then laments that the king has been defeated and his crown thrown down, asking how long God will hide.
89.lookfor: Notice how often the words loving kindness and faithfulness appear, the detailed promises to David, and the shocking reversal at verse 38.

names.name: Rahab
names.gloss: Here the chaos monster of the sea, also a poetic name for Egypt.

names.name: Tabor
names.gloss: A rounded mountain in Galilee, rising from the Jezreel plain.

names.name: Hermon
names.gloss: The great snow-capped mountain on Israel's northern border.

insights.title: Love and faithfulness
insights.body: Loving kindness (hesed) and faithfulness (emunah) each appear seven times in Psalm 89, starting in its first verse. They are the twin pillars of the covenant with David. The question the psalm raises is whether they still stand.

insights.title: The covenant with David
insights.body: Verses 19–37 expand Nathan's promise to David: his offspring will reign forever, God will be his Father, and sin will be punished but the covenant never broken (89:30-34). The psalm quotes God's oath at length before questioning it.

insights.title: The crown in the dust
insights.body: "You have renounced the covenant of your servant. You have defiled his crown in the dust" (89:39). The scene fits the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC, when the Davidic king was taken captive. "You have shortened the days of his youth" (89:45) may refer to young King Jehoiachin.

insights.title: Firstborn and faithful witness
insights.body: God promises to make David "my firstborn, the highest of the kings of the earth" (89:27), and calls the moon "the faithful witness in the sky" (89:37). Revelation greets readers from Jesus Christ, "the faithful witness, the firstborn of the dead, and the ruler of the kings of the earth", drawing on this psalm.

insights.title: Rahab the sea monster
insights.body: "You rule the pride of the sea... You have broken Rahab in pieces" (89:9-10). Here Rahab is the monster of chaos that ancient myths said the gods defeated. The God who controls the sea is the God who swore to David.

insights.title: End of Book 3
insights.body: Psalm 89 ends Book 3 with a doxology (89:52) right after the cry "Lord, where are your former loving kindnesses?" (89:49). Book 4, beginning with a prayer of Moses, responds by turning back to God's kingship before there were kings.

insights.title: Ethan the Ezrahite
insights.body: The title names Ethan the Ezrahite, a wise man compared with Solomon and also a temple singer. Ezrahite may mean a native of the land.

insights.title: When promises seem broken
insights.body: The psalmist quotes God's promises back to him (89:49). How can people of faith hold on to God's word when events seem to contradict it?

90.summary: Moses' prayer sets the eternal God against short, troubled human lives, and asks him to teach us to number our days, to satisfy us with his love, and to establish the work of our hands.
90.lookfor: Notice the contrast between God's eternity and human shortness, the image of grass, and the requests at the end.

insights.title: Book 4 begins with Moses
insights.body: Psalm 90 is the only psalm credited to Moses and opens Book 4 (Psalms 90–106). After the fall of David's kingdom in Psalm 89, the Psalter goes back to Moses, before Israel had kings. Moses is named seven times in Book 4 and only once in Books 1–3.

insights.title: Our dwelling place
insights.body: "Lord, you have been our dwelling place for all generations" (90:1) echoes Moses' blessing: the eternal God is your dwelling place. For a people who wandered and later lost their land, God himself is home.

insights.title: Return to dust
insights.body: "You turn man to destruction, saying, 'Return, you children of men'" (90:3) recalls God's words to Adam: you will return to dust. The word for destruction can also mean dust or crushed matter.

insights.title: A thousand years
insights.body: "A thousand years in your sight are just like yesterday" (90:4). Peter quotes this when people mock the delay of Christ's return: with the Lord a day is as a thousand years, and a thousand years as a day.

insights.title: Seventy years
insights.body: "The days of our years are seventy, or even by reason of strength eighty years" (90:10). This was a long life in the ancient world, where many died young. The psalm does not complain about the number but about the toil and sorrow that fill it.

insights.title: Counting our days
insights.body: "So teach us to count our days, that we may gain a heart of wisdom" (90:12). Counting days means taking seriously that life is limited. Wisdom begins with that honesty.

insights.title: O God, our help
insights.body: Isaac Watts' hymn O God, Our Help in Ages Past (1719) is a paraphrase of this psalm. It is often sung at funerals and remembrance services. The psalm is also commonly read at Jewish and Christian funerals.

insights.title: Establish our work
insights.body: The prayer ends asking God to "establish the work of our hands" (90:17), twice. In a life so short, what kind of work would one want God to make last?

91.summary: Whoever takes shelter in the Most High is promised protection from snares, plague and terrors by night and day, with angels to guard them, and God himself promises to answer and rescue.
91.lookfor: Notice the four names for God at the start, the list of dangers, the angels, and God's own voice in the last three verses.

insights.title: Four names for God
insights.body: The first two verses use four names: Most High (Elyon), Almighty (Shaddai), Yahweh, and my God. Each adds a facet of protection: supremacy, power, covenant faithfulness and personal relationship. The secret place and shadow (91:1) picture a hiding place under God's care.

insights.title: Terrors of night and noon
insights.body: "The terror by night... the pestilence that walks in darkness... the destruction that wastes at noonday" (91:5-6) reflect ancient fears of disease and evil powers at certain hours. The Greek translation spoke of a noonday demon, which monks later identified with acedia, the listless despair of midday.

insights.title: A song against harm
insights.body: The Talmud calls Psalm 91 a song against afflictions, and Jews have long recited it for protection, including at night before sleep. In Christian tradition it is a Compline psalm, prayed at the close of the day.

insights.title: The devil quotes a psalm
insights.body: In Jesus' temptation, the devil quotes verses 11–12 to urge him to jump from the temple. Jesus answers that one must not put God to the test. The psalm promises protection for those who trust, not for those who try to force God's hand.

insights.title: Treading on serpents
insights.body: "You will tread on the lion and cobra" (91:13). Jesus tells his disciples he has given them authority to tread on serpents and scorpions. Genesis promised that a descendant of the woman would crush the serpent's head.

insights.title: God answers
insights.body: In the last three verses God speaks: "Because he has set his love on me, therefore I will deliver him" (91:14). The verb for set his love means to cling with desire. God's promises include "I will be with him in trouble" (91:15), not a promise of no trouble.

insights.title: When harm comes
insights.body: The psalm promises that "no evil shall happen to you" (91:10), yet faithful people do fall ill and suffer. How might verse 15, "I will be with him in trouble", help in reading the rest of the psalm?

92.summary: A Sabbath song gives thanks for God's works, contrasts the brief flourishing of the wicked with the lasting fruitfulness of the righteous, planted like palms and cedars in God's house.
92.lookfor: Notice the morning-and-night rhythm of praise, the grass and the trees, and the promise of fruit in old age.

names.name: Lebanon
names.gloss: The mountains north of Israel, famous for great cedars.

insights.title: A song for the Sabbath
insights.body: Psalm 92 is the only psalm whose title names a day. The Mishnah says the Levites sang it in the temple on the Sabbath, and it is still central to the synagogue's Friday evening and Saturday services. Rest is filled with thanksgiving.

insights.title: Seven times Yahweh
insights.body: The divine name Yahweh appears seven times in the psalm, a number linked with the seventh day. Verse 8, "But you, Yahweh, are on high forever more", stands at the centre of the poem.

insights.title: Morning and night
insights.body: "To proclaim your loving kindness in the morning, and your faithfulness every night" (92:2). Love is celebrated as the day begins; faithfulness as it ends, looking back on how God kept his word.

insights.title: The senseless man
insights.body: "A senseless man doesn't know" (92:6) uses a word related to animals: brutish, without reflection. Such a person sees the wicked spring up like grass and misses that grass withers (92:7).

insights.title: Palm and cedar
insights.body: "The righteous shall flourish like the palm tree. He will grow like a cedar in Lebanon" (92:12). The date palm thrives in hot oases and bears fruit for decades; the cedar grows tall and long-lived in the mountains. Together they picture fruitfulness and strength.

insights.title: Planted in God's house
insights.body: "They are planted in Yahweh's house" (92:13) echoes Psalm 52, where the psalmist is a green olive tree in God's house, and Psalm 1, where the righteous is a tree by streams of water.

insights.title: Fruit in old age
insights.body: "They will still produce fruit in old age" (92:14). What kind of fruit might the later years of life bear that earlier years cannot?

93.summary: A short hymn proclaims that Yahweh reigns, robed in majesty and enthroned from eternity, mightier than the roaring floods, and that his statutes and his house stand firm.
93.lookfor: Notice the opening cry "Yahweh reigns!", the rising floods, and the move from cosmic power to God's statutes and house.

insights.title: Yahweh reigns
insights.body: Psalm 93 begins a group of psalms that celebrate God's kingship (Psalms 93–99), many starting with "Yahweh reigns!" Coming after the collapse of David's throne in Psalm 89, they answer that the true King has never lost his throne (93:2).

insights.title: Reigns or has become King
insights.body: The Hebrew phrase can be translated Yahweh reigns or Yahweh has become King. Some scholars, especially Sigmund Mowinckel, proposed that Israel held an annual festival celebrating God's enthronement. Others think the psalms simply declare God's eternal rule; the debate continues.

insights.title: The floods lift their voice
insights.body: "The floods have lifted up their voice" (93:3). Canaanite myths described the storm god Baal fighting Prince Sea and Judge River. Here the waters roar, but Yahweh on high is mightier (93:4). No battle is needed: he is simply greater.

insights.title: Friday's psalm
insights.body: The Mishnah lists Psalm 93 as the psalm for the sixth day of the week, and the Greek title connects it with the day before the Sabbath, when the earth was founded. On the day creation was completed, God is hailed as King.

insights.title: Clothed with majesty
insights.body: "He is clothed with majesty! Yahweh is armed with strength" (93:1). God is pictured dressed as a king for his coronation. Isaiah and Psalm 104 also describe God's royal clothing.

insights.title: From sea to statutes
insights.body: After the roaring waters comes a quiet line: "Your statutes stand firm" (93:5). The God who steadies the world also gives a reliable word. His house is marked by holiness.

insights.title: It can't be moved
insights.body: "The world also is established. It can't be moved" (93:1). When the world feels shaky, what does it mean to believe that God's rule holds it steady?

94.summary: The psalmist calls on the God of vengeance to judge the arrogant who crush widows and orphans, rebukes fools who think God doesn't see, and testifies that God's love held him up.
94.lookfor: Notice what the wicked say about God, the psalmist's arguments from the ear and eye, and the personal testimony from verse 16.

insights.title: God of vengeance
insights.body: "You God to whom vengeance belongs" (94:1) can sound harsh. In the Bible vengeance belongs to God as the rightful judge, not to individuals. It means putting wrongs right for victims. Paul quotes Deuteronomy, "Vengeance belongs to me", to tell believers not to take revenge.

insights.title: The widow and the alien
insights.body: "They kill the widow and the alien, and murder the fatherless" (94:6). These three groups had no family protection. Israel's law repeatedly placed them under God's special care. The wicked here may be Israel's own powerful people.

insights.title: He who made the ear
insights.body: "He who implanted the ear, won't he hear? He who formed the eye, won't he see?" (94:9). The argument is simple: the Creator of senses cannot be less aware than his creatures. The wicked assume "Yah will not see" (94:7).

insights.title: Futile thoughts
insights.body: "Yahweh knows the thoughts of man, that they are futile" (94:11). Paul quotes this in 1 Corinthians, applying it to the wisdom of the wise, to warn against boasting in human leaders.

insights.title: Blessed discipline
insights.body: "Blessed is the man whom you discipline, Yah" (94:12). Proverbs and Hebrews also teach that God's discipline is a sign of love. Here it is teaching from God's law that gives rest in hard days.

insights.title: Mischief by statute
insights.body: "Shall the throne of wickedness have fellowship with you, which brings about mischief by statute?" (94:20) describes injustice made legal. Isaiah condemns those who write unjust decrees to rob the poor. The Mishnah lists this as the temple psalm for Wednesday.

insights.title: My foot is slipping
insights.body: "When I said, 'My foot is slipping!' Your loving kindness, Yahweh, held me up" (94:18). The large public complaint gives way to a personal testimony. God's comfort meets the "multitude of my thoughts" (94:19).

insights.title: Who will stand up for me?
insights.body: "Who will rise up for me against the wicked?" (94:16). When no human defender comes, what does it mean to find that God is one's help (94:17)?

95.summary: A call to sing, kneel and worship the great King who made the earth and shepherds his people is followed by a warning not to harden hearts as Israel did in the wilderness.
95.lookfor: Notice the two invitations "Oh come", the turn at "Today", and the memories of Meribah and Massah.

names.name: Meribah
names.gloss: Quarrel: the place where Israel argued with God over water.

names.name: Massah
names.gloss: Testing: another name for the same place in the wilderness.

insights.title: The Venite
insights.body: For centuries Psalm 95, called the Venite from its first Latin word, has opened Christian morning prayer; the Rule of St Benedict prescribes it daily. In the synagogue it begins the Friday evening service welcoming the Sabbath, followed by Psalms 96–99.

insights.title: Two invitations
insights.body: The psalm invites twice: "Oh come, let's sing" (95:1) because God is great Creator, and "Oh come, let's worship and bow down" (95:6) because he is our Shepherd. Joyful shouting and humble kneeling belong together.

insights.title: Kneel
insights.body: "Let's kneel before Yahweh, our Maker" (95:6). The Hebrew verb for kneel is related to the word for blessing. Kneeling was the posture of a subject before a king.

insights.title: Meribah and Massah
insights.body: "Don't harden your heart, as at Meribah, as in the day of Massah" (95:8). At those places, whose names mean quarrel and testing, Israel complained that God had brought them out to die of thirst. Their hearts were hard even after seeing his works.

insights.title: Today
insights.body: Hebrews quotes verses 7–11 at length and dwells on the word "Today" (95:7): the invitation is still open. It argues that the "rest" (95:11) was never fully reached in Canaan, so a Sabbath rest remains for God's people.

insights.title: Forty years
insights.body: "Forty long years I was grieved with that generation" (95:10). Because the generation that left Egypt refused to trust God at the border of Canaan, they died in the wilderness. The psalm uses their story as a warning to worshippers.

insights.title: Worship and warning
insights.body: The psalm moves from joyful worship to a sober warning. Why might those who sing loudest to God also need to be reminded not to harden their hearts?

96.summary: All the earth is called to sing a new song, declare Yahweh's glory among the nations, and rejoice, because he reigns and comes to judge the world in righteousness.
96.lookfor: Notice the triple calls to sing and to ascribe, the contrast with idols, and creation's joy at God's coming.

insights.title: Sung for the ark
insights.body: Most of Psalm 96 appears in 1 Chronicles 16 as part of the song David appointed when the ark was brought to Jerusalem. The psalm takes a celebration of Israel's worship and opens it to all the earth.

insights.title: Gods and nothings
insights.body: "All the gods of the peoples are idols" (96:5) contains a wordplay: gods is elohim, and idols is elilim, which sounds similar but means worthless things or nothings. Yahweh, by contrast, made the heavens.

insights.title: From Psalm 29 to the nations
insights.body: "Ascribe to Yahweh, you families of nations" (96:7-9) reuses Psalm 29, which called on heavenly beings to ascribe glory. Here the summons goes to every nation on earth.

insights.title: Reigning from the tree
insights.body: In the 2nd century Justin Martyr quoted verse 10 with the added words from the tree, so that it read the Lord reigns from the tree, accusing Jewish teachers of removing the last words. The phrase is not in Hebrew or most Greek manuscripts, but it entered some old Latin versions and Christian hymns about the cross.

insights.title: Creation rejoices
insights.body: The heavens, earth, sea, fields and trees all rejoice (96:11-12) because God "comes to judge the earth" (96:13). Judgment here is good news: the setting right of all things. Paul speaks of creation waiting to be set free.

insights.title: A Christmas psalm
insights.body: In Catholic and Anglican tradition, Psalm 96 is sung at the Christmas midnight service: "Let the heavens be glad, and let the earth rejoice" (96:11). The new song for all nations is heard as celebrating Christ's birth.

insights.title: Say among the nations
insights.body: "Say among the nations, 'Yahweh reigns'" (96:10). What might it mean in practice to declare God's rule among people who do not know him?

97.summary: Yahweh reigns in clouds, fire and lightning; idol-worshippers are put to shame, Zion rejoices, and light and gladness are sown for the righteous.
97.lookfor: Look for the storm imagery of God's appearing, the shaming of idols, and the seed of light at the end.

names.name: Zion
names.gloss: Jerusalem's temple hill.

insights.title: Clouds and darkness
insights.body: "Clouds and darkness are around him. Righteousness and justice are the foundation of his throne" (97:2). The cloud and fire recall Sinai, when God came down on the mountain. Mystery surrounds him, but his rule rests on justice.

insights.title: Mountains like wax
insights.body: "The mountains melt like wax at the presence of Yahweh" (97:5). Micah uses the same image when God comes down. The firmest things in the world cannot stand in his presence.

insights.title: Let all the angels worship
insights.body: "Worship him, all you gods!" (97:7) The Greek translation reads all his angels, and Hebrews quotes a similar line, from this psalm or from Moses' song, when the Firstborn is brought into the world.

insights.title: Love God, hate evil
insights.body: "You who love Yahweh, hate evil" (97:10). Love for God is not neutral about wrong. Amos and Paul give the same pairing.

insights.title: Light is sown
insights.body: "Light is sown for the righteous" (97:11) pictures light scattered like seed, waiting to sprout. Jewish tradition recites this verse before the Kol Nidre prayer at the start of Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement.

insights.title: The islands
insights.body: "Let the multitude of islands be glad!" (97:1) The islands or coastlands meant the distant lands of the Mediterranean, the edge of the known world. Isaiah often speaks of the islands waiting for God's law.

insights.title: Glad judgment
insights.body: "Zion heard and was glad... because of your judgments" (97:8). Why might God's judgments be a cause for joy rather than fear for his people?

98.summary: A new song celebrates Yahweh's saving victory seen by all the earth, and calls people, instruments, seas, rivers and mountains to greet the coming King and Judge.
98.lookfor: Notice the three stages: God's salvation, the people's music, and creation's joy.

insights.title: His holy arm
insights.body: "His right hand, and his holy arm, have worked salvation for him" (98:1) echoes the song at the Red Sea. Isaiah uses almost the same words for God's return to Zion: all the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of our God.

insights.title: Mary's song
insights.body: "He has remembered his loving kindness and his faithfulness toward the house of Israel" (98:3) is echoed in Mary's Magnificat, where God has helped Israel, remembering his mercy. The Anglican Book of Common Prayer sets Psalm 98 as an alternative to the Magnificat at Evening Prayer.

insights.title: Trumpet and ram's horn
insights.body: "With trumpets and sound of the ram's horn" (98:6). The trumpets were straight silver instruments blown by priests; the ram's horn, shofar, was used for signals and festivals. Both were used to hail a king.

insights.title: Joy to the World
insights.body: Isaac Watts' carol Joy to the World (1719) is a paraphrase of the second half of this psalm. Watts read it as celebrating Christ's coming as King, which is why it became a Christmas song.

insights.title: Rivers clap their hands
insights.body: "Let the rivers clap their hands. Let the mountains sing for joy together" (98:8). Creation is pictured as an audience at a coronation. Isaiah gives the trees of the field hands to clap as well.

insights.title: Psalm 96 again
insights.body: Psalm 98 shares its opening and closing with Psalm 96: a new song, and God coming to judge the world with righteousness (98:9). The repetition reinforces the message of Book 4 that God reigns and will put the world right.

insights.title: Seen by all
insights.body: "All the ends of the earth have seen the salvation of our God" (98:3). What does it mean that God's saving acts are meant to be public, not private?

99.summary: The King enthroned above the cherubim is holy, loves justice, and answered Moses, Aaron and Samuel, forgiving yet disciplining; so all are called to worship at his holy hill.
99.lookfor: Listen for the refrain about holiness, the footstool, and the three great intercessors.

names.name: Zion
names.gloss: Jerusalem's temple hill.

names.name: Samuel
names.gloss: The prophet and last judge, who anointed Saul and David and prayed for Israel.

insights.title: Holy, holy, holy
insights.body: The refrain "He is Holy!" comes three times (99:3, 99:5, 99:9), the last time expanded. It recalls the seraphim crying holy three times in Isaiah's vision and the living creatures in Revelation.

insights.title: Above the cherubim
insights.body: "He sits enthroned among the cherubim" (99:1) refers to the ark of the covenant, with two golden cherubim on its lid. The ark was pictured as God's throne or his footstool (99:5) in the Most Holy Place.

insights.title: Great intercessors
insights.body: "Moses and Aaron were among his priests, Samuel among those who call on his name" (99:6). All three prayed for Israel in crisis and were answered. Jeremiah names Moses and Samuel as the greatest intercessors.

insights.title: Forgiving and avenging
insights.body: "You are a God who forgave them, although you took vengeance for their doings" (99:8). Moses and Aaron were forgiven, yet neither entered the promised land. Forgiveness and consequences can go together.

insights.title: The King loves justice
insights.body: "The King's strength also loves justice" (99:4). God's power is defined by its love of what is right. He establishes equity and executes justice in Jacob.

insights.title: Close of the King psalms
insights.body: Psalm 99 completes the series beginning "Yahweh reigns" (Psalms 93, 96–99). It moves from the whole earth to Zion and to Israel's history, showing that the universal King is also the God who spoke from the pillar of cloud (99:7).

insights.title: Holiness and nearness
insights.body: God is high and holy, yet he answered those who called (99:6-8). How do awe and closeness belong together in worship?

100.summary: All the earth is invited to serve Yahweh with joy, know that he made us and we are his sheep, and enter his gates with thanksgiving, for his love endures forever.
100.lookfor: Count the commands in this short psalm, and notice the reasons given for them in verses 3 and 5.

insights.title: A psalm for the thank offering
insights.body: The title calls it a psalm of thanksgiving, todah, the name of a sacrifice of thanks. Jews recite it daily in the morning service but leave it out on the Sabbath and festivals, when individual thank offerings were not brought in the temple.

insights.title: We are his, or not we ourselves
insights.body: "It is he who has made us, and we are his" (100:3). The Hebrew words for and we are his and and not we ourselves sound the same and differ by one letter. Jewish scribes marked the reading followed by WEB; older versions like the King James chose not we ourselves.

insights.title: Seven commands
insights.body: In five verses the psalm gives seven commands: shout, serve, come, know, enter, give thanks, bless. Every one is joyful. Even "Serve Yahweh" (100:2) is to be done with gladness.

insights.title: Sheep of his pasture
insights.body: "We are his people, and the sheep of his pasture" (100:3) repeats Psalm 95. Jesus calls himself the good shepherd who knows his own sheep.

insights.title: Old Hundredth
insights.body: William Kethe's 1561 paraphrase All People That on Earth Do Dwell set this psalm to a tune now called Old Hundredth. It is one of the most widely sung hymns in English, and the same tune carries the common doxology.

insights.title: His love endures forever
insights.body: "His loving kindness endures forever, his faithfulness to all generations" (100:5). This confession becomes a refrain in later psalms, especially Psalm 136, where it is repeated in every verse.

insights.title: Joyful service
insights.body: The psalm commands gladness (100:2). Can joy be commanded, and what does the psalm offer as reasons for it?

101.summary: A king vows to rule with integrity: to keep his own heart and home blameless, to have nothing to do with slanderers and liars, and to fill his court with the faithful.
101.lookfor: Notice the series of "I will" promises, the focus on the king's house, and who will and will not serve him.

insights.title: A king's vows
insights.body: Psalm 101 sounds like a new king's pledge at his coronation. He begins with his own life (101:2-4), then turns to whom he will allow in his court (101:5-7). Personal integrity comes before public justice.

insights.title: A mirror for princes
insights.body: Martin Luther wrote a long exposition of Psalm 101 in 1534, treating it as a guide for Christian rulers. Medieval and Reformation writers called such texts mirrors for princes. The psalm has often been read to those taking public office.

insights.title: Within my house
insights.body: "I will walk within my house with a blameless heart" (101:2). The test of character begins at home, where no one is watching. Paul makes the same point about church leaders managing their households well.

insights.title: No vile thing
insights.body: "I will set no vile thing before my eyes" (101:3) is literally no thing of Belial, a word for worthlessness that later became a name for evil. What a person chooses to look at shapes what they become.

insights.title: Morning by morning
insights.body: "Morning by morning, I will destroy all the wicked of the land" (101:8). Kings heard legal cases in the morning at the city gate. Jeremiah urges the house of David to execute justice in the morning.

insights.title: When will you come?
insights.body: In the middle of his vows the king asks God, "When will you come to me?" (101:2). Why might someone determined to live well still need God to come?

102.summary: An afflicted person pours out a complaint of wasting life and loneliness, then turns to the eternal God who will rebuild Zion, and whose years never end even when the heavens wear out.
102.lookfor: Notice the images of smoke, withered grass and lonely birds, the turn to Zion's restoration, and the contrast between creation wearing out and God remaining.

names.name: Zion
names.gloss: Jerusalem, whose stones and dust God's servants love.

insights.title: A prayer for anyone
insights.body: The title is unique: it names no author, only a situation: a prayer of someone afflicted and overwhelmed. It offers itself to anyone in that condition. It is the fifth of the seven penitential psalms.

insights.title: Birds of the ruins
insights.body: "I am like a pelican of the wilderness... an owl of the waste places... a sparrow that is alone on the housetop" (102:6-7). The first two are unclean birds that haunt ruins; the identification of the species is uncertain. All three picture loneliness and desolation.

insights.title: Ashes for bread
insights.body: "I have eaten ashes like bread, and mixed my drink with tears" (102:9). Mourners sat in ashes and put dust on their heads. The psalmist's grief has become his daily food.

insights.title: The set time for Zion
insights.body: "It is time to have pity on her. Yes, the set time has come" (102:13). The psalm seems to come from the exile, when God's servants loved even the stones and dust of ruined Jerusalem (102:14). Jeremiah had promised a set time for return.

insights.title: A people yet to be created
insights.body: "This will be written for the generation to come. A people which will be created will praise Yah" (102:18). The prayer is written down for the future. The word created suggests God will make a new people.

insights.title: You are the same
insights.body: Verses 25–27 contrast the heavens, which wear out like clothes, with God, whose years have no end. Hebrews quotes these verses as spoken to the Son, the Creator who remains the same.

insights.title: Short days, endless years
insights.body: The psalmist's days are like a long shadow (102:11), but God's years are throughout all generations (102:24). How can the eternity of God comfort someone whose life feels short?

103.summary: David calls his own soul to bless Yahweh for all his benefits: forgiveness, healing, compassion like a father's, and love that outlasts frail human life, then calls angels and all creation to join in.
103.lookfor: Notice the list of benefits, the images of distance and fatherhood, the contrast between grass and God's love, and the widening circle of praise at the end.

insights.title: Speaking to my soul
insights.body: The psalm begins and ends with "Praise Yahweh, my soul!" (103:1, 103:22). The psalmist speaks to himself, stirring up his own heart. Between those lines the praise widens from personal benefits to Israel to the angels and all creation.

insights.title: Youth renewed like the eagle's
insights.body: "Your youth is renewed like the eagle's" (103:5). Eagles and vultures moult and grow fresh feathers, and they can live a long time, which made them a picture of renewed vigour. Isaiah says those who wait for Yahweh will mount up with wings like eagles.

insights.title: His ways to Moses
