insights.body: "He made known his ways to Moses" (103:7) answers Moses' request, "show me your ways". God's reply was the description of his character quoted in verse 8: merciful and gracious, slow to anger, abundant in loving kindness.

insights.title: East from west
insights.body: "As far as the east is from the west, so far has he removed our transgressions from us" (103:12). The distance is immeasurable. Micah says God casts sins into the depths of the sea.

insights.title: A father's compassion
insights.body: "Like a father has compassion on his children" (103:13) uses racham, a word related to the womb, describing deep, protective tenderness. The reason follows: "he remembers that we are dust" (103:14), recalling Adam formed from the ground.

insights.title: Like grass
insights.body: "As for man, his days are like grass" (103:15). Isaiah and Peter use the same picture, contrasting withering grass with the word of God that stands forever. Here the lasting thing is God's loving kindness (103:17).

insights.title: Don't forget
insights.body: "Don't forget all his benefits" (103:2). Why is forgetting God's goodness so easy, and what helps people remember?

104.summary: A great creation hymn praises Yahweh, robed in light, who set the earth on its foundations, tamed the waters, and feeds every creature from lions to sea monsters, all of which depend on his breath.
104.lookfor: Follow the order of creation, notice the many animals and their homes, and the dependence of all life on God's breath.

names.name: Lebanon
names.gloss: The mountains north of Israel, famous for great cedars.

insights.title: Genesis 1 as a song
insights.body: The psalm roughly follows the days of creation: light (104:2), sky (104:2-3), waters and dry land (104:5-9), plants (104:14), sun and moon (104:19), sea creatures (104:25) and humans at work (104:23). Genesis lists; the psalm marvels.

insights.title: An Egyptian parallel
insights.body: Scholars have long noted similarities with the Great Hymn to the Aten, the sun disc, from the time of Pharaoh Akhenaten in the 14th century BC: lions prowling at night, people going to work at dawn, ships on the sea. Psalm 104 praises the Creator, not the sun, which simply "knows when to set" (104:19).

insights.title: Winds and flames
insights.body: "He makes his messengers winds; his servants flames of fire" (104:4). The Hebrew word for messengers also means angels. Hebrews quotes the verse in its Greek form to contrast angels with the Son.

insights.title: Wild goats and rock badgers
insights.body: "The high mountains are for the wild goats. The rocks are a refuge for the rock badgers" (104:18). The rock badger is the hyrax, a small furry animal still common among the rocks around En Gedi. Every creature has a place made for it.

insights.title: Leviathan at play
insights.body: "There the ships go, and leviathan, whom you formed to play there" (104:26). Elsewhere Leviathan is a monster of chaos God defeats; here it is a creature frolicking in the sea God made for it. God asks Job whether he can play with it as with a bird.

insights.title: Spirit and breath
insights.body: "You take away their breath: they die... You send out your Spirit and they are created" (104:29-30). The same Hebrew word, ruach, means breath, wind and Spirit. Christians sing this psalm at Pentecost, and Orthodox evening prayer, Vespers, begins with it.

insights.title: The first Hallelujah
insights.body: The psalm ends with "Praise Yah!" (104:35), in Hebrew hallelu-yah. This is the first time the word appears in the Psalms. From here it becomes more and more frequent, until the final psalms are filled with it.

insights.title: Let Yahweh rejoice
insights.body: "Let Yahweh rejoice in his works" (104:31). What does it suggest that God delights in creatures like wild goats and sea monsters that have no use to people?

105.summary: A call to give thanks retells how God kept his covenant with Abraham, protecting the patriarchs, sending Joseph ahead, bringing Israel out of Egypt with wonders, and giving them the land.
105.lookfor: Notice how the psalm focuses on what God did rather than on Israel's failures, the story of Joseph, and the purpose stated in the last verse.

names.name: Ham
names.gloss: Noah's son, ancestor of the Egyptians; a poetic name for Egypt.

names.name: Canaan
names.gloss: The land west of the Jordan promised to Abraham's descendants.

insights.title: Sung for the ark
insights.body: Verses 1–15 appear in 1 Chronicles 16 as part of the song sung when David brought the ark to Jerusalem, followed by parts of Psalms 96 and 106. The historical psalms were used to remind worshippers who their God was.

insights.title: Twin psalms
insights.body: Psalms 105 and 106 tell the same history from two sides. Psalm 105 tells of God's faithfulness and does not mention a single sin of Israel. Psalm 106 tells of Israel's repeated unfaithfulness. Both end with "Praise Yah!"

insights.title: Anointed ones and prophets
insights.body: "Don't touch my anointed ones! Do my prophets no harm!" (105:15) refers to the patriarchs, protected from kings like Pharaoh and Abimelech. God called Abraham a prophet. The verse is not about later kings or church leaders.

insights.title: The iron entered his soul
insights.body: "His neck was locked in irons" (105:18) is literally his soul came into iron. Older English versions, following the Latin, read the iron entered into his soul, a phrase that became an English idiom for deep suffering. Joseph was held "until the time that his word happened" (105:19).

insights.title: Plagues in a new order
insights.body: The plagues are retold selectively (105:28-36), beginning with darkness, the ninth plague in Exodus, and omitting the death of livestock and the boils. As with Psalm 78, the poet shapes the story freely.

insights.title: Given in order to obey
insights.body: The psalm ends by stating why God gave the land: "that they might keep his statutes, and observe his laws" (105:45). Grace comes first, and obedience is the grateful response.

insights.title: Remembering the covenant
insights.body: "He has remembered his covenant forever" (105:8). How might telling a story of God's faithfulness, without dwelling on failures, shape a community's hope?

106.summary: A national confession recalls Israel's sins from the Red Sea to the land, and God's repeated mercy, and ends with a plea to gather the scattered people; it closes Book 4.
106.lookfor: Notice the pattern of rebellion and rescue, the people who stood in the gap, and the cry to be gathered from the nations.

names.name: Dathan
names.gloss: A Reubenite who rebelled against Moses with Korah and Abiram.

names.name: Abiram
names.gloss: Dathan's brother and fellow rebel; both were swallowed by the earth.

names.name: Horeb
names.gloss: Another name for Mount Sinai.

names.name: Baal Peor
names.gloss: The Baal worshipped at Peor in Moab, where Israel fell into idolatry.

names.name: Phinehas
names.gloss: Aaron's grandson, a priest who stopped the plague at Peor.

names.name: Meribah
names.gloss: The place where Israel quarrelled over water.

insights.title: We have sinned with our fathers
insights.body: "We have sinned with our fathers" (106:6). The speakers do not blame earlier generations but join them. The final plea, "gather us from among the nations" (106:47), suggests the psalm was prayed in exile. Daniel and Nehemiah pray similar confessions.

insights.title: Exchanging glory
insights.body: At Horeb "they exchanged their glory for an image of a bull that eats grass" (106:20). Paul uses the same language in Romans 1: people exchanged the glory of God for images of humans and animals.

insights.title: Leanness into their soul
insights.body: "He gave them their request, but sent leanness into their soul" (106:15). When Israel craved meat, God sent quails, but a plague followed. Getting what they demanded left them poorer.

insights.title: Standing in the breach
insights.body: Moses "stood before him in the breach" (106:23), like a soldier filling a gap in a city wall, to turn away God's wrath after the golden calf. Ezekiel later says God looked for someone to stand in the gap and found none.

insights.title: Credited as righteousness
insights.body: Phinehas' zeal at Baal Peor "was credited to him for righteousness" (106:31), the same phrase used of Abraham's faith in Genesis 15. The episode is violent and troubling; the psalm presents it as stopping a plague that was killing thousands.

insights.title: Sacrifices to demons
insights.body: "They sacrificed their sons and their daughters to demons" (106:37). Child sacrifice was practised in Canaanite and Phoenician religion, and some kings of Judah did it in the valley of Hinnom. Israel's law and prophets condemned it utterly.

insights.title: End of Book 4
insights.body: The doxology "Blessed be Yahweh, the God of Israel, from everlasting even to everlasting! Let all the people say, 'Amen'" (106:48) closes Book 4. Chronicles quotes it, with verses 1 and 47, in David's song for the ark.

insights.title: Mercy after mercy
insights.body: "He rescued them many times, but they were rebellious" (106:43), "Nevertheless he regarded their distress" (106:44). What does this long pattern say about God's patience, and about human memory?

107.summary: Opening Book 5, the redeemed are called to give thanks, and four scenes show people in desert, prison, sickness and storm who cry to Yahweh and are rescued.
107.lookfor: Watch the repeated pattern in each scene: trouble, crying out, rescue and a refrain of thanks; then the wisdom ending.

insights.title: Book 5 answers Book 4
insights.body: Psalm 106 ended with "gather us from among the nations" (Psalm 106:47). Psalm 107, opening Book 5, begins with the redeemed "gathered out of the lands, from the east and from the west, from the north and from the south" (107:3). The prayer has been answered.

insights.title: Four rescues
insights.body: Four groups are described: lost travellers (107:4-9), prisoners (107:10-16), the sick (107:17-22) and sailors (107:23-32). Each time "they cried to Yahweh in their trouble, and he delivered them", followed by the refrain "Let them praise Yahweh for his loving kindness".

insights.title: Some by their own fault
insights.body: The prisoners "rebelled against the words of God" (107:11), and the sick were "Fools... afflicted because of their disobedience" (107:17). The wanderers and sailors are not blamed. God rescues in both cases when people cry out.

insights.title: He sends his word
insights.body: "He sends his word, and heals them" (107:20). The centurion asked Jesus only to say the word and his servant would be healed. God's word is pictured as a messenger that goes out and acts.

insights.title: Calming the storm
insights.body: "He makes the storm a calm, so that its waves are still" (107:29). When Jesus calmed the storm on the Sea of Galilee, his disciples asked who this was that even the wind and sea obey. The psalm had given that power to Yahweh.

insights.title: Those who go down to the sea
insights.body: Israel was not a seafaring nation, and the sea was feared as a place of chaos. The vivid scene of ships rising to the sky and sailors staggering like drunk men (107:23-27) shows real knowledge of storms. Verses 23–30 are often read at services for seafarers.

insights.title: Let the redeemed say so
insights.body: "Let the redeemed by Yahweh say so" (107:2) uses ga'al, the verb for a kinsman buying back a relative. Being rescued creates an obligation to tell. The psalm ends by calling the wise to consider these loving kindnesses (107:43).

insights.title: At wits' end
insights.body: The sailors are "at their wits' end" (107:27) when they cry out. Why do people often turn to God only when they have run out of their own resources, and does God mind?

108.summary: A new psalm made from two older ones: the praise of Psalm 57 is joined to God's promise and the plea for help from Psalm 60.
108.lookfor: Compare it with Psalm 57:7-11 and Psalm 60:5-12, and notice what is left out.

names.name: Shechem
names.gloss: An ancient city in the central hill country west of the Jordan.

names.name: Succoth
names.gloss: A town in the Jordan valley east of the river.

names.name: Gilead
names.gloss: The hill country east of the Jordan.

names.name: Moab
names.gloss: A kingdom east of the Dead Sea.

names.name: Edom
names.gloss: A kingdom south-east of the Dead Sea, descended from Esau.

names.name: Philistia
names.gloss: The land of the Philistines on the southern coast.

insights.title: Two psalms joined
insights.body: Verses 1–5 repeat the end of Psalm 57, and verses 6–13 repeat the second half of Psalm 60. The editors combined a song of confidence with a prayer for victory to make a new prayer.

insights.title: Praise first
insights.body: Psalm 60 opened with "God, you have rejected us". Psalm 108 leaves out that bitter opening and begins instead with "My heart is steadfast" (108:1). The same promises are now read in the light of praise.

insights.title: Why Edom again?
insights.body: "Who has led me to Edom?" (108:10). Edom became especially hated after it joined in the plunder of Jerusalem in 586 BC, as Obadiah and Psalm 137 show. Reusing this old prayer may reflect that later bitterness.

insights.title: Your beloved
insights.body: "That your beloved may be delivered" (108:6) uses yedidim, beloved ones. The same root appears in Jedidiah, beloved of Yah, the name Nathan gave to Solomon. God's people are described as his beloved.

insights.title: Wash pot and sandal
insights.body: "Moab is my wash pot. I will toss my sandal on Edom" (108:9). A wash basin was a menial household item, and casting a sandal over land may have symbolised taking possession. Israel's proud neighbours become God's household servants.

insights.title: Reusing old prayers
insights.body: Psalm 108 shows God's people taking older prayers and reshaping them for new needs. What prayers from the past might be worth reusing in the present?

109.summary: Repaid with hatred for his love, the psalmist faces a torrent of curses, asks God to deal with his accusers and to save him, and trusts that God stands at the right hand of the needy.
109.lookfor: Notice the change from "they" to "him" at verse 6, the long series of curses, and the contrast between the accuser at the right hand and God at the right hand.

insights.title: Whose curses?
insights.body: Verses 6–19 are a long string of curses on one person, while the enemies before and after are plural. Many scholars think these verses quote what the enemies say against the psalmist, which he then hands back to God: "This is the reward of my adversaries" (109:20). Others read them as the psalmist's own prayer.

insights.title: An accuser at his right hand
insights.body: "Let an adversary stand at his right hand" (109:6) uses satan, which means accuser. In a court the accuser stood at the defendant's right. In Zechariah, the Satan stands at the high priest's right hand to accuse him.

insights.title: But I am in prayer
insights.body: "In return for my love, they are my adversaries; but I am in prayer" (109:4). The Hebrew is simply but I, prayer. The psalmist's whole response to hatred is to pray.

insights.title: Another takes his office
insights.body: Peter quotes verse 8, "Let another take his office", when the apostles choose Matthias to replace Judas. The early church read this psalm of betrayal in light of Judas.

insights.title: Left out of daily prayer
insights.body: Psalm 109 is the most severe of the cursing psalms. When the Catholic Liturgy of the Hours was revised after the Second Vatican Council, Psalms 58, 83 and 109 were left out of the cycle of daily prayer because of their curses, though they remain in the Bible.

insights.title: God at the right hand
insights.body: The psalm ends with God who "will stand at the right hand of the needy, to save him from those who judge his soul" (109:31). Where an accuser was asked to stand (109:6), God takes his place as defender.

insights.title: Clothed in cursing
insights.body: "He clothed himself also with cursing as with his garment" (109:18). How does a habit of cursing others come to surround and soak into the one who practises it?

110.summary: Yahweh invites the king to sit at his right hand until his enemies are subdued, and swears that he is a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek.
110.lookfor: Notice the two divine speeches, the mention of Melchizedek, and the warrior images at the end.

names.name: Zion
names.gloss: Jerusalem, from which the king's rule extends.

names.name: Melchizedek
names.gloss: The ancient priest-king of Salem who blessed Abraham.

insights.title: The New Testament's favourite psalm
insights.body: Psalm 110 is quoted or echoed in the New Testament more than any other Old Testament passage. Its first verse is the source of the creed's confession that Christ sits at the right hand of the Father.

insights.title: David's Lord
insights.body: "Yahweh says to my Lord" (110:1). Jesus asked how the Messiah could be David's son if David calls him Lord. In Hebrew the first word is the divine name and the second is adoni, my lord, a title for a king or master.

insights.title: Enemies as a footstool
insights.body: "Until I make your enemies your footstool" (110:1). Egyptian art shows pharaohs resting their feet on images of bound enemies; a footstool from Tutankhamun's tomb is decorated this way. The image is of total victory.

insights.title: Priest like Melchizedek
insights.body: "You are a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek" (110:4). Melchizedek was both king of Salem and priest of God Most High. A king in Jerusalem could claim his double role. Hebrews builds a long argument from this verse about Christ's priesthood.

insights.title: Dew from the womb of the morning
insights.body: Verse 3 is one of the most obscure in the Psalms. The Hebrew seems to picture the king's youthful strength fresh like the dew of dawn. The Greek translation reads from the womb before the morning star I have begotten you, which church fathers read of the Son's eternal birth.

insights.title: Jewish readings
insights.body: Rabbinic tradition read the psalm in various ways: of Abraham, to whom Melchizedek's priesthood was said to pass, of David, and of the Messiah. Christian interpretation from the start read it of Jesus.

insights.title: Drinking from the brook
insights.body: "He will drink of the brook on the way; therefore he will lift up his head" (110:7). The warrior king pauses in pursuit to refresh himself and goes on with renewed strength. Samson and Gideon's men drank in the middle of battle.

insights.title: A sworn promise
insights.body: "Yahweh has sworn, and will not change his mind" (110:4). Why might it matter that this priesthood rests on God's oath rather than on family descent?

111.summary: An alphabet hymn praises Yahweh's great works, his faithfulness to his covenant and his trustworthy precepts, ending with the fear of Yahweh as the beginning of wisdom.
111.lookfor: Notice how many times God's works are mentioned, and compare the phrases with those in Psalm 112.

insights.title: Twin acrostics
insights.body: Psalms 111 and 112 are both alphabet poems in which each half-line begins with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet, 22 lines each. Both begin "Praise Yah!" Psalm 111 describes God; Psalm 112 describes the person who fears him.

insights.title: Righteousness endures forever
insights.body: "His righteousness endures forever" (111:3) is said of God here and of the God-fearing person twice in Psalm 112. The righteous person comes to share God's character.

insights.title: Gracious and merciful
insights.body: "Yahweh is gracious and merciful" (111:4) again echoes God's self-revelation to Moses. Psalm 112:4 uses the same words of the upright person.

insights.title: Food to those who fear him
insights.body: "He has given food to those who fear him" (111:5). The word for food usually means prey, food torn by a hunting animal. It may recall the manna and quail in the wilderness, given in remembrance of his covenant.

insights.title: Beginning of wisdom
insights.body: "The fear of Yahweh is the beginning of wisdom" (111:10) is the motto of Proverbs. Fear here means reverent awe and obedience, not terror. Wisdom starts with taking God seriously.

insights.title: Works pondered
insights.body: "Yahweh's works are great, pondered by all those who delight in them" (111:2). This verse has been inscribed over the entrance of the old Cavendish Laboratory in Cambridge, inviting scientists to study creation as God's work.

insights.title: Remembered wonders
insights.body: "He has caused his wonderful works to be remembered" (111:4). Through festivals, stories and songs God builds memory into worship. What practices help people remember what God has done?

112.summary: A matching alphabet poem describes the blessed person who fears Yahweh: generous, just and steady, unafraid of bad news, whose righteousness endures forever.
112.lookfor: Compare each line with Psalm 111, and notice how generosity and fearlessness belong together here.

insights.title: Picking up where 111 ended
insights.body: Psalm 111 ended with the fear of Yahweh as the beginning of wisdom. Psalm 112 begins: "Blessed is the man who fears Yahweh" (112:1). It describes what that wisdom looks like in a life.

insights.title: Like God
insights.body: Phrases used of God in Psalm 111 are now used of the righteous person: his righteousness endures forever (112:3), he is "gracious, merciful, and righteous" (112:4). People who fear God come to resemble him.

insights.title: Lending and giving
insights.body: "It is well with the man who deals graciously and lends" (112:5). Israel's law required interest-free loans to the poor and cancelled debts every seventh year. Generosity was part of righteousness.

insights.title: He has given to the poor
insights.body: Paul quotes verse 9, "He has dispersed, he has given to the poor. His righteousness endures forever", when encouraging the Corinthians to give generously to the poor believers in Jerusalem.

insights.title: A steadfast heart
insights.body: "He will not be afraid of evil news. His heart is steadfast, trusting in Yahweh" (112:7). The word steadfast means firmly established. This person's security is not that bad news never comes but that the heart is anchored.

insights.title: Light in darkness
insights.body: "Light dawns in the darkness for the upright" (112:4). The righteous are not spared darkness but find light within it. Isaiah promises that those who pour themselves out for the hungry will see their light rise in darkness.

insights.title: Wealth and righteousness
insights.body: The psalm says "Wealth and riches are in his house" (112:3), yet the righteous person gives freely (112:9). How does this psalm connect blessing with generosity rather than accumulation?

113.summary: The first Hallel psalm praises Yahweh's name from sunrise to sunset: he is enthroned on high, yet stoops to lift the poor from the dust and give the childless woman a home.
113.lookfor: Notice the contrast between God's height and his stooping, and who he lifts up.

insights.title: The Passover Hallel
insights.body: Psalms 113–118 are called the Hallel, praise, or the Egyptian Hallel because Psalm 114 recalls the exodus. They are sung at Passover and other festivals. According to the Mishnah, Psalm 113, and in one view 114, was sung before the Passover meal and the rest afterward.

insights.title: The hymn at the Last Supper
insights.body: After the Last Supper, Matthew and Mark say Jesus and his disciples sang a hymn before going out to the Mount of Olives. If the meal was a Passover, this was probably the second part of the Hallel, Psalms 115–118.

insights.title: High and stooping
insights.body: "Who is like Yahweh, our God, who has his seat on high, who stoops down to see in heaven and in the earth?" (113:5-6). God is so high that he must stoop even to look at the heavens, and yet he does look, all the way down to the dust.

insights.title: Hannah's song
insights.body: "He raises up the poor out of the dust. Lifts up the needy from the ash heap; that he may set him with princes" (113:7-8) repeats Hannah's song almost word for word. Mary's Magnificat sings the same reversal.

insights.title: The ash heap
insights.body: The ash heap was a town's rubbish dump outside the walls, where outcasts and beggars sat. Job sat among the ashes in his suffering. God lifts people from the dump to the royal court.

insights.title: The barren woman
insights.body: "He settles the barren woman in her home, as a joyful mother of children" (113:9). In a society where a woman's security often depended on having children, childlessness was a deep grief. Sarah, Rachel, Hannah and Elizabeth all experienced it.

insights.title: Who is like Yahweh?
insights.body: The psalm's answer to "Who is like Yahweh?" is that his greatness shows itself in lifting the lowly. How does that change what greatness means?

114.summary: A short, vivid poem retells the exodus as nature's reaction: the sea flees, the Jordan turns back, mountains skip like rams, and the earth trembles before the God of Jacob.
114.lookfor: Notice the paired images, the playful questions to the sea and mountains, and the final miracle of water from rock.

insights.title: Sea and river
insights.body: "The sea saw it, and fled. The Jordan was driven back" (114:3) joins the beginning and end of the wilderness journey: the Red Sea crossing and the Jordan crossing under Joshua.

insights.title: Judah his sanctuary
insights.body: "Judah became his sanctuary, Israel his dominion" (114:2). God's holy place is not first a building but a people. The psalm never names God until verse 7, building suspense about who caused all this.

insights.title: Skipping mountains
insights.body: "The mountains skipped like rams, the little hills like lambs" (114:4) pictures Sinai quaking when God came down. The poem then playfully asks the sea and mountains what happened to them (114:5-6).

insights.title: Rock into water
insights.body: "Who turned the rock into a pool of water, the flint into a spring" (114:8) recalls the water from the rock in the wilderness. Paul says the rock that followed Israel was Christ.

insights.title: Dante's psalm
insights.body: In Dante's Purgatorio, the souls arriving by boat at the mountain of Purgatory sing In exitu Israel de Aegypto, the Latin opening of this psalm. Medieval readers saw the exodus as a picture of the soul's release from sin.

insights.title: One psalm or two
insights.body: The Greek and Latin Bibles join Psalms 114 and 115 into one psalm, while splitting Psalm 116 into two. This is one more reason the numbering differs between Hebrew-based and Greek-based Bibles.

insights.title: Tremble, earth
insights.body: "Tremble, you earth, at the presence of the Lord" (114:7). If even mountains respond to God's presence, how should people respond?

115.summary: Giving glory to God's name and not to themselves, the people mock lifeless idols and call all Israel, the priests and all who fear Yahweh to trust him and receive his blessing.
115.lookfor: Notice the description of idols, the three groups called to trust, and the blessing that follows.

insights.title: Non nobis
insights.body: "Not to us, Yahweh, not to us, but to your name give glory" (115:1) is known in Latin as Non nobis. In Shakespeare's Henry V the king orders it sung after the victory at Agincourt. It has often been sung to give God credit for success.

insights.title: Idols that can't
insights.body: Idols have mouths, eyes, ears, noses, hands and feet, but cannot speak, see, hear, smell, feel or walk (115:5-7). The list mocks the effort of human hands. Psalm 135 repeats it, and Isaiah develops it at length.

insights.title: Becoming like what you worship
insights.body: "Those who make them will be like them" (115:8). People become like what they trust: worship of the lifeless makes people lifeless. Jeremiah says Israel went after worthless things and became worthless.

insights.title: Three groups
insights.body: The call to trust goes to Israel, the house of Aaron, and "You who fear Yahweh" (115:9-11). The third group may mean all the faithful, or Gentiles who worshipped Israel's God, like the God-fearers in Acts. Psalms 118 and 135 use the same three groups.

insights.title: Heaven and earth
insights.body: "The heavens are the heavens of Yahweh; but the earth has he given to the children of men" (115:16) echoes Genesis, where humans are given rule over the earth. Responsibility for the earth is a gift from its Owner.

insights.title: We will bless
insights.body: "The dead don't praise Yah... But we will bless Yah" (115:17-18). The living have a task the dead cannot do. The psalm ends with the community's resolve to praise from now on.

insights.title: Where is their God?
insights.body: The nations ask "Where is their God, now?" (115:2), since Israel's God has no image. How does the psalm answer, and what does it suggest about a God who cannot be seen?

116.summary: Rescued from the cords of death, the psalmist declares his love for Yahweh, asks what he can give in return, and resolves to lift the cup of salvation and pay his vows in public.
116.lookfor: Notice the first words of the psalm, the question about repaying God, and the cup and vows at the temple.

names.name: Sheol
names.gloss: The realm of the dead.

insights.title: I love Yahweh
insights.body: The psalm opens abruptly: "I love Yahweh, because he listens to my voice" (116:1). It is one of very few places where someone says directly that they love God. Love grows from being heard.

insights.title: Return to your rest
insights.body: "Return to your rest, my soul" (116:7). The psalmist speaks to his own soul, as in Psalms 42 and 103. Rest here is the calm after danger, restored because God has dealt generously.

insights.title: I believed, therefore I said
insights.body: "I believed, therefore I said" (116:10) is quoted by Paul in its Greek form: we also believe, and therefore we also speak. Faith that has been tested must speak.

insights.title: The cup of salvation
insights.body: "I will take the cup of salvation" (116:13) probably refers to a cup of wine raised at a thanksgiving meal or poured out as an offering. Since this psalm belongs to the Passover Hallel, Christians have connected it with the cup Jesus took at the Last Supper.

insights.title: Precious death
insights.body: "Precious in Yahweh's sight is the death of his saints" (116:15). Precious here means costly or weighty: God does not let his faithful ones die cheaply or unnoticed. It is God's reason for rescuing the psalmist from death.

insights.title: Vows in public
insights.body: The psalmist will pay his vows "in the presence of all his people, in the courts of Yahweh's house" (116:18-19). Thanksgiving was public; the rescued person brought an offering and shared a meal with others, telling them the story.

insights.title: What can I give?
insights.body: "What will I give to Yahweh for all his benefits toward me?" (116:12). The answer is to take, to call, and to pay vows (116:13-14). Why might receiving be the first way to repay God?

117.summary: The shortest psalm calls all nations and peoples to praise Yahweh for his great love and lasting faithfulness.
117.lookfor: Notice who is invited to praise, and the reason given in only two lines.

insights.title: Short and wide
insights.body: Psalm 117 has only two verses, the shortest chapter in the Bible. Yet its reach is the widest: "all you nations... all you peoples" (117:1). Israel's experience of God's love is a reason for the whole world to praise.

insights.title: Gentiles praising
insights.body: Paul quotes verse 1 in Romans 15 among several Old Testament texts showing that God always intended the Gentiles to glorify him for his mercy.

insights.title: Great toward us
insights.body: "His loving kindness is great toward us" (117:2) uses a verb meaning to prevail or be mighty. God's love has overpowered everything against it. The pair of loving kindness and faithfulness sums up God's covenant character.

insights.title: Laudate Dominum
insights.body: In Latin the psalm begins Laudate Dominum omnes gentes. Mozart's setting in his Vespers of 1780 is among the best-known pieces of church music. By a common count of chapters in Protestant Bibles, Psalm 117 is also the middle chapter of the Bible.

insights.title: Inside the Hallel
insights.body: Psalm 117 sits within the Hallel psalms sung at Passover. After Psalms 115–116, focused on Israel and one person, it opens the circle to all nations before the great thanksgiving of Psalm 118.

insights.title: Why the nations?
insights.body: The nations are told to praise God for his love "toward us" (117:2), that is, toward Israel. How can God's faithfulness to one people be good news for everyone?

118.summary: A festival thanksgiving tells how Yahweh rescued the speaker when surrounded by enemies, and ends with a procession through the temple gates, celebrating the rejected stone that became the cornerstone.
118.lookfor: Notice the call-and-response refrain, the gates of righteousness, the stone, and the cry "Save us now" with the blessing on the one who comes.

insights.title: A procession
insights.body: Psalm 118 is the last of the Hallel psalms and was sung at festivals, especially Tabernacles. It seems to follow a procession: a call-and-response refrain (118:1-4), a testimony (118:5-18), entry through the gates (118:19-20) and a festive offering at the altar (118:27).

insights.title: The rejected stone
insights.body: "The stone which the builders rejected has become the cornerstone" (118:22) is quoted by Jesus after his parable of the wicked tenants, by Peter before the council, and in 1 Peter. It became a key text for Jesus' rejection and vindication.

insights.title: Hosanna
insights.body: "Save us now, we beg you, Yahweh!" (118:25) is in Hebrew hoshia na, which became Hosanna. The crowds shouted it, with "Blessed is he who comes in Yahweh's name" (118:26), as Jesus rode into Jerusalem.

insights.title: Around the altar
insights.body: "Bind the sacrifice with cords, even to the horns of the altar" (118:27) is hard to translate; it may mean bind the festival procession with branches up to the altar. The Mishnah describes priests circling the altar at Tabernacles with willow branches, crying the words of verse 25.

insights.title: What can man do?
insights.body: "Yahweh is on my side. I will not be afraid. What can man do to me?" (118:6) is quoted in Hebrews to encourage contentment and courage.

insights.title: Luther's own psalm
insights.body: Martin Luther called Psalm 118 his own beloved psalm and wrote a commentary on it in 1530 while confined at Coburg Castle. Verse 17, "I will not die, but live, and declare Yah's works", was one he especially treasured.

insights.title: The day Yahweh has made
insights.body: "This is the day that Yahweh has made. We will rejoice and be glad in it!" (118:24) refers to the day of rescue and celebration. Christians sing it especially at Easter, the day of the rejected stone's vindication.

insights.title: Severe but not to death
insights.body: "Yah has punished me severely, but he has not given me over to death" (118:18). How can hardship and rescue both be seen as coming from God's hand?

119.summary: The Bible's longest chapter is an alphabet poem of 22 stanzas in which the psalmist, often under pressure from proud enemies, delights in God's word, asks to be taught and revived by it, and ends confessing he is a lost sheep.
119.lookfor: Notice the eight different words for God's instruction, the mix of love and lament, and how the poem ends.

skim.advice: Each eight-verse stanza circles the same themes; read a few stanzas slowly rather than racing through all 176 verses, and pay special attention to the verses listed here.

insights.title: An alphabet of devotion
insights.body: Psalm 119 has 176 verses in 22 stanzas, one for each letter of the Hebrew alphabet. All eight verses in a stanza begin with the same letter, which is why WEB prints headings like ALEPH and BET. The form suggests completeness: devotion to God's word from A to Z.

insights.title: Eight words for God's word
insights.body: The psalm uses eight main terms: law (torah), testimonies, precepts, statutes, commandments, ordinances, word and promise. Nearly every verse contains at least one. Each highlights a different side of God's instruction: teaching, witness, charge, decree, command, judgment and spoken word.

insights.title: Love, not mere rule-keeping
insights.body: The psalm is full of love and longing: "How I love your law! It is my meditation all day" (119:97), and "I rejoice at your word, as one who finds great plunder" (119:162). The law is a relationship with its Giver, addressed as "you" throughout.

insights.title: A lamp to my feet
insights.body: "Your word is a lamp to my feet, and a light for my path" (119:105). Ancient oil lamps were small clay bowls that lit only a few steps ahead. God's word gives enough light for the next step, not the whole road.

insights.title: Under pressure
insights.body: The psalm is not written from comfort. Princes slander and persecute the psalmist (119:23, 119:161), the proud dig pits (119:85), and he is like "a wineskin in the smoke" (119:83), dried out and shrivelled. Yet he says "It is good for me that I have been afflicted" (119:71).

insights.title: Midnight and seven times a day
insights.body: "At midnight I will rise to give thanks to you" (119:62) and "Seven times a day, I praise you" (119:164) shaped Christian monastic prayer. St Benedict's Rule cites these verses for the night office and the seven daytime hours, and assigns parts of Psalm 119 to be prayed each day.

insights.title: A lost sheep
insights.body: After 175 verses of devotion, the psalm ends: "I have gone astray like a lost sheep. Seek your servant" (119:176). Love for God's word does not make the psalmist self-sufficient. Isaiah says all we like sheep have gone astray, and Jesus tells of the shepherd who seeks the lost one.

insights.title: Hidden in the heart
insights.body: "I have hidden your word in my heart, that I might not sin against you" (119:11). What might it mean to carry God's words inside, so that they are present when they are needed?

120.summary: The first of the Songs of Ascents: a person surrounded by lying tongues and people who hate peace cries to Yahweh, feeling like an exile among hostile strangers.
120.lookfor: Notice the focus on deceitful speech, the strange place names, and the contrast between peace and war.

names.name: Meshech
names.gloss: A people of the far north, in what is now eastern Turkey.

names.name: Kedar
names.gloss: Nomadic Arab tribes of the Syrian-Arabian desert, descended from Ishmael.

insights.title: Songs of Ascents
insights.body: Psalms 120–134 each carry the title A Song of Ascents. Most scholars think they were sung by pilgrims going up to Jerusalem for the festivals. The Mishnah links them with fifteen steps in the temple on which the Levites sang, and some connect them with the return from exile.

insights.title: Starting far away
insights.body: The collection begins far from Jerusalem, among liars and people who want war (120:6-7). The journey of the Ascents moves from exile and distress toward the house of God, ending with blessing in the temple at night in Psalm 134.

insights.title: Meshech and Kedar
insights.body: "Woe is me, that I live in Meshech, that I dwell among the tents of Kedar!" (120:5). Meshech was far north near the Black Sea and Kedar in the Arabian desert. No one could live in both, so the names are probably a figure for living among hostile, foreign people.

insights.title: Coals of juniper
insights.body: The punishment for the deceitful tongue is "Sharp arrows of the mighty, with coals of juniper" (120:4). The plant is the broom tree, whose wood makes long-burning, intensely hot charcoal. Elijah rested under a broom tree.

insights.title: I am peace
insights.body: "I am for peace" (120:7) is literally I am peace. The psalmist's whole identity is shalom, yet every word he speaks is met with hostility. Jesus blesses peacemakers.

insights.title: Lying lips
insights.body: The danger in this psalm is speech: "lying lips... a deceitful tongue" (120:2). The pilgrim sets out longing to leave a world of deceit for the place where God's truth is honoured.

insights.title: Too long
insights.body: "My soul has had her dwelling too long with him who hates peace" (120:6). What is it like to feel out of place in one's own surroundings, and how might that start a journey toward God?

121.summary: A pilgrim looks to the hills and finds that help comes from Yahweh, the Maker of heaven and earth, who never sleeps and will keep him in every going out and coming in.
121.lookfor: Count how many times the word "keep" or "keeper" appears, and notice the dangers of the road mentioned.

insights.title: Looking to the hills
insights.body: "I will lift up my eyes to the hills. Where does my help come from?" (121:1). For a pilgrim, the hills meant a hard climb, possible robbers, and perhaps the hilltop shrines of other gods. The question is answered at once: help comes from the Maker of the hills (121:2).

insights.title: The keeper
insights.body: The Hebrew verb shamar, keep or guard, appears six times (121:3-8). It is the word in the priestly blessing, Yahweh bless you and keep you. God is pictured as a watchman on duty.

insights.title: Neither slumbers nor sleeps
insights.body: "He who keeps Israel will neither slumber nor sleep" (121:4). Elijah mocked the prophets of Baal that their god might be asleep. The God of Israel needs no rest and is never off duty.

insights.title: Sun and moon
insights.body: "The sun will not harm you by day, nor the moon by night" (121:6). Sunstroke was a real danger for travellers. Many ancient people also believed the moon caused illness; the Greek word for epileptic in Matthew literally means moonstruck.

insights.title: Shade on the right hand
insights.body: "Yahweh is your shade on your right hand" (121:5). In a land of strong sun, shade meant survival. The right hand was the side of a protector or defender.

insights.title: Going out and coming in
insights.body: "Yahweh will keep your going out and your coming in" (121:8) covers every journey and all of life's activities, from leaving home in the morning to returning at night. It echoes the blessings of Deuteronomy. Many Jews and Christians pray this psalm before travelling.

insights.title: Where does my help come from?
insights.body: The psalm asks a question everyone faces. What hills do people today look to for help, and what difference does it make to look past them to their Maker?

122.summary: A pilgrim recalls the joy of setting out for Yahweh's house, now stands inside Jerusalem's gates, and prays for the peace and good of the city.
122.lookfor: Notice the moment of arrival, the description of the city, and how often the word peace appears.

insights.title: From invitation to arrival
insights.body: "I was glad when they said to me, 'Let's go to Yahweh's house!'" (122:1) recalls the invitation; "Our feet are standing within your gates" (122:2) celebrates arrival. The journey of the Ascents reaches its goal.

insights.title: Where the tribes go up
insights.body: "Where the tribes go up... according to an ordinance for Israel" (122:4). The law required Israelite men to appear before God three times a year at the festivals of Passover, Weeks and Tabernacles. Jerusalem was the meeting point of the whole nation.

insights.title: Peace and Jerusalem
insights.body: "Pray for the peace of Jerusalem" (122:6) is full of wordplay in Hebrew: shalom (peace), Yerushalayim (Jerusalem) and the words for prosper and security all sound alike. The city's name was popularly heard as containing the word peace.

insights.title: Compact together
insights.body: "Jerusalem, that is built as a city that is compact together" (122:3) describes tightly packed buildings within the walls. It may also suggest a people bound together in unity.

insights.title: I was glad
insights.body: Hubert Parry's anthem I was glad, setting this psalm, has been sung at the entrance of the monarch at every British coronation since 1902. The psalm's joy at entering God's house has been heard in many settings of arrival.

insights.title: Thrones of judgment
insights.body: "For there are set thrones for judgment, the thrones of David's house" (122:5). Jerusalem was both the place of worship and of royal justice. A city at peace needs both God's presence and fair courts.

insights.title: Seeking the city's good
insights.body: "For the sake of the house of Yahweh our God, I will seek your good" (122:9). Jeremiah told the exiles to seek the peace of Babylon too. What might it look like to seek the good of the place one lives?

123.summary: Worn out by the scorn of the proud, the people lift their eyes to God enthroned in heaven, like servants watching their master's hand, and ask for mercy.
123.lookfor: Notice the picture of servants watching a hand, and the repeated plea for mercy.

insights.title: Watching the master's hand
insights.body: "As the eyes of servants look to the hand of their master... so our eyes look to Yahweh" (123:2). A household servant watched for a signal, a gift or a command from the master's hand. The people wait attentively, dependent on God's next move.

insights.title: Lifting the eyes again
insights.body: "To you I do lift up my eyes" (123:1) picks up Psalm 121, where the pilgrim lifted his eyes to the hills. Here the gaze goes higher, to the one who sits in the heavens.

insights.title: Contempt of the comfortable
insights.body: "Our soul is exceedingly filled with the scoffing of those who are at ease, with the contempt of the proud" (123:4). This fits the time after the exile, when neighbours like Sanballat mocked the Jews rebuilding Jerusalem's walls.

insights.title: Have mercy on us
insights.body: "Have mercy on us, Yahweh, have mercy on us" (123:3) uses a verb meaning to show favour or grace. In the Greek translation the cry is eleeson, the root of the ancient Christian prayer Kyrie eleison, Lord, have mercy.

insights.title: Until he has mercy
insights.body: The servants watch "until he has mercy on us" (123:2). Prayer here is persistent attention, not a single request. The psalm ends without an answer, still waiting.

insights.title: Enduring contempt
insights.body: The psalm does not answer scorn with scorn but looks to God. How might looking to God change the way someone bears contempt?

124.summary: Israel is invited to say that if Yahweh had not been on their side, they would have been swallowed alive and swept away, but they escaped like a bird from a snare.
124.lookfor: Notice the repeated "if it had not been Yahweh", the flood and trap images, and the closing confession.

insights.title: Let Israel now say
insights.body: "If it had not been Yahweh who was on our side, let Israel now say" (124:1). A leader speaks the first line and the people repeat it (124:2). The whole community confesses that its survival is God's doing.

insights.title: Swallowed alive
insights.body: "They would have swallowed us up alive" (124:3) recalls the earth swallowing Korah's rebels and the great fish swallowing Jonah. Enemies are pictured as a monstrous mouth.

insights.title: Proud waters
insights.body: "Then the proud waters would have gone over our soul" (124:5). Floodwaters are given human arrogance. A flash flood in a dry wadi can sweep away everything in minutes, a picture of sudden disaster.

insights.title: The fowler's snare
insights.body: "Our soul has escaped like a bird out of the fowler's snare" (124:7). Bird-catchers used nets and spring traps. A trapped bird cannot free itself; only a broken snare lets it go.

insights.title: Our help is in the name
insights.body: "Our help is in Yahweh's name, who made heaven and earth" (124:8) became a standard opening in Christian worship, especially before confession and at night prayer, often answered by the people. Calvin's Geneva service began with it.

insights.title: If not for God
insights.body: The psalm imagines what would have happened without God. What does looking back on near disasters, and seeing God's hand in them, do for faith?

125.summary: Those who trust Yahweh are as unshakable as Mount Zion and surrounded by him as Jerusalem is by mountains, and the psalm asks God to do good to the upright and bring peace on Israel.
125.lookfor: Notice the picture of mountains around the city, the concern about wicked rule, and the closing blessing.

names.name: Zion
names.gloss: Jerusalem's temple hill.

insights.title: Mountains around Jerusalem
insights.body: "As the mountains surround Jerusalem, so Yahweh surrounds his people" (125:2). Jerusalem sits on hills that are lower than the ridges around it, including the Mount of Olives to the east. Pilgrims arriving would see the city ringed by heights.

insights.title: Like Zion
insights.body: "Those who trust in Yahweh are as Mount Zion, which can't be moved" (125:1). It is not the mountain's height that makes it secure but God's presence there. Trust gives people the same stability.

insights.title: The sceptre of wickedness
insights.body: "The scepter of wickedness won't remain over the allotment of the righteous; so that the righteous won't use their hands to do evil" (125:3). Foreign or corrupt rule could pressure people into compromise. The psalm trusts it will not last long enough to corrupt the faithful.

insights.title: Crooked ways
insights.body: "Those who turn away to their crooked ways" (125:5) uses a word for twisted, winding paths. The upright walk straight; the faithless wander off on side roads.

insights.title: Peace be on Israel
insights.body: The psalm closes with "Peace be on Israel" (125:5), as does Psalm 128. Paul ends Galatians with a similar blessing of peace on the Israel of God.

insights.title: Surrounded
insights.body: The image of God surrounding his people (125:2) speaks of protection on every side. In what situations might that picture be most needed?

126.summary: Remembering the dreamlike joy when Yahweh brought the exiles back to Zion, the people ask him to restore them again, trusting that those who sow in tears will reap with songs of joy.
126.lookfor: Notice the laughter and dreaming, the streams in the desert, and the farmer sowing in tears.

names.name: Zion
names.gloss: Jerusalem.

names.name: Negev
names.gloss: The dry southern desert of Judah, where streambeds fill only after rain.

insights.title: Like those who dream
insights.body: "When Yahweh brought back those who returned to Zion, we were like those who dream" (126:1) probably remembers the return from Babylon after Cyrus' decree in 538 BC. It was so wonderful it seemed unreal. Then reality set in, and the people pray for further restoration (126:4).

insights.title: Great things
insights.body: First the nations say "Yahweh has done great things for them" (126:2), then Israel echoes, "Yahweh has done great things for us" (126:3). The outsiders' testimony comes first. Mary's song says the Mighty One has done great things for me.

insights.title: Streams in the Negev
insights.body: "Restore our fortunes again, Yahweh, like the streams in the Negev" (126:4). The Negev's dry streambeds are empty for most of the year, but winter rains can fill them suddenly with rushing water and the desert blooms. The people ask for that kind of sudden renewal.

insights.title: Sowing in tears
insights.body: "Those who sow in tears will reap in joy" (126:5). Seed was precious in hard times; sowing it instead of eating it was an act of sorrowful hope. Jesus says his disciples' grief will turn to joy, and Paul says in due season we will reap.

insights.title: Sung before grace
insights.body: Jewish families sing Psalm 126 before the blessing after meals on Sabbaths and festivals. A song about joy after exile becomes part of thanks for every festive meal.

insights.title: Joy remembered and hoped for
insights.body: The psalm both remembers past joy and asks for joy again. How does remembering past mercy help people keep sowing in difficult seasons?

127.summary: Unless Yahweh builds the house and guards the city, human effort is in vain; he gives rest to those he loves, and children are his gift.
127.lookfor: Notice the building, guarding and working that come to nothing without God, and the image of children as arrows.

insights.title: By Solomon
insights.body: This is the only Song of Ascents credited to Solomon, the builder of the temple and of much of Jerusalem. A psalm about building houses and guarding cities suits him. "House" can mean a building, a temple or a family line.

insights.title: His loved ones
insights.body: "He gives sleep to his loved ones" (127:2) uses yedid, beloved, the root of Jedidiah, the name God gave Solomon. The phrase can also be read he gives to his beloved while they sleep, recalling Solomon receiving wisdom in a dream.

insights.title: Vain labour
insights.body: The word "vain" appears three times (127:1-2): building, guarding and working long hours. The psalm does not reject work but anxious toil that forgets God. Jesus warns against worry about what we will eat.

insights.title: Arrows and a full quiver
insights.body: "As arrows in the hand of a mighty man, so are the children of youth" (127:4). In a society without police or pensions, grown sons protected their parents and spoke for them "with their enemies in the gate" (127:5), where legal disputes were settled.

insights.title: Nisi Dominus
insights.body: The Latin opening, Nisi Dominus, has been used as a motto by cities and institutions, including the city of Edinburgh, whose motto shortens it to Nisi Dominus frustra, without the Lord, in vain.

insights.title: Children as a gift
insights.body: "Children are a heritage of Yahweh. The fruit of the womb is his reward" (127:3). The Bible repeatedly describes children as gifts from God, not achievements. Hannah gave her son back to God in gratitude.

insights.title: Sleep as a gift
insights.body: The psalm suggests that sleep, not endless work, is a sign of God's love (127:2). What would it mean to trust God enough to rest?

128.summary: The one who fears Yahweh will enjoy the fruit of his work, a fruitful family around his table, and the blessing of Zion through long life.
128.lookfor: Notice the domestic images of table, vine and olive shoots, and how blessing widens from home to Jerusalem.

names.name: Zion
names.gloss: Jerusalem, the source of blessing.

insights.title: Eating your own labour
insights.body: "You will eat the labor of your hands" (128:2) reverses the curses of Deuteronomy, where enemies eat what you have grown. The blessing is to enjoy the results of your own work in peace.

insights.title: Vine and olive shoots
insights.body: "Your wife will be as a fruitful vine... your children like olive plants, around your table" (128:3). Young olive shoots sprout around the base of an old olive tree, which keeps the grove alive for centuries. Vine and olive were the two great crops of the land.

insights.title: A wedding psalm
insights.body: Psalm 128 is often sung or read at Jewish and Christian weddings. Its picture of a household at peace, gathered around the table, has made it a favourite blessing for new families.

insights.title: From home to Zion
insights.body: The blessing moves from the man (128:1) to his household (128:3), to Jerusalem (128:5), to future generations (128:6), and finally to all Israel. Family life is part of the larger life of God's people.

insights.title: Children's children
insights.body: "Yes, may you see your children's children" (128:6). Living to see grandchildren was a sign of a long and blessed life. Proverbs says grandchildren are the crown of the aged.

insights.title: Blessed and blessed
insights.body: The psalm begins with ashre, blessed or happy (128:1), describing the good life, and moves to barak, to be blessed by God (128:4-5), describing its source. The happy life flows from God's blessing.

insights.title: Ordinary blessing
insights.body: This psalm finds God's blessing in work, meals and family. How might seeing these ordinary things as gifts change how people live them?

129.summary: Israel recalls how often it has been afflicted since its youth, as if ploughed across its back, yet never defeated, and asks that those who hate Zion wither like grass on a roof.
129.lookfor: Notice the ploughing image, the cords cut by God, and the missing harvest blessing at the end.

names.name: Zion
names.gloss: Jerusalem.

insights.title: Afflicted from youth
insights.body: "Many times they have afflicted me from my youth up" (129:1). Israel's youth was slavery in Egypt, and its history continued with one oppressor after another. Yet "they have not prevailed against me" (129:2). The nation's survival is itself a testimony.

insights.title: Ploughed on my back
insights.body: "The plowers plowed on my back. They made their furrows long" (129:3) pictures the scars of whipping as furrows cut by a plough. Isaiah uses a similar image for Israel's back laid like the ground for passers-by to walk on.

insights.title: Cords cut
insights.body: "He has cut apart the cords of the wicked" (129:4). The cords may be the ropes that harnessed the ox to the plough. When God cuts them, the ploughing stops.

insights.title: Grass on the housetops
insights.body: "Let them be as the grass on the housetops, which withers before it grows up" (129:6). Flat roofs were made of packed earth, and seeds sprouted in them after rain but dried out quickly in the thin soil. Isaiah uses the same picture for Assyria's victims.

insights.title: The harvest greeting
insights.body: Passers-by would greet reapers with a blessing, and the reapers answered. Boaz greeted his workers, "Yahweh be with you", and they replied, "Yahweh bless you". The enemies will have no harvest to bless (129:8).

insights.title: Not prevailed
insights.body: The psalm holds together long suffering and survival (129:2). What does it take for a community to tell its history honestly, including both the scars and the endurance?

130.summary: From the depths, the psalmist cries for mercy, finds forgiveness in God, waits for him more than watchmen wait for morning, and calls Israel to hope in his abundant redemption.
130.lookfor: Notice the move from personal cry to community hope, the question about keeping a record of sins, and the watchmen.

insights.title: Out of the depths
insights.body: "Out of the depths I have cried to you" (130:1) uses a word for deep waters, the place of drowning. In Latin it begins De profundis, and it is the sixth of the seven penitential psalms. Catholics have traditionally prayed it for the dead.

insights.title: Who could stand?
insights.body: "If you, Yah, kept a record of sins, Lord, who could stand?" (130:3). If God kept accounts, everyone would be condemned. Paul says no one will be justified by works of the law.

insights.title: Forgiveness that creates awe
insights.body: "But there is forgiveness with you, therefore you are feared" (130:4). Surprisingly, forgiveness leads not to carelessness but to reverence. Being forgiven makes God's holiness and mercy both more real.

insights.title: Watchmen for the morning
insights.body: "My soul longs for the Lord more than watchmen long for the morning" (130:6). City watchmen and temple guards watched through the night, waiting for dawn and the end of their shift. The repetition captures the long wait.

insights.title: From all their sins
insights.body: "He will redeem Israel from all their sins" (130:8). The angel told Joseph that Mary's son would be called Jesus because he would save his people from their sins.

insights.title: Luther and Owen
insights.body: Martin Luther turned this psalm into the hymn Aus tiefer Not, From Deep Distress, in 1523–24. The Puritan John Owen wrote a lengthy exposition of it after his own spiritual crisis. It has been one of the most loved psalms of repentance.

insights.title: Waiting with hope
insights.body: "I wait for Yahweh. My soul waits. I hope in his word" (130:5). How is waiting with hope different from simply waiting?

131.summary: In three verses the psalmist lays aside pride and ambition and rests quietly in God like a weaned child with its mother, then calls Israel to hope.
131.lookfor: Notice what the psalmist refuses to do and the gentle image of the weaned child.

insights.title: No lofty eyes
insights.body: "My heart isn't haughty, nor my eyes lofty; nor do I concern myself with great matters, or things too wonderful for me" (131:1). The psalmist chooses to accept the limits of what can be understood. Job came to a similar point.

insights.title: A weaned child
insights.body: "Like a weaned child with his mother" (131:2). In ancient Israel children were often weaned around age two or three; Hannah weaned Samuel before bringing him to the temple. A weaned child no longer cries to be fed but simply rests with its mother.

insights.title: Stilled and quieted
insights.body: "I have stilled and quieted my soul" (131:2). The calm is a deliberate act, not a passing mood. Some scholars suggest the speaker may be a mother, carrying her child up to Jerusalem.

insights.title: Like a child
insights.body: Jesus told his disciples that unless they turned and became like little children they would not enter the Kingdom, and that whoever humbles himself like a child is greatest.

insights.title: Personal to communal
insights.body: The last verse turns from the individual to "Israel, hope in Yahweh" (131:3), repeating the call of Psalm 130. A personal experience of quiet trust becomes an invitation for the whole community.

insights.title: Things too wonderful
insights.body: What might it look like to stop striving to understand or control everything, and to rest in God like a child?

132.summary: The people ask Yahweh to remember David's oath to find a home for the ark, and recall Yahweh's own oath to David to keep his line on the throne and to dwell forever in Zion.
132.lookfor: Notice the two oaths, David's and Yahweh's, and the procession of the ark to its resting place.

names.name: Ephrathah
names.gloss: The region of Bethlehem, David's home town.

names.name: Jaar
names.gloss: Probably Kiriath Jearim, where the ark stayed for twenty years.

names.name: Zion
names.gloss: Jerusalem, chosen as God's resting place.

insights.title: David's vow
insights.body: The psalm recalls David's determination to find "a place for Yahweh, a dwelling for the Mighty One of Jacob" (132:5). David brought the ark to Jerusalem and wanted to build God a house. It may have been sung in a festival re-enacting the ark's arrival.

insights.title: Found in the field of Jaar
insights.body: "We heard of it in Ephrathah. We found it in the field of Jaar" (132:6). After the Philistines returned the ark, it stayed for twenty years at Kiriath Jearim, the town of forests, until David brought it up.

insights.title: Solomon's dedication
insights.body: "Arise, Yahweh, into your resting place; you, and the ark of your strength" (132:8-10) is quoted at the end of Solomon's prayer at the temple's dedication in Chronicles.

insights.title: Two oaths
insights.body: David swore to Yahweh (132:2), and Yahweh swore to David (132:11). God's oath includes a condition: "If your children will keep my covenant" (132:12). Psalm 89 had asked how the promise could fail; this psalm holds both the promise and the responsibility.

insights.title: A horn that buds
insights.body: "There I will make the horn of David to bud" (132:17). The verb for bud is related to tsemach, Branch, a title the prophets gave the coming king from David's line. A lamp for the anointed also signals a continuing dynasty.

insights.title: Fruit of his body
insights.body: "I will set the fruit of your body on your throne" (132:11). At Pentecost Peter says David knew God had sworn to seat one of his descendants on his throne, and that he spoke of the resurrection of the Messiah.

insights.title: Resting place
insights.body: God says of Zion, "This is my resting place forever. Here I will live" (132:14). What does it mean that God chooses a place, and a people, to live among?

133.summary: A short song celebrates how good it is for brothers to live in unity, comparing it to fragrant oil flowing down Aaron's beard and to the dew of Hermon falling on Zion.
133.lookfor: Notice the two images of things flowing down, and where the blessing is located.

names.name: Hermon
names.gloss: The great mountain in the far north, known for heavy dew.

names.name: Zion
names.gloss: Jerusalem's temple hill.

insights.title: Brothers together
insights.body: "How good and how pleasant it is for brothers to live together in unity!" (133:1). For pilgrims from all the tribes gathered in Jerusalem, the festival was a moment of national unity. The phrase also recalls family land held together by brothers.

insights.title: Oil on Aaron's beard
insights.body: "Like the precious oil on the head, that ran down on the beard, even Aaron's beard" (133:2). Aaron was anointed as high priest with a special perfumed oil poured on his head. The abundance of oil flowing down pictures generous, consecrating blessing.

insights.title: The dew of Hermon
insights.body: Mount Hermon is famous for heavy dew, which waters the land in the dry summer. Hermon is about 200 kilometres from Zion, so its dew falling on Jerusalem (133:3) is a poetic picture of abundant blessing coming down from above.

insights.title: Flowing down
insights.body: Three times something "ran down" or "came down" (133:2-3): the oil on the head, on the beard, on the robe, and the dew on Zion. Unity is a blessing that comes from above, not something people manufacture.

insights.title: That they may be one
insights.body: Jesus prayed that his followers would be one, as he and the Father are one. The early church in Jerusalem was described as being of one heart and soul.

insights.title: Life forever
insights.body: "For there Yahweh gives the blessing, even life forever more" (133:3). Where God's people live in unity, God commands his blessing. The phrase life forever is rare in the Old Testament.

insights.title: Good and pleasant
insights.body: Unity is called both good and pleasant (133:1). Why might unity among believers be so hard to achieve, and so beautiful when it happens?

134.summary: The last Song of Ascents calls the temple servants on night duty to lift their hands and bless Yahweh, and asks Yahweh, Maker of heaven and earth, to bless them from Zion.
134.lookfor: Notice the night setting, the exchange of blessing between people and God, and how the Ascents end.

names.name: Zion
names.gloss: Jerusalem's temple hill.

insights.title: Servants by night
insights.body: "All you servants of Yahweh, who stand by night in Yahweh's house" (134:1) probably refers to the priests and Levites who kept watch in the temple through the night. Chronicles mentions Levite singers on duty day and night.

insights.title: A two-way blessing
insights.body: The people call the servants to bless Yahweh (134:1-2), and then the blessing comes back: "May Yahweh bless you from Zion" (134:3). Worship moves up to God and blessing flows down from him.

insights.title: Lifting hands
insights.body: "Lift up your hands in the sanctuary" (134:2) describes the posture of prayer and praise, open hands raised toward God. It appears throughout the Psalms and in Paul's letters.

insights.title: End of the journey
insights.body: The Songs of Ascents began among liars far from home (Psalm 120) and end at night inside the temple, with blessing (134:3). The pilgrimage is complete. The Maker of heaven and earth, named also in Psalms 121 and 124, blesses his people.

insights.title: A bedtime psalm
insights.body: Because of its night setting, Psalm 134 has been prayed at Compline, the last service of the day, in Western monastic tradition, along with Psalms 4 and 91.

insights.title: Night worship
insights.body: Some served God through the night when no crowds were present. What might it mean to keep praising God in the dark hours when no one sees?

135.summary: The temple servants are called to praise Yahweh, who chose Israel, rules nature, struck Egypt and the kings of Canaan, and is utterly unlike the lifeless idols of the nations.
135.lookfor: Notice how much of this psalm echoes other Scriptures, the list of defeated kings, and the call to every group of worshippers at the end.

names.name: Sihon
names.gloss: An Amorite king east of the Jordan defeated by Israel under Moses.

names.name: Amorites
names.gloss: A people of Canaan and the land east of the Jordan.

names.name: Og
names.gloss: The giant king of Bashan defeated by Israel under Moses.

names.name: Bashan
names.gloss: The fertile region east of the Jordan and north of Gilead.

insights.title: A mosaic of Scripture
insights.body: Psalm 135 is woven from other texts: its opening echoes Psalm 113, verse 7 matches Jeremiah, verse 14 quotes Moses' song, and verses 15–18 repeat the idol passage of Psalm 115. A worship leader gathered familiar words into a new hymn.

insights.title: His own possession
insights.body: "Yah has chosen Jacob for himself; Israel for his own possession" (135:4) uses segullah, a word for a king's private treasure. At Sinai God called Israel his treasured possession among all peoples. Peter applies similar words to the church.

insights.title: Wind from the storehouses
insights.body: God "brings the wind out of his treasuries" (135:7). Ancient people pictured wind, rain, snow and hail kept in heavenly storehouses. The psalm uses the picture to show God's direct control over the weather that others credited to Baal.

insights.title: Sihon and Og
insights.body: Sihon and Og were the first kings defeated on the way to the promised land, east of the Jordan. Their defeat became a regular part of Israel's remembered history and gave confidence for the battles ahead.

insights.title: Unlike the idols
insights.body: Idols have mouths but "neither is there any breath in their mouths" (135:17). The God who sends wind from his storehouses is set against idols with no breath at all. The contrast is between a living God and dead images.

insights.title: Everyone called
insights.body: The psalm ends by calling the house of Israel, Aaron, Levi, and all who fear Yahweh to praise him (135:19-20). Psalm 115 named three groups; this adds the Levites, the temple singers themselves.

insights.title: Becoming like idols
insights.body: "Those who make them will be like them" (135:18). What does it look like when people become like the things they trust?

136.summary: A litany of thanks retells creation, the exodus, the wilderness and the gift of the land, answering every line with the refrain "for his loving kindness endures forever".
136.lookfor: Read the first half of each verse in order to follow the story, and notice where the story reaches "us" near the end.

names.name: Sihon
names.gloss: An Amorite king defeated by Israel east of the Jordan.

names.name: Amorites
names.gloss: A people of Canaan and the land east of the Jordan.

names.name: Og
names.gloss: The king of Bashan defeated by Israel under Moses.

names.name: Bashan
names.gloss: The fertile region east of the Jordan.

skim.advice: The refrain repeats in every verse; read the first half-lines in order to see the story from creation to the present, and treat the refrain as a response.

insights.title: The Great Hallel
insights.body: Jewish tradition calls Psalm 136 the Great Hallel, and it is sung at the Passover meal and in Sabbath morning prayers. The refrain was probably sung by the congregation or a second choir in answer to a leader.

insights.title: His loving kindness endures forever
insights.body: The refrain, "for his loving kindness endures forever", comes in all 26 verses. Hesed, God's covenant love, is the thread through every event. The same refrain was sung when the ark entered the temple, when fire fell on Solomon's sacrifice, and when the second temple's foundation was laid.

insights.title: Singing into battle
insights.body: When Judah faced a huge invading army under King Jehoshaphat, singers went ahead of the soldiers singing "Give thanks to Yahweh, for his loving kindness endures forever". Chronicles says the enemy was defeated as they sang.

insights.title: Creation to now
insights.body: The psalm moves from creation (136:4-9) to the exodus (136:10-15), the wilderness (136:16), the conquest (136:17-22), and finally to "us" in our low estate (136:23-24). Israel's present is part of the same story of God's faithful love.

insights.title: Food for every creature
insights.body: Near the end the psalm widens: God "gives food to every creature" (136:25). The love that rescued Israel also feeds all living things. Jesus points to God feeding the birds.

insights.title: God of gods, Lord of lords
insights.body: "Give thanks to the God of gods... to the Lord of lords" (136:2-3) echoes Deuteronomy. Revelation names the Lamb King of kings and Lord of lords.

insights.title: Thanks in every line
insights.body: Even the defeat of enemies and the deaths of the Egyptian firstborn are followed by the refrain (136:10). What does it mean to see God's love running through the hard parts of the story too?

137.summary: Exiles by Babylon's rivers weep for Zion, refuse to sing the songs of Zion for their captors, swear never to forget Jerusalem, and cry out for vengeance on Edom and Babylon.
137.lookfor: Notice the hung-up harps, the captors' mocking request, the oath of memory, and the shocking final verse.

names.name: Zion
names.gloss: Jerusalem, destroyed by Babylon in 586 BC.

names.name: Edom
names.gloss: Judah's neighbour to the south-east, which cheered Jerusalem's fall.

insights.title: By the rivers of Babylon
insights.body: This is one of the few psalms that can be dated with confidence: it comes from the Babylonian exile after 586 BC, or soon after. Babylon lay on the Euphrates, with a network of irrigation canals. The exiles sat by them and wept (137:1).

insights.title: Harps on the willows
insights.body: "On the willows in that land, we hung up our harps" (137:2). The trees were probably Euphrates poplars. Hanging up the lyres meant refusing to play. Captors demanded "Sing us one of the songs of Zion!" (137:3) as entertainment or mockery.

insights.title: If I forget you
insights.body: "If I forget you, Jerusalem, let my right hand forget its skill" (137:5). A musician swears by his playing hand and his singing tongue (137:6). At many Jewish weddings, the groom recites these verses before breaking a glass, remembering Jerusalem's destruction at the height of joy.

insights.title: Edom's betrayal
insights.body: "Remember, Yahweh, against the children of Edom, the day of Jerusalem; who said, 'Raze it!'" (137:7). Edom, descended from Jacob's brother Esau, cheered and joined in the plunder. Obadiah and Lamentations condemn it.

insights.title: The terrible last verse
insights.body: "Happy shall he be, who takes and dashes your little ones against the rock" (137:9) is among the hardest lines in Scripture. Ancient conquerors did such things, and Isaiah had foretold the same for Babylon. The psalm voices the raw rage of victims who had seen it done to their own children, and hands it to God rather than acting on it.

insights.title: How Christians have read it
insights.body: Church fathers such as Origen and Augustine read the little ones as sinful thoughts to be dashed against the rock, Christ, and the Rule of St Benedict echoes this reading. Others take the verse as an honest record of human anger, not as an example to imitate, set against Jesus' command to love enemies.

insights.title: Singing in a foreign land
insights.body: "How can we sing Yahweh's song in a foreign land?" (137:4). When people feel exiled, from home, from health or from belonging, how can they still worship?

138.summary: David gives wholehearted thanks for answered prayer, foresees the kings of the earth praising Yahweh, and trusts God, who is high yet cares for the lowly, to complete his purpose for him.
138.lookfor: Notice the praise before the gods and kings, God's care for the lowly, and the confident final request.

insights.title: David's last collection
insights.body: Psalm 138 begins the final group of psalms credited to David (Psalms 138–145) before the closing hallelujahs. After Book 5's pilgrim songs and history psalms, David's voice returns with thanks, lament and praise.

insights.title: Before the gods
insights.body: "Before the gods, I will sing praises to you" (138:1). The psalmist praises Yahweh openly in the face of every rival power, whether other nations' gods or heavenly beings. The Greek translation reads before the angels.

insights.title: Your Name and your Word
insights.body: "You have exalted your Name and your Word above all" (138:2) is difficult in Hebrew; it may mean God's promise has surpassed even his reputation. God has done more than people expected of him.

insights.title: High yet near
insights.body: "Though Yahweh is high, yet he looks after the lowly; but the proud, he knows from afar" (138:6). Isaiah says God dwells in the high place and with the contrite. Mary's song praises God who looked on her humble state.

insights.title: Fulfilling what concerns me
insights.body: "Yahweh will fulfill that which concerns me" (138:8). Paul expresses the same confidence: he who began a good work in you will complete it.

insights.title: Kings giving thanks
insights.body: "All the kings of the earth will give you thanks" (138:4). A personal answer to prayer (138:3) becomes part of a vision of all rulers hearing God's words. The psalms often move from the individual to the nations.

insights.title: Works of your hands
insights.body: "Don't forsake the works of your own hands" (138:8). What does it mean to ask God not to abandon what he has made, including oneself?

139.summary: David marvels that Yahweh knows him completely, is present everywhere he could go, and formed him in the womb, then asks God to deal with the wicked and to search his own heart.
139.lookfor: Follow the four movements: God knows, God is present, God made, and search me; and notice the sudden turn at verse 19.

names.name: Sheol
names.gloss: The realm of the dead.

insights.title: Known completely
insights.body: God knows the psalmist's sitting and rising, his thoughts and his words before he speaks (139:2-4). "You hem me in behind and before" (139:5) could feel threatening, but the psalmist calls such knowledge wonderful (139:6).

insights.title: Nowhere to flee
insights.body: "Where could I go from your Spirit?" (139:7). Heaven, Sheol, the far sea, darkness: God is there (139:8-12). Jonah tried to flee to the sea; Amos said no one could escape God by climbing to heaven or digging to Sheol.

insights.title: Wings of the dawn
insights.body: "If I take the wings of the dawn, and settle in the uttermost parts of the sea" (139:9). Dawn rises in the east and the sea lies to the west of Israel. Flying as fast as morning light from east to west still would not escape God.

insights.title: Knit in the womb
insights.body: "You knit me together in my mother's womb" (139:13) and "woven together in the depths of the earth" (139:15). The weaving image pictures bones and sinews formed by a skilled hand. The depths of the earth is a poetic phrase for the hidden place of formation. The passage is often cited in Christian reflection on the value of human life before birth.

insights.title: Written in your book
